#6195. Guide: United Airlines Has Starlink On More Than Half Its Flights, But These Aircraft Offer The Best Odds

United Airlines has reached an impressive milestone: Starlink is now available on more than half of its daily flights. I increasingly choose United when I know Starlink will be onboard, but customers generally cannot determine that when booking. Here is what United should change and which aircraft currently offer your best chance of getting Starlink.

United announced last week that Starlink had crossed the 50% threshold across its daily schedule. The airline expects that number to approach 64% by the end of 2026 and plans to complete fleetwide installations by the end of 2027.

That is an extraordinarily fast rollout for an airline with more than 1,000 mainline aircraft plus a large regional fleet.

The announcement was packaged around Thanksgiving travel, with United expecting to carry more than 6.6 million passengers between November 19 and December 1. But the more consequential development is that Starlink is no longer a novelty you might encounter on a regional jet. Instead, it is becoming a defining part of the United experience.

I have used just about every major inflight internet system, and Starlink is clearly the best.

The connection is fast, latency is low, and it works well enough that I can complete almost everything onboard that I would ordinarily do from my office. Large files load quickly, video calls are possible (but thankfully not allowed on United), and the service supports multiple devices. It is also free for MileagePlus members.

If two departures are similarly priced and one has Starlink, I will choose the Starlink flight. I may even accept a slightly less convenient departure time because several productive hours in the air are worth far more to me than leaving an hour earlier.

That is precisely the sort of customer behavior United wants. Scott Kirby has repeatedly suggested that Starlink will persuade customers loyal to other airlines to try United, after which the rest of the experience will convince them to stay.

I understand his confidence. Once you experience internet that works almost like it does on the ground, returning to a slow or unreliable connection is painful.

Here is the problem: United generally does not confirm Starlink availability until three days before departure.

The airline offers a useful Starlink tracker, but it is designed to check an upcoming flight rather than help someone choose among flights several weeks or months in advance. By the time the tracker confirms the aircraft, most passengers have already purchased their tickets.

Aircraft substitutions will always occur, and no airline can guarantee that a particular tail number will operate a flight. But that does not prevent United from displaying the expected connectivity during booking.

United already identifies many onboard features in the reservation process. It could add a Starlink indicator based on the scheduled aircraft, accompanied by a clear disclaimer that equipment may change. Even an imperfect forecast would be useful.

United carefully says Starlink is available on more than half of its daily flights, which is not the same as saying more than half of its aircraft or passenger seats have Starlink. Regional jets and narrowbody aircraft generally operate more flights per day than widebody aircraft, allowing each installation to influence a larger number of departures.

United’s entire two-cabin regional fleet now has Starlink. If you want the best chance of getting it, book a flight operated by a Bombardier CRJ-550 or Embraer E175.

If you are traveling on a mainline aircraft, the Airbus A321neo is most likely to have Starlink, with 88% of that fleet equipped. The Boeing 737-800 follows at 77%, while 67% of the Boeing 737-900 fleet has it.

Avoid the Airbus A319, Airbus A320, and Boeing 757-300 if connectivity is important to you. None currently have Starlink, and the aging Panasonic systems installed on some of those aircraft are most likely not to work at all.

Personally, I avoid 757-300s and go out of my way to fly on A321neos. You should too if onboard connectivity is important to you.

Progress on the widebody fleet remains slow. Only 2% of United’s Boeing 787 fleet and 5% of its Boeing 777 fleet currently have Starlink, while none of its Boeing 767s are equipped.

Delta Air Lines has selected Amazon Leo for its next-generation internet, with installations scheduled to begin in 2028. As I discussed yesterday, a rocket failure that destroyed 40 Amazon satellites illustrates the risk of selecting a network that is still being constructed.

Delta already offers free Wi-Fi on most of its fleet, and I have found it perfectly usable on many flights. This is not a choice between internet and no internet. But in terms of functionality, Starlink is better. It is not even a contest.

United may complete its fleetwide rollout before Delta installs Amazon Leo on its first aircraft. That gives United time to turn a technical advantage into a behavioral one: customers try Starlink, discover they can be more productive in the air, and begin considering connectivity when selecting future flights.

That is why displaying Starlink during booking would be valuable. If the product is strong enough to influence purchasing decisions, United should make it easier for customers to find before purchasing.

It would also help reduce disappointments. I was recently on a Boeing 777-200 with old-school Panasonic Wi-Fi, and a business class passenger across the aisle from me was fuming that there was no Starlink. Better to underpromise and overdeliver than the other way around.

Starlink is now available on more than half of United Airlines flights and should reach nearly 64% by the end of the year. That is impressive progress and gives United a genuine advantage over its domestic competitors.

I increasingly choose flights based on whether Starlink will be onboard. The frustration is that United generally cannot confirm it until three days before departure, long after the booking decision has been made.

A Starlink indicator during booking would not need to be a guarantee. It could simply tell customers what United reasonably expects to offer. In the meantime, regional jets, Airbus A321neos, and Boeing 737-800s give you the best shot at Starlink on United.

#6194. Lufthansa Unveils Spacious Business Class Seats And Starlink For Select A320 Flights

Lufthansa is finally adding proper business class recliners to a small portion of its Airbus A320 fleet. The new seats will cost extra, even for passengers already booked in business class, but I welcome the option. After years of selling an economy seat with a blocked middle as business class, this is an upgrade worth getting excited about. It is a welcome change for an airline more accustomed to following competitors than setting the standard.

Lufthansa has opened bookings for its new “Premium Business Seat,” which will initially be installed on six Airbus A320ceo aircraft.

Each aircraft will receive eight recliners in the first two rows, arranged 2-2. Features include:

The six aircraft will also receive Starlink Wi-Fi during the retrofit.

These are recliners rather than flat beds, but they will represent a substantial improvement over the standard European business class seat, particularly on longer flights, which for those unaware is simply a regular economy class seat with the adjacent seat blocked.

The first modified aircraft is scheduled to enter service on December 16, 2026, initially operating various routes.

Dedicated deployment begins in February 2027, with seat reservations now available for flights from March 1, 2027:

Look for the Premium Business Seat designation when booking:

Lufthansa is retaining its standard business class offering behind the recliners. Business class passengers can select the larger seat during booking or subsequently through seat reservations, subject to the buy-up price: buying business class will not automatically get you a business class recliner on these routes.

I can already hear the objections: passengers are paying a premium for business class and then being asked to pay again for a better seat. But this is quite different than what intra-Europe business class has been for as long as I can remember on Lufthansa (except for the old A300s) and I would still rather have this option than continue with the blocked-middle arrangement as the only choice.

Lufthansa calls this a “commercial test.” Demand and the response to its booking options will determine whether the concept expands, but I think this concept is going to do great.

I wrote about the Eurowings Premium BIZ concept when it was announced last year. It was rather amusing that the budget carrier would introduce proper narrowbody business class seating before its “full service” Lufthansa Group siblings.

That project was intended to test the concept for other airlines within the group. Now we are seeing a similar approach at Lufthansa itself. The conventional European model has an operational advantage: airlines can move the curtain to adjust the size of business class. Dedicated recliners make that space less flexible.

Installing a small permanent cabin while retaining conventional business class behind it strikes me as a reasonable compromise. Lufthansa can sell the larger seats to passengers willing to pay for them and still expand the rest of business class when demand warrants. I would particularly like to see this spread to longer routes across the group. An empty middle seat is welcome, but it becomes a rather thin comfort proposition when you are spending several hours onboard, especially with those uncomfortable Recaro slimline seats.

One Mile At A Time suggests that Air France should introduce proper business class seats throughout its Airbus A220 fleet. I love that idea…SWISS should do the same.

The A220 offers an especially compelling opportunity because its economy cabin is arranged 2-3. With adjacent seats blocked in business class, Air France sells only three seats per row.

A proper 2-2 business class cabin would allow it to sell four seats across while giving passengers a wider seat. Additional legroom would consume more cabin length, of course, so the calculation is not quite as simple as adding another paying passenger in every existing row, but I think the math would work.

For illustration, replacing three conventional business class rows with two recliner rows would reduce capacity from nine passengers to eight. That is a modest reduction in exchange for a much better product, though the actual economics would depend on the seat dimensions and final layout.

I have already experienced what this could look like on my Bulgaria Air A220-300 flight from Sofia to Amsterdam. The airline offered proper recliners in a 2-2 layout, with leg rests and power outlets. I found it an excellent way to spend three hours flying within Europe.

Air France and SWISS have invested heavily in its premium reputation. A small recliner cabin on the A220 would extend that investment to the European flights that often begin or end a longhaul business class journey.

We do not need a flat bed from Paris to Amsterdam or Zurich to London, but on longer European routes, a comfortable recliner would give me another reason to choose one carrier over another.

Lufthansa will install eight Premium Business Seats on each of six Airbus A320s, with bookings now open for select Frankfurt flights to Athens, Nice, and Cairo from March 2027.

The surcharge will bother some passengers, understandably, but I think it makes sense and am pleased to see Lufthansa offer a better seat and hope the test succeeds.

Eurowings demonstrated a willingness to try something different. Lufthansa is following. Perhaps Air France, SWISS, and others will see an opportunity too. European business class has room to improve, and a seat that is actually different from economy is a very good place to start.

#6193. Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

California Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#6192. How to Plan a Trip to the World’s Largest Ski Resort, Les Trois Vallées

Standing at the top of a steep gully, I looked down at the line ahead. A handful of tracks cut through 10 inches of powder to my left, telling the story of the skiers who arrived before me. But I couldn’t help but notice untouched snow under an overhanging cliff face to my right.

Before I dropped in, I looked out at the view ahead. I could make out tiny chairlift towers on the snow-capped peaks and ridgelines on the horizon. It felt as if the entire mountain range belonged to the Les Trois Vallées Ski Resort, one of the best—and the biggest—ski destinations in Europe.

Les Trois Vallées (also known as Les 3 Vallées, or the 3 Valleys) began with the construction of a 19-passenger open-air “chairlift” in 1938 in the small town of Méribel. But it wasn’t until 1971, with the creation of the joint ski pass that offers access to the seven resorts that make up Les Trois Vallées, that the ski area took its current form.

Today, the resort spans three main valleys and has 169 chairlifts accessing nearly 26,000 acres of skiable terrain (for comparison, Park City has 7,300 acres of skiable terrain). That makes it the world’s largest interconnected ski area—and it’s all accessible via a single ski ticket. Lift tickets for each of the seven resorts are available, but the cost savings don’t make it worthwhile—for a couple of extra euros, you can buy a pass that gives you access to the entire resort. Les Trois Vallées is also a convenient destination for Epic Pass holders, who get seven days of skiing at Les Trois Vallées.

Given the destination is so vast, here are some tips for navigating the expansive terrain and various villages that make up Les Trois Vallées, based on my most recent trip in 2026.

An aerial view of the skiing area of Les Trois Vallees, also known as The 3 Valleys.

“We need to ski over there today,” our guide and former ski racer, Timothée “Timy” Theaux, says as he pointed toward a distant ridgeline. “The wind is coming from Italy, so that side of the ridge is where we’ll find the best snow.”

We skied seamlessly from lift to lift until we reached an open bowl with untouched powder. Theaux knew exactly where to go given the current conditions, and how to get there.

Les Trois Vallées isn’t like a typical US resort. The terrain is so vast and complex that skiing it without a guide can be more of a chore than skiing with one. Guides—which you can hire through each resort’s ski school, like ESF Val Thorens—not only know how to navigate the resort and keep you safe off-piste, but also know exactly where to go to score skiers the best possible conditions and overall experience.

I pictured myself without a guide at the resort, spending day after day staring at trail maps, hopping on lifts that dropped me a mile from where I thought they would. Thankfully, our guide’s expertise spared us from what could’ve been a logistical nightmare.

On our third day at the resort, low visibility made it hard to see more than 15 feet ahead. As we impatiently waited for the fog to lift, lapping groomed runs outside of our hotel, Theaux decided to head toward Courchevel.

“Courchevel and Méribel are good to ski when visibility is low,” he told us, explaining that they’re both at a lower elevation and have more tree skiing.

Even if it’s just for a day or two, hiring a guide at the beginning of the trip will help skiers and riders get a feel for Les Trois Vallées and each individual resort. While all seven resorts offer a good mix of terrain for every ability level, some, like Val Thorens, sit at a higher elevation and have more alpine terrain than resorts like Courchevel, which are lower and have more tree skiing.

The terrain is also so vast that it’s not hard to avoid crowds—which typically stick to the pistes at each resort (Courchevel, Val Thorens, and Méribel are some of the more popular ones). Focusing on one resort per day, rather than spending an entire day riding lifts from one side of the resort to the other, is a stellar way to maximize time on snow.

Backcountry skiers can enjoy the vast off-piste areas beyond the resort's groomed runs.

Unlike many US ski areas, there aren’t dedicated off-piste areas marked on a map—everything within (and really, outside of) the resort’s boundaries is fair game. But leaving the pistes requires a guide, or at the very least, knowledge of how to navigate backcountry terrain. A low-angle, mellow backcountry slope can quickly steepen enough to raise avalanche concerns, and skiers who leave the pistes should be able to recognize and manage backcountry hazards. And while not all off-piste terrain at Les Trois Vallées requires the chops of an expert skier, it doesn’t take much to get yourself in trouble. When it came to navigating the resort, keeping us out of trouble, and scoring the best conditions away from the crowds, Theaux took out all of the guesswork.

After several lift rides and traverses, we finally found ourselves in Courchevel, on the opposite side of the resort from where we were staying in Val Thorens. We immediately left the groomed runs and headed for the trees, leaving the crowded pistes behind.

As a New Englander, I feel at home in tight, scrappy tree runs. But leaving the pistes to explore the vast terrain and big lines encompassed by Les Trois Vallées was special. Unlike the runs I’ve grown accustomed to at my local ski areas, pistes at Les Trois Vallées don’t have a hard line defined by thick trees and icy trail edges; almost everything is skiable.

“Dropping into an off-piste line alone, with just your guide, is one of the most special feelings in the world,” says Dan Egan, a pro skier who has been spending winters in France for nearly three decades. He was skiing with us for the week. “You really get to connect with the place in a way you never would on a groomed run filled with people.”

At the top of nearly every chairlift, I spotted about a dozen distant backcountry lines I wanted to explore. Saw-toothed peaks gave way to steep chutes and couloirs, many of which funneled into open powder fields. “I need to come back and ski that,” I found myself thinking about a dozen times per day.

Courchevel is perhaps the spiffiest resort at The Three Valleys—but there are budget-friendly villages nearby.

Each resort town has its own feel, so it’s important to know your priorities before booking. Courchevel, for example, is the most luxurious destination, while Col de la Chambre is perfect for skiers who want to spend their evenings partying. Budget-conscious skiers should consider Brides-les-Bains or Orelle; whereas Les Menuires might be better for families. Saint-Martin and Méribel both have a cozy European village vibe, but Méribel might have the slight advantage for off-piste skiers.

Val Thorens is known for its vibrant aprés-ski scene.

When we first arrived at the Fahrenheit Seven hotel in Val Thorens, I felt like I was in an early 2000s ski movie. The back deck was packed shoulder to shoulder, and the DJ knew just what to play to keep the crowd going. It was the middle of the afternoon on a random Sunday.

While there is plenty of partying to be done all over Les Trois Vallées (the parties at La Folie Douce Val Thorens and La Folie Douce Méribel are not to be missed), there are also more laid-back places to stay. Of the seven resorts and villages, each has its own unique feel and caters to different types of skiers. And all of them offer lift access to the pistes.

“Courchevel is my favorite place to ski because it has a lot of luxury restaurants and accommodations, so hardcore skiers think it’s not for them,” Theaux told us during our low-visibility day. “The off-piste terrain is always empty.”

But if you’re heading to Courchevel for the accommodations over the skiing, Les Airelles Courchevel is about as luxurious as it gets.

Saint-Martin-de-Belleville, slightly below Val Thorens in the Belleville Valley, has the quiet feel of a quaint European hamlet. Like Val Thorens (and most villages around the resort), it’s very walkable, but it's better for skiers who value history and culture over parties. Orelle, made up of 10 hamlets and less popular than other villages, and Brides-les-Bains, known for its thermal waters and spa culture, are also quiet options; the latter is great for budget-conscious travelers.

Méribel, next to Courchevel's high-end restaurants and parties, is known as a family-friendly resort village with plenty of restaurants, bars, shops, and easy lift access. Similarly, Les Menuires is also known as a family destination, but is ideal for skiers looking to explore some of Les Trois Vallées’ bigger off-piste terrain.

Food across the resort is locally sourced, even at on-hill dining options, like Caron 3200.

No matter which village you stay in, good food is never more than a couple of steps or a chairlift ride away.

“I really love the jamon because it requires patience,” says Vincent Suchet, the cheesemaker and grandson of Pépé Nicolas at family-owned, Michelin-starred Chez Pépé Nicolas—located just below Val Thorens in the Belleville Valley. He told us as we sipped wine and tasted local cheeses in a cool, stone-walled cellar: “And I favor the cheeses because you have to wait two years; the flavor is the best when you have to wait.”

The culinary experience stood in stark contrast to what I was used to at US ski areas—fast service, overpriced, yet mediocre cheeseburgers and pizza, and ingredients sourced hundreds, if not thousands, of miles away. At Les Trois Vallées, home to ten Michelin-starred restaurants like Hotel La Bouitte, the food is just as important as the skiing.

During my week at the resort, I couldn’t find a single fast-food or chain restaurant in any of the seven villages. Restaurants are all family-owned, and thought goes into where ingredients are sourced. It’s not uncommon for cheeses to be made by a local farmer whose family has been doing it for generations.

Caron 3200, perched above Val Thorens, is the highest wine bar in Europe.

Even on-hill dining options, like Caron 3200, perched above Val Thorens at 10,500 feet (making it the highest wine bar in Europe), emphasize the culinary experience.

“We have 150 different wines, and most are French,” Eric Bonnel, managing director of Val Thorens Tours, told us as we sipped wine and admired the views of Mont Blanc and the surrounding Alps through the oversized windows. “And we store them at three different altitudes. The reds are aged at a higher altitude because there’s less oxygen.”

On our last evening at Les Trois Vallées, it finally started snowing. I momentarily felt a slight sense of disappointment about leaving ahead of a huge storm. But as I sipped my post-meal Génépi with new and old friends, I realized it didn’t matter. The skiing was only a small part of the Les Trois Vallées experience.

Les Trois Vallées is accessible via train, plane, or car.

For international travelers, the most convenient airport to fly into is Geneva, which is located just a couple of hours from the resort (depending on where you’re staying). While the Swiss airport has the most international flight options, it’s also possible to fly into Lyon, Chambéry, and Grenoble.

Companies like Alpine Fleet offer shuttle transfers from the airports to the resorts in Les Trois Vallées. You can also rent a car, but with the lifts and shuttles available in each resort town, you don’t really need one once you arrive.

Those traveling within Europe or from one of the area’s international airports can access Les Trois Vallées by train, with the Moûtiers﻿ train station serving major cities like London, Paris, Geneva, and Lyon. From the train station, travelers can get to each resort by taxi or bus.

#6191. Trump Blames Buttigieg For FAA Meltdown While Elon Musk Blames Sean Duffy

President Donald Trump blames Pete Buttigieg for the nationwide FAA meltdown. Elon Musk, meanwhile, is pointing at the tTransportation Secretary Trump appointed, claiming Sean Duffy rejected an offer of free Starlink service. The finger-pointing continues, but neither accusation tells stranded passengers exactly why a router installation brought the system down.

Speaking to reporters on November 16, Trump singled out his predecessor’s transportation secretary for the failure that halted departures across the United States:

“Buttigieg ruined the system. He totally ruined it.”

When asked what personal responsibility he accepted, Trump responded:

He also praised Duffy and attributed the disruption to aging equipment. I have already addressed the problem with blaming the previous administration. America’s air traffic control infrastructure has suffered from decades of deferred investment. That includes the Biden administration, but also Trump’s first term and the administrations before it.

Friday’s failure, however, occurred during work performed under the current administration. An explanation of what Buttigieg allegedly did wrong would be useful, but of course Buttigieg is just the whipping boy for an administration that shows no personal responsibly for any of its deleterious actions.

Musk has offered a different accusation. In a post on X, he wrote:

“Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were.”

Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were. https://t.co/OZwDeiXOAr

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 16, 2026

That is a pointed criticism of the same official Trump says handled the situation well, but Musk does not explain when the offer was made, what equipment or service was included, where it would have been deployed, or how it would have prevented this particular failure…what a surprise.

I would like Duffy to answer the allegation directly. Was there an offer? What did it cover? Why was it declined? If the proposal was unsuitable, explain why.

Musk should also substantiate his assertion that the service would have been needed here. Being able to offer satellite internet does not establish that his proposed “gift” would have kept this particular network operating.

I love Starlink as an airline passenger. It is easily the best inflight internet service available now, and it increasingly influences which flights I book. But that does not mean it is or would have been a solution to an air traffic control network failure.

According to the FAA’s explanation, excessive connection attempts flooded its telecommunications network, destabilizing aircraft communications and radar feeds. Investigators identified sites in El Dorado, Arkansas, and Amarillo, Texas. L3Harris had been working at El Dorado, including installing a new router. Blocking those locations apparently stabilized the network. The broadcasting function on the new routers was also disabled as a precaution.

To support Musk’s claim, we would need to know whether his proposed Starlink connections would have bypassed the affected equipment and preserved the necessary communications.  Perhaps Starlink could have provided useful redundancy…but maybe the proposed installation would have had no bearing on this failure.

Buttigieg has defended his record, pointing to improvements in controller staffing, runway safety, and flight cancellations during his tenure.

He also says he launched the communications modernization project that the current administration is continuing. His response asks for an accounting of the money already authorized and an explanation of why the execution of that work triggered such a widespread failure.

As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived. We reversed a decade of decline in air traffic controller staffing, drove down runway safety incidents, and when I left office we were experiencing the lowest flight cancellation rates in… https://t.co/68KleIhFEc

— Pete Buttigieg (@PeteButtigieg) November 16, 2026

They do not mean Buttigieg’s tenure should escape scrutiny. The January 2023 nationwide ground stop occurred on his watch, and the system still required enormous investment when he left office while his boss prioritized student loan forgiveness and federal mask mandates instead of accelerating infrastructure programs like Air Traffic Control modernization.

But acknowledging those shortcomings does not relieve the current administration of responsibility for its own decisions. Duffy has been Transportation Secretary for nearly two years. He oversees the department responsible for explaining this failure and should be held accountable for the actions under his watch.

There is an obvious temptation to enjoy the spectacle: Trump blames Buttigieg while Musk suggests Trump’s own transportation secretary rejected help. I find the contradiction revealing, but passengers deserve something more useful than competing accusations.

The investigation must establish what changed in the network, why that change caused such a widespread disruption, and whether the safeguards surrounding the work were adequate. Congress should examine the Starlink allegation too, if Musk can provide a concrete proposal and evidence supporting his account.

Duffy may have had reasonable grounds to decline whatever Musk offered, but he should be able to articulate them. Likewise, Musk may have identified a missed opportunity, but he should be able to demonstrate his rather glaring accusation.

And Trump should stop treating an investigation as unnecessary because he has already identified a political opponent to blame. The age of the equipment was known. The difficult task was upgrading it while maintaining reliable service. That is the work his administration undertook, and that is the work it must explain to a weary public.

Trump says Buttigieg ruined the system and accepts no personal responsibility. Musk says Duffy rejected free Starlink service that was needed. Both claims deserve scrutiny and neither establishes the technical cause of Friday’s meltdown.

I would be far more receptive to an administration that acknowledged a failure during a difficult modernization project and explained how it would improve the process. Instead, we keep receiving accusations, praise for the response, and demands for more money.

The passengers who lost days getting home deserve a candid explanation of what went wrong. So do the taxpayers being asked to fund the repair. Is this really a political issue that should divide us?

#6190. Starlux Adds First Route to Australia, New Zealand

Taiwanese carrier Starlux is branching out to Australia and New Zealand with a new, one-stop connection.

Starting March 23, 2027, the airline will fly from Taipei to Sydney to Auckland. Flights will initially operate four times weekly, then switch to daily on May 1. Starlux will operate the route using Airbus A330-900 aircraft.

Taipei-Sydney-Auckland will be the airline’s first one-stop or through route; all other flights are nonstop from Taiwan. Officials said the one-stop approach will give travelers access to “two incredible destinations in one journey.”

Starlux said it is working with Qantas to arrange connecting flights to other destinations in Australia, New Zealand, and Fiji.

Starlux is headquartered in Taipei and mainly flies within East and Southeast Asia, though it also offers service to North America and Europe. In the U.S., it serves Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Phoenix, and Ontario, California.

#6189. At Dior’s First Spa in Venice, Old Glamour Gets the Hi-Tech Treatment

The buzz of the Venice Film Festival has only just died down, when I step out of a Riva boat that bobs at the berth of the Hotel Cipriani Venice on Giudecca Island. I’m excited but also exhausted after spending the previous ten days on several long-haul flights, and I fear it’s beginning to affect my conversational skills—and my collagen levels. Luckily, I’m not here to attend a premiere or hop between Biennale events. I'm here to experience Cipriani's newly opened Dior Spa, the fashion house's first in Venice.

Venice’s links with Dior go back to 1951 when the French couture brand’s eponymous founder fell in love with the city after attending the Ball of the Century costume party at the Palazzo Labia, hosted by art collector Charles de Beistegui.

The views from my suite's private terrace

A welcome Dior takeover on Cip's ground floor

Sophia Loren and Julia Roberts are just a few of the starry names to have stayed at this classic hotel, which launched its new spa in July 2026 as part of ongoing renovations led by New York architect Peter Marino. The cream and pastel palette channels an 18th-century Venetian Rococo spirit, with elegant mid-century Italian stucco and terrazzo flooring. Science-driven skincare nerds tend to believe that fashion houses can’t run beauty departments worthy of their approval, but Dior has the potential to persuade them otherwise. Many luxury spas are often either visually stunning temples that offer underwhelming treatments, or medically-driven centers that leave you glowing but feeling as if you’re in a hospital. Dior combines the best of both worlds, recalling an old-school glamour while deploying higher-tech treatments that aren’t geared towards “maxxing” but aim for clients to look and feel their best in a tranquil environment.

The Dior Spa's La Collection Privée island

After spending the morning in Murano watching the world’s most talented glassblowers at work, I head down to the spa’s marbled entrance where a Murano chandelier dangles above a centerpiece table festooned with beautiful bottles of parfums from Dior’s La Collection Privée, including Tobacolore and, my favorite fragrance, La Colle Noire. I’m handed a rose infusion before slipping into cloud-soft Dior slippers and waiting outside my treatment room for one of the signature treatments, which include Le Théâtre Corporal, a four-handed, Ayurvedic-inspired massage (which couples can do together), and the Golden Aura hydrafacial. But I’m here for what feels like the most apt option in a city famed for its masked balls: the Mascarade facial.

Setting up for a canalside Dior masterclass

Developed by the brand’s global skincare ambassador, Hadda Akrim, the Mascarade aims to regenerate the skin and soothe the mind. I’m in need of it now that my circadian rhythm is disrupted after back-to-back flights, cabin pressure and changing time zones. The treatment is more than just a facial: it involves 90 minutes of drainage, rebalancing, and re-boosting with the help of devices that encourage the nutrients being massaged into your skin to sink deeper. Firstly, I lie on the treatment table to receive an abdominal massage, which rebalances my nervous system (the gut is our second brain, after all) and restores my inner harmony to maximize my radiance.

Next, ultrasound waves are applied across my face to improve the skin’s elasticity and circulation, followed by microcurrent muscle stimulation during which I literally feel my cells awakening. The procedure soothes my mind so much I fall into a contented sleep. It’s all designed to boost my complexion’s glow—and it works. Dior’s global spa director, Olivier Hahn, told me he’s most proud of the sonic component of the spa offering, which does its job by calming me down without me even noticing.

A heavenly breakfast in my top-floor suite

The best kind of antioxidants at Oro restaurant

I wake up for the next stage of the treatment, a technical jaw massage, which the facialist carries out to counteract my nighttime teeth-grinding. She then places cryogenic stones over a cooling mask to firm, drain, and reoxygenate my skin. It’s a perfect way to re-enter the world, cognitively and physically. I feel snatched as I sip coffee by the pool after the treatment. The Mascarade facial is great for a morning-after depuffing, but, given the OMGs I receive from fellow spa-goers, I conclude that it’s also perfect for an evening out. I head out into the Venetian night with nothing but a touch of mascara and a post-facial luminosity.

Feeling like a kid on Christmas morning, the staff sent me on my way with a bag of the Dior Prestige products to keep up my skincare routine back home. The ingredients are mainly organic, something I hadn’t expected. In the same way that historic French vineyards downplay their organic practices for fear of alienating clients disdainful of natural wines, Dior also keeps its products' natural roots on the down low. It all comes as a pleasant surprise and further cements this spa’s authority in the world of regenerative beauty therapy.

Situated halfway between San Francisco and the Oregon border, California's Mendocino Coast has managed to remain a relatively hidden gem, of sorts. While it's certainly not a secret, its remote location has kept it from getting overrun with tourists — but new direct flights and millions of dollars in roadwork funding are making it more accessible than ever. And that's just one reason the coastal town of Mendocino made our list of top destinations to visit in 2027.

Nestled between rugged cliffs, redwood forests and rich wine terroirs, Mendocino has it all. No matter what you get up to out here — and there’s more to do than you might expect — it’s virtually impossible not to feel your blood pressure drop. The area’s relaxed pace of life is infectious, and during a recent two-day trip, this type-A traveler found herself hopping on the slow travel train.

From how to get there and where to stay to the best things to do and eat, here’s how to spend a long weekend (or longer!) on the Mendocino Coast. I dare you not to fall in love.

Travelers have several airports to choose from when flying to Mendocino.

The closest, albeit smallest, option is Charles M. Schulz–Sonoma County Airport (STS), which puts you only a two-to-three-hour drive from Mendocino. Alaska Airlines, Delta and Southwest have all launched new routes to STS this year from Austin, Phoenix, Salt Lake City and more.

You’ll have more options if you fly into San Francisco International Airport (SFO), Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) or Sacramento International Airport (SAC). All are roughly the same distance from Mendocino — three to four hours depending on traffic — and offer plenty of direct flights from around the country through various airlines. A local I spoke to recommended SAC, saying that the drive is less stressful because it doesn’t go through a city.

No matter where your flight lands, you’ll need to rent a car. The drive can be tiring, especially as the roads get windier approaching the coast. Thankfully, there are plenty of wineries and cideries along the way where you can stop for a restroom break (and maybe a drink or two, if you’re not the driver).

One of the many facets of Mendocino’s appeal is the charming, walkable downtown — complete with views of Mendocino Bay.

You’ll find no shortage of souvenirs here, from bookshops and toy stores to clothing and home decor. Art lovers will enjoy perusing the handful of galleries. Coffeeshops, bakeries and chocolate shops abound, so you needn't worry about finding caffeine or snacks to sustain you during your wanderings.

If you wear jewelry (or are in the market for a unique gift that will fit in your suitcase), you won’t want to miss Mendocino Sandpiper, which offers a wide variety of work by local artists.

And that’s just the town of Mendocino. Its slightly larger neighbor, Fort Bragg, located about a 15-minute drive north along the coast, has even more boutiques to browse.

Related: 9 tertiary cities in the US that are both charming and affordable

You will need a car to get around the Mendocino Coast area, but you won’t have to spend much time in the car once you arrive. That’s because the area’s best outdoors activities are within easy reach of Mendocino and Fort Bragg.

The expansive Mendocino Coast Botanical Gardens were a highlight for me, and would probably be stunning in the spring and summer when most of the flowers are in bloom.

Mendocino Headlands State Park is literally steps from downtown, and there are several other state parks under 20 minutes away, including Jug Handle State Natural Reserve and Russian Gulch State Park. To commune with the area’s famous redwoods, head to Otis R. Johnson Wilderness Park, a glorious corner of green tucked away on the edge of Fort Bragg. Or head to MacKerricher State Park for a stroll along a black-sand beach and views of the aptly named Seal Rocks.

February to March is peak whale-watching season due to the gray whale migration, but this area gets visits from various whale species year-round, so keep your eyes peeled. I didn’t spot any whales, but I did see some seals and sea lions bobbing in the waves, as well as flocks of pelicans and other waterbirds.

You may also hear about a place called Glass Beach, which served as a community garbage dump at the beginning of the 20th century; over several decades, the waves tumbled some of the debris into colorful sea glass. Locals warned me that most of the glass is gone now, snatched up by tourists over the years. You’re better off going to the International Sea Glass Museum in Fort Bragg — with over 3,000 pieces on display, it boasts the world’s largest permanent sea glass exhibit.

Related: 7 warm-weather expedition cruises that will wow nature and adventure lovers

Both Mendocino and Fort Bragg have surprisingly varied food scenes, from the casual organic Good Life Cafe & Bakery and elevated all-vegan Fog Eater to the Irish-inspired Patterson’s Pub and Asian fusion Gnar Bar. And foodies won’t want to miss the local farmers’ markets, held on summer Fridays in Mendocino and Wednesdays year-round in Fort Bragg.

However, the main draws for foodies are, of course, the seafood — I heard Fort Bragg’s Sea Pals described as “the best fish ‘n’ chips outside of the U.K.” — and the thriving beverage scene.

Oenophiles will want to take the Highway 128 Wine Road to sample the fruits of the nearby Anderson Valley and Yorkville Highlands wine regions. But you’ll get plenty of opportunities to sample local wines in town as well. My hotel even offered a lobby wine machine where you can get wine samples with the press a button and tap of a keycard.

If wine isn’t your thing, don’t worry, there are plenty more local beverages to try. Gowan’s Cider Garden, which brews both alcoholic and non-alcoholic varieties, bills itself as California's first-ever cider tasting orchard. Meanwhile, the zero-waste, solar-powered North Coast Brewing Co. has been brewing unique beers (and winning awards for them) since 1988.

Related: The best credit cards for dining

The Mendocino Coast is also home to some fascinating history, and it has an array of museums and other attractions where visitors can learn more.

Fort Bragg’s Guest House Museum is a great starting point to learn about local history, from the logging industry to the Great 1906 Earthquake. Or visit during Labor Day weekend to experience lumberjack games at the annual Paul Bunyan Days festival.

If you have young travelers in tow, check out Fort Bragg’s Noyo Center for Marine Science, which offers interactive exhibits like tide pools and a full orca skeleton. Or climb to the top of a lighthouse and see a real Fresnel lens at either Point Cabrillo Light Station State Historic Park or the 156-year-old Point Arena Lighthouse.

Train enthusiasts won’t want to miss the historic Skunk Train, which started carrying timber in the late 1800s and now carries passengers through scenic redwood forests. While the train’s traditional 35-mile route has a reputation for jaw-dropping scenery, a tunnel collapse in recent years has shortened the route to a sliver of its former glory. However, I still enjoyed the nostalgic vibes of the Redwood Presidential Class, which made me feel like I had been dropped into one of my favorite Agatha Christie murder mysteries.

Related: The world's most scenic train rides

The Mendocino Coast has been leaning into slow and wellness travel, and for obvious reasons. With ancient redwoods on one side and windswept cliffs on the other — and blessedly few tourists crowding the trails — the landscape itself is therapeutic.

If you want something more structured, there are plenty of wellness activities if you know where to look. Many are offered by locals hotels but open to the public.

A few examples include yoga classes at Stanford Inn by the Sea, redwood hot tub and sauna sessions at Sweet Water Inn & Spa, sound healing in a geodesic dome at Mendocino Grove, and guided shinrin-yoku (forest bathing) walks at Brewery Gulch Inn & Spa.

Related: 9 wellness trends and where to experience them

Summer is Mendocino’s most popular season. It will also be the most expensive and busiest time to go — though I don’t expect the area to get too packed at any time of year, given its remoteness.

For adventure seekers looking to make the most of the area’s hiking, water sports and more, it’s probably worth planning your trip in summer for longer days and maximum sunshine. And with average highs topping out in the mid-70s Fahrenheit, Mendo could make a nice coolcation spot.

However, you can save money and all but guarantee a quiet vacation by traveling in the shoulder seasons from mid-October to November and April to early June. During these times, you can still expect warm enough weather for outdoor exploits, though temperatures will drop at night and more frequent rains may wash out hiking trails occasionally.

The hotel scene in Mendocino is characterized by quiet luxury. Its neighbor, Fort Bragg, has more variety and more budget-friendly options.

I spent three nights in the new Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino, a half-century-old property that was recently renovated before joining the Trailborn nature lodge collection and Marriott Bonvoy program. Other points options include Holiday Inn Express Fort Bragg by IHG and Baymont by Wyndham Fort Bragg.

If, like me, you love a good independent or boutique hotel, Mendocino is full of them. For instance, you could book a seaside cottage at Agate Cove Inn through Amex Travel or Capital One Travel, earning 5 points per dollar with your or 10 miles per dollar with your Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, respectively.

Or consider staying at SCP Mendocino Inn and Farm, a 19th-century manor turned B&B where guests can enjoy complimentary breakfast sourced from the onsite farm. Even better, you can redeem your points for more than 1 cent apiece via Chase Points Boost.

Overall, one of the things I loved most about the Mendocino Coast was its manageable size. From the downtown areas to the state parks, everything I visited was small but high-quality.

So instead of running around a city trying to cram in as much as possible, you can spend a leisurely weekend (or longer) exploring charming boutiques, quirky museums, local dining or natural wonders. You won’t run out of things to do, but the close proximity between attractions and “island time” mentality will help you savor the activities you choose.

That’s what slow travel is all about, right?

#6187. Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep. Celeste Maloy, R-Utah, walking alongside him. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, said they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”

The new leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

#6186. Review: Park Hyatt Vienna, My Favorite Hotel In The Austrian Capital

The Park Hyatt Vienna is not only my favorite hotels in Vienna, but one of my favorite Hyatt properties in the world. With excellent service, nice amenities, delicious breakfast, and central location, our latest stay was another great reminder of what a superb property this is.

Although we could have connected directly to Zürich after landing in Vienna, I was able to force a 23.5-hour layover into the itinerary, which gave us a chance to stay to the Park Hyatt Vienna, a hotel I’ve enjoyed many times over the years but it was the first time my children had come along.

I booked this for 35,000 World of Hyatt points (versus a cash rate of over €700) and applied a “Guest of Honor” to the reservation, which essentially marks me as “Globalist” in the system.

Our Austrian flight landed at 11:30 am into VIE and I had emailed the hotel requesting an early check-in, specifically noting that we would be happy to forgo an upgrade in order to access our room a few hours early. Our request was honored.

The Park Hyatt Vienna is ideally located on Am Hof in the heart of the old town, an easy walk from St. Stephen’s Cathedral and many of the places I most enjoy visiting in Vienna.

Checking in, I was welcomed back to the hotel and the amenities were explained, including breakfast and pool hours (most important to my kids!).

We were assigned room 331, a standard room with two twins beds. While not an upgrade, the room was spacious enough and quite comfortable with a desk, round table, chair, and the two beds.

My daughter jumped right into bed to go to sleep (it was, after all, about 3:15 am in Los Angeles), but I pulled her out: no napping today would hopefully mean no jet lag tomorrow.

The bathroom featured really beautiful stonework behind the bathtub and included two sinks, a separate water closet, and walk-in shower.

The room had a wardrobe that included a coffee machine, hot water kettle, and mini-bar including snacks and drinks.

A welcome amenity was also waiting for us including various chocolates and candies.

The room had plenty of 220-volt outlets and also a safe to lock valuables. Unfortunately, the room did not have any USB-C ports or wireless chargers.

A primary reason I booked this hotel was for the pool and wellness. My kids love to swim and I can’t think of a better hotel pool than this one: we spent a lot of time here in the afternoon and evening.

The entire pool and spa area is posh, with a full-range of treatments available but nice say chairs with fresh peaches and plums, a locker room, and a wellness area with a sauna and steam room available to all guests.

Side note: the hotel has a cryogenic machine in the spa that will let you stand in -110ºC temperatures for three minutes…I was tempted and probably would have tried it had I been alone.

Thankfully, there was no drama this time in the sauna!

> Read More: Accused Of Being A Child Predator at Park Hyatt Vienna!

The fitness center is located in the spa area on the lower level, but accessible 24/7 with your room card and includes TechnoGym equipment. I awoke an hour before the kids and went down to workout…a nice way to start the day and fight jet lag.

You mustn’t skip breakfast here, for it is truly a treat.

The Bank is the most beautiful part of the hotel: an ornate dining room that was once the grand lobby when this hotel was still a bank. Breakfast is served from 7:00 am each morning until 10:30 am (11:00 am on weekends) and includes a delicious buffet plus an additional a la carte menu. If breakfast isn’t clouded in your rate, it is €58 each, which while steep is really worthwhile considering all you get with it.

There’s a bar section in The Bank that includes alcohol, including a large cocktail menu, and lighter food. It’s open from 9:00 am to 1:00 am on Monday – Wednesday, till 2:00 am on Thursday – Saturday, and from 5:00 pm to 1:00 pm on Sunday (good luck finding anything open on Sunday in Vienna…).

The hotel’s Viennese café includes cakes, coffee and chocolates, as well as alcoholic drinks and snacks, with an outdoor terrace. Open each day from 9:00 am to 8:00 pm.

Open from 9:00 am to 6:00 pm daily, the Lounge offers a more informal dining experience where you can enjoy hot and cold drinks plus a variety of food. Menu here.

Finally, 24/7 room service is available. Menu here.

There used to be really posh cigar lounge in this hotel, but now it is a beauty salon (Vienna has banned indoor smoking after being a smoker’s haven for so many years).

Our entire say was marked by one pleasant service encounter after another. I had a nice extended conversation with teh doorman and another great conversation with the agent who checked me in. We had a nice chat with our waitress in The Bank and the spa staff was also very friendly. I do speak German, albeit with an American accent, and appreciated that the staff was willing to engage in my less-than-perfect German as opposed to switching to English.

This was another wonderful stay at the Park Hyatt Vienna and I’ll sum it up by saying simply that I cannot wait to return.

My original review is below, dating all the way back to August 2014. Heidi and I went for my birthday just weeks after we got married…the hotel had recently opened and we had a great stay. It’s nice to see this hotel age so gracefully and what a joy it is to share this property and the lovely city of Vienna with my children.

Vienna is a stately city rich with majestic architecture, an erudite culture, and a regal sense of style. In the center of the old city, replete with cobblestone walkways, horse drawn carriages, and glistening statues of historical luminaries, a new Park Hyatt hotel has opened on the site of a former monarchical bank. My wife and I celebrated my birthday in Vienna last weekend and stayed for two nights at Park Hyatt’s newest property.

A historic property located on Am Hof 2 in the heart of the First District of Vienna, a UNESCO World Heritage site, the hotel’s location cannot be beat. Within a few paces is the Goldenes Quartier shopping district, St. Stephan’s Cathedral, Hofburg Palace, Spanish Riding School, and many museums.

We began the day in Frankfurt with an early flight on Austrian Airlines to Vienna. I sent a note to the main hotel e-mail, park.vienna@hyatt.com, just before takeoff requesting an early check-in and had a response waiting when I landed in Vienna – the room was ready.

From Vienna Airport you have two public transportation options for getting into the city – the City Airport Train (CAT) which travels non-stop to the heart of Vienna or a suburban train (S-Bahn) which calls at several stations on the way into town, taking about 15 minutes longer than the direct service. The CAT is 14EUR one-way while the S-Bahn is 4.40EUR. We took the S-Bahn into town, then connected on the underground train (U-Bahn) to Herrengasse Station, which is just a short walk from the hotel.

A smiling porter greeted us outside the door and took our luggage. Inside, a friendly young man checked us in, speaking first in English when he noticed my American passport but then switching to German upon the request of my wife that I practice my Deutsch! He escorted us upstairs and demonstrated the hi-tech features of our room. Like many Park Hyatt properties, lighting and draperies are electronically controlled by a central push-button unit.

I loved the room – a spacious standard room with tremendous natural light, a great view, and functionality. The room featured copious electrical outlets – an essential amenity when taking my business on the road, as I did here even on my birthday weekend. The layout of the couch in front of the bed in front of the desk nicely utilized the space in the room and the separate entry hall insulated the room from outside noise.

Two doors decorated in geometric art-deco style, closed off the bathroom and entry hall from the bedroom. The bathroom was very large (and well-placed mirrors made it appear even larger) and featured a sizeable bathtub, walk-in rain shower, two sinks, and a separate water closet.

A minibar featured an Illy coffee machine with several packets of complimentary espresso and snack and drink for purchase. The refrigerator did make a rather loud humming sound that could be heard even when the bedroom door was closed. I am a heavy sleeper, but my wife woke me up one night to “turn the climate off” yet it was not the air conditioning, it was the refrigerator! It was not terrible, just noticeable.

It was warm outside and we had a problem getting the air conditioning to activate. Turns out one of the windows was open just ajar – just make sure all your windows are tightly shut and your room key is in the slot by the door or else your air conditioning will not function. Once on, the room cooled down rapidly. Vienna boasts exceptional weather so most of the year there is no need for a/c anyway.

The hotel offers three dining options in addition to 24-hour room service; The Bank, Pearl, and The Lobby Lounge. Pearl bar features an outdoor terrace in addition to a contemporary indoor seating area and specializes in cocktails. A tapas menu is available with food as substantial as Wiener Schnitzel also available.

The Lobby Lounge offers drinks and light meals and sits next to the Living Room, a cigar and whiskey lounge that is one of the hotel’s best features. Admittedly, I see little value in setting fire to and then inhaling a plant that is linked to lung cancer but many of my friends and my brother hold a different opinion, so I find myself in cigar bars quite often. If you are a conneousier of cigars or just enjoy an opulent room to enjoy a drink in with friends, this bar is not to be missed. With plush couches and rich wooden paneling on the walls, I felt like I was part of the gentry mulling over world affairs in the cigar and brandy room onboard the Titanic.

Finally, The Bank is the hotel’s most opulent restaurant and central to the character of the property. Here, on the site of the former cashier’s hall, we had breakfast each morning. Breakfast was 33EUR and the buffet was expansive with all that you would expect in a comprehensive breakfast—fresh squeezed juices, cereals, fruits, breads, cold-cuts, cheeses, breakfast meats, and eggs. Coffee (it was tremendous) as well as pancakes, waffles, French Toast, and eggs are included in the buffet and can be ordered from your server.

We spent hours in here each morning enjoying a leisurely breakfast (breakfast ends at 10:30a during the week and 11:00a on weekends) and found the service to be warm, personal, and punctual. I thought everything was great – my wife had a problem with her eggs on the first morning (soft boiled eggs came out hard-boiled, then an omelet ordered with no cheese was delivered with cheese) but the issues were quickly remedied and did not reoccur the next morning. The juices were remarkably tasty (apple, orange, and even grapefruit were exceptional) and my favorite part of the breakfast was the cheese-covered cooked tomatoes.

Lunch and dinner are also offered each night in The Bank and you will find no menu posted online because the menu, sourced with local ingredients, changes often. Prices were moderate and I was prepared to dine at the restaurant for my birthday, but when mentioning that I was especially looking for fish, the concierge directed me to a restaurant called Kornat about 15 minutes away by foot, which specializes in fish and seafood.

So I missed trying out The Bank for an evening meal, but I did appreciate the restaurant recommendation for the food was amazing and we enjoyed a prime outdoor table thanks to a call ahead from the concierge.

I do have one gripe and only one true gripe about the property: the in-room wireless internet speed was unreliable. The Park Hyatt Vienna offers complimentary wired and wi-fi internet, which is a nice feature, but I found myself on multiple occasions banging my hand on the desk with disgust as poor connectivity led to unacceptably long page load times and the inability to make internet-based telephone calls. Other times, though, the interent worked perfectly well with pages loading fast and no issue with Skype calls or viewing YouTube videos. Admittedly, I did not not bring my ethernet cable converter for my MacBook Air so I was unable to test the wired internet speed.

A large fitness studio with state-of-the-art, brand new equipment was much appreciated. Several bikes, treadmills, and ellipticals filled one side of the room while strength training equipment and free weights filled out the other. The room itself, with brass candelabras and wooden floors was an elegant place to work out and apples, bottled water, refrigerated towels, newspapers, and magazines were available.

The gym overlooks the swimming pool below, which sits on the site of the former bank vault. With an ornate frieze relief and elongated white leather couches, it offers a refreshing antidote to the hot afternoon sun (or cold). Adjacent to the pool is a lounge with chairs to relax and also steam room and sauna facilities. My one regret is that we did not spend an extra day in Vienna just to lounge around the spa. Certainly, seeing Vienna is the priority if your time is limited, but this is a great complimentary benefit of the hotel that seems to go unutilized, as I saw many hotel guests and no one using the pool or spa lounge. Full spa services are available here in the Arany Spa and you can even see the original 3-ton bank vault door.

This hotel is a category six property, meaning it is 25,000 Hyatt Gold Passport points per night or 12,500 points plus a $150 co-pay (my preferred method of payment to help stretch out my points). The daily rate during the summer is about 375EUR or $500. Gold Passport availblity is good.

I can’t tell you how much I enjoyed the city of Vienna and both my wife (who is not usually a city person) and I wish to return soon. When we do, we will definitely choose the Park Hyatt again, allowing an extra day for the spa and enjoying at a more leisurely pace one of Europe’s greatest capital cities.
