#6176. Inside NYC’s Pool Scene, the City’s Great Equalizer

Just when we thought New York had seen it all, I caught wind that the first-ever five-borough pool tournament—in the city’s history—was about to kick off.

It was all thanks to Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break. Tran has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade and has played on more than 130 tables out of the 400 to 500 he estimates are in NYC (he even catalogs them out of his own goodwill for other New Yorkers, on Pool Tables NYC). He’s just that guy: an absolute force of nature with a heavy case of do-the-impossible syndrome. One day over summer, at a league night with fellow pool-playing regulars, he wondered if there was a way to get folks like these together for one big game—to unite New York’s pool-playing dive bar families and play as one.

Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break, has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade.

The idea was a tournament “built by pool players, run by pool players,” says Tran, who you’ll most often find playing at George & Jacks in Williamsburg. “No money changing hands, no ulterior motive.” Just bringing together this community, which Tran is the first to admit existed long before he stepped on the scene.

So this powerhouse did it: 2,256 players, 16 venues, all five boroughs, over two days in early November. When I caught up with Tran the week before the tournament, he still couldn’t believe he was bringing the idea to life. “I was like, 'What am I signing up to do once I post this?' But then I posted it, and it just took off—like completely took off. And everybody was like, 'Yeah, we can totally do this.'”

Entry was set at just $25, and anyone could sign up once the link went live. Volunteers were coordinated to run the tournament at each of the 16 bars, and local businesses chipped in more than $6,000 in giveaways. The New York Sign Museum even donated the grand prize: a street sign naming the winner Five Boro Champion.

I rode the wave of Tran’s infectious energy and spent an entire weekend hopping between dives watching the tournament’s pool players do what they do best.

The audience at NYC bar Sugar Mouse applauds Five Boro Break creator Dan Tran at the finals.

On Saturday, November 8, you could feel it in the air. There was something electric about knowing the grittiest corners of New York City were locked in on the same game. That distinct four o’clock autumn sunlight was shining on Bushwick Ice House, one of the 16 venues, when I walked in with Traveler’s Julia Abbonizio and Skyli Alvarez, who were ready to photograph the scene. Gathered around a red-felt table were a dozen or so players who shot us “what’s up” nods as we entered; the bartender moseyed over with “what’s it gonna be?” eyes. Without a word exchanged, we were already part of the bar’s family.

The crowd around us was dressed in their dive-bar best (jeans), and glowing under the neon-red Budweiser lights. The energy in the room matched the game unfolding. One moment, the place roared with Miller High Life clinks and friends catching up. The next it would go pin-drop silent as someone bent over and lined up a shot. More often than not, we’d hear a “nice” before the cue even struck, or a congratulatory clap before someone sank the 8-ball, because everyone knew the game well enough to see exactly what was coming.

Will Pay, a Bushwick Ice House regular, designed the tournament's felt-green shirts.

Satoe Onizuka plays Netta Rawner (left) at Bushwick Ice House.

Will Pay, a Bushwick resident and the creative mind behind the tournament’s T-shirt and site design—dark green, like a pool table’s felt, and featuring a solid orange 5-ball to nod to the boroughs—was running the show. He jokingly told me he’s something of a pool scout around the city, sniffing out the best shooters to join his league. Pay attested that, when Tran initially announced the tournament, interest at his local dive Bushwick Ice House was immediate. Within 10 minutes of the link being live, the waitlist to play at the venue had passed 100.

While Satoe Onizuka, the stealthiest star of the regulars, shook another hand after winning yet another round, I snuck outside of Bushwick Ice House to chat with Pay, who was wearing the Five Boro Break shirt he designed. We got into the type of conversation you do at a dive bar or around a pool table. The love of the game. The importance of dives as sacred spaces. The alluring seediness of it all. Pay knows how we got here: “The game itself is called billiards, but it got casualized to ‘pool’ because people used to throw a ton of money on the table—pool their money—and gamble,” Pay said. “Obviously, that’s gone out the window because everyone’s super chill these days, but what’s cool is that it still has that air of danger, of being something a bit forbidden.” Will’s right: it’s never corny to shoot pool. No matter who you are, it makes you feel like the slickest person in the room.

There’s also that sense that you’re part of something bigger. Back inside, Pay gestured around the room. “Look at this place,” he said in admiration. “There’s literally no real estate for this table. But it’s here. And without it, this place would simply not be what it is. These people would probably not be here in this bar. I don’t even think this bar would exist.”

The enthusiasm at Bushwick Ice House reminded me of how this tournament could only have happened because NYC dive bars already operate as tight-knit communities of their own. They’re the ultimate third places, the spots that aren’t home or work—and the pool table is, in fact, their beating heart.

By 9 p.m. on Saturday, when we stumbled into LES’ Sadie’s Ward, '80s dance-pop shook the walls. Drinks were flowing, the room glowed disco-lit, and everyone was having such a good time you had to shout to be heard by the person next to you. A group of hodge-podge regulars stood two and three deep around the pool table, watching the small, curly-haired Amanda Andries, one of the bar’s most beloved shooters, sink her way toward Sunday’s finals.

Andries is one of the Ladies of Sadie’s, a magnetic group of female regulars at this bar, who were gassing each other up and out-shooting all the 6-foot-something men in flannels that dared to play them. For all the history that tables at bars like Sadie’s have absorbed, it’s the people gathered around them who make the pool scene so captivating—and at this bar, the social fabric is very tightly knit.

East Williamsburg's Anchored Inn was one of the 16 bars that hosted Five Boro Break games.

We sat in the small hideaway across from the bar as the games rolled on, reflecting on the players we’d met throughout the tournament so far: soft-spoken, sharp-shooting Audrey Jones at Anchored Inn over loaded Carmen fries; Allegra “Legz” Fierro outside the graffied, mirrorless bathroom at Blue Ruin Bar; and Elvin Estevez, a polite killer on the table, in the leather booths at Twins Lounge. I’d asked each to tell me their golden rule of playing pool in this city, but it all came back to one recurring theme: be a good person. There’s a camaraderie in wanting to keep NYC’s pool scene a sacred place.

It’s easy not to suck, though. Sam Shumway of Pool Table Archive said to me by phone in the days following the event. Five years ago, he started posting photos of the pool tables he’d played on in cities across the US, but his hobby grew into a living record of pool culture.

“Pool tables are special because they’re a snapshot of a time and a place in a bar,” he told me. “A lot of these tables are older than you are. Like, that’s a 40-year-old table. Imagine how much life it’s seen around it.” You can picture a montage of scenes immediately: 4 a.m. closings, birthday toasts, new friendships, awkward first dates, breakups, and more than a few questionable decisions. Maybe a win in the first-ever cross-city tournament.

Allegra “Legz” Fierro in Hell's Kitchen's Blue Ruin Bar, just before a match

Come Sunday, we walked into a jam-packed, purple-lit Sugar Mouse for the finals. The winners from each of the 16 bars would go head-to-head across six pool tables. A live dad rock band jammed in the corner, and all I saw were familiar faces from Saturday’s hijinks, smiling, watching respectfully, nodding when a friend nailed a shot, and hugging and shaking hands when one missed. As the field dwindled to four semifinalists, then just two, the crowd drew tighter around the remaining table. Two large projectors cast a live feed onto the wall, as former WPBA No. 1 Jennifer Barretta commented and Hall of Famer John Leyman refereed with a stern eye.

We were all there for the moment Brennan Brooks of the BCA Brooklyn Travel League took the inaugural win, cementing his right to take home that iconic sign. But as I took in the room around me, what stood out most was seeing people packed in like sardines to watch their fellow dive bar regulars take the stage. It was a kaleidoscope of communities, each representing their local with love. The Five Boro Break was never just about winning; it was about creating a space where everyone could be part of something.

A triumphant moment at Sadie's Ward on the Lower East Side

The East Village's Sugar Mouse hosted the tournament final.

It was a fresh alternative to life on a screen—maybe that’s part of why so many people showed up. “People are craving human connection again; people are craving something to do with their hands,” Shumway had said. And though it might look too cool, or intimidating, everyone has a place if they want it. “Pool brings together people who would normally have nothing in common. And there are no pre-qualifications for putting your name on a chalkboard. You might get beat, and that’s okay.”

At the end of the Finals night, all of us riding a collective high, Tran stood next to the championship table to thank everyone who helped bring his vision to life. He couldn’t get a word out before the room burst into applause. Thirty seconds of it, and it showed no signs of letting up. Humble as he is, he just smiled.

Tran rattled off the bars, businesses, and people who stepped up to make the tournament possible, shaking his head happily. “This is what pool does,” he said. “It brings people together rather than pushes people apart.”

Or as Shumway likes to put it: “Pool is the great equalizer.”

#6175. Allegiant, Sun Country Add New Destinations, 16 Routes

Allegiant and Sun Country are adding new destinations and a combined 16 routes ahead of the summer of 2027.

Allegiant said Tuesday that it will resume service to Minneapolis, while Sun Country will expand to Belleville, Illinois (via MidAmerica St. Louis Airport), Gulf Shores, Alabama, and Knoxville, Tennessee.

Notably, Minneapolis is Sun Country’s main operating base; renewed service from Allegiant is expected to bring their networks closer together.

Allegiant acquired Sun Country in May, though for the time being they are continuing to operate as separate airlines.

“Minnesota is an essential part of the future of our combined company, and today’s announcement is another step in delivering on that commitment,” Allegiant CEO Greg Anderson said in a news release. “MSP is our largest base of operations by a wide margin, and we see opportunities for continued growth there. Combining Sun Country’s strong foundation in the Twin Cities with Allegiant’s nationwide network of communities will provide Minnesota travelers with more convenient, affordable nonstop travel options.”

The new routes will come online in April and May.

Additionally, Allegiant said it will operate four routes currently flown by Sun Country:

Allegiant and Sun Country are expected to eventually merge operations, with the Sun Country brand phased out, though it is not clear exactly when this will happen. Allegiant said Tuesday that it will continue operating separately from Sun Country “until 2028 or later.”

#6174. Review: Austrian Airlines A320 Economy Class

After a lovely stay in Vienna, we continued our journey to Zürich onboard an Austrian Airlines A320 in economy class.

We arrived at the airport around 9:30 am, figuring there would be no need to get there early to use a lounge when we had just enjoyed an excellent breakfast at the Park Hyatt Vienna.

The airport was busy but we used the Star Gold corridor to enjoy expedited security and were soon at the gate, ready to board our short flight to Switzerland.

Stepping onboard, we headed to the back to find our seats in row 22.

The Austrian A320 has 180 seats arranged in a 3-3 configuration (same in business class, though the middle seat is blocked).

The Recaro BL3520 “NEK” slimline seats are very uncomfortable with very little padding. These are familiar seats if you have flown within Europe on Lufthansa Group carriers, with a literature pocket and a folding tray table on the seatback ahead.

Legroom varies by aircraft and row. Austrian lists a minimum economy class seat pitch of just 28 inches across its A320 fleet, so do not expect much room to stretch out, though it felt like we had 29 inches.

There are no power ports or USB ports on this aircraft. Thankfully, however, there are individual air vents, unlike on the 777.

In economy class, passengers receive a free glass of water and Austrian chocolate.

For those peckish, buy-on-board is available. I pre-ordered a hot meal from the carrier’s Austrian Melangerie menu.

What else would I order on Austrian Airlines but Wiener Schnitzel? While a proper Wiener Schnitzel is made with veal, Austrian uses chicken onboard, describing the dish as:

Golden-brown chicken schnitzel with parsley potatoes

The price was €13.80, though I received a 10% discount for pre-ordering.

Presentation was very much like economy class: the schnitzel and potatoes were served together in a cardboard box, but sometimes you have to look beyond the presentation. The chicken was tender, the breading remained surprisingly crisp, and the parsley potatoes were a nice accompaniment…my son Augustine and I both enjoyed it.

I highlighted this meal in a recent Meal of the Week feature.

> Read More: Austrian Airlines’ €13.80 Wiener Schnitzel On An 80-Minute Flight

I had also hoped to try the Julius Meinl Wiener Melange, a €5.20 coffee served with milk foam in a proper ceramic cup on a silver tray. Alas, Austrian only offers the Melange on flights of at least 80 minutes and our Vienna to Zürich flight was apparently five minutes too short according to the flight attendant.

Before landing I used the lavatory in the rear of the aircraft and it was messy by that point, with paper towels overflowing from the waste receptacle.

While there is no seatback screens or streaming movies and TV shows, Wi-Fi was available for purchase onboard. A high speed pass (Viasat) was 6€ while messaging was free. I had trouble connecting, initially, but ultimately was able to pay the 6€ and connect.

This was a quick, boring flight with a delicious lunch onboard thanks to the buy-on-board menu. I’d never go out of my way to fly Austrian shorthaul in economy class, but if you are stuck behind the curtain, do take advantage of the pre-order menu to make the flight go by a bit faster.

My original review, covering an Austrian Airlines A320 journey from Vienna to Yerevan, Armenian (fun trip!) in 2019 is below.

What is Austrian Airlines like on a mid-haul flight in economy class?

My business partner, John, and I spent a weekend in Yerevan, Armenia last month. We were in Vienna earlier in the week, so the nonstop Austrian flight from VIE to EVN made the most sense. We booked for 15,000 United miles each in economy class.

Business class would have been an extra 10,000 miles, but I figured 1.) the seat is the same, 2.) I already had lounge access, and 3.) we would be eating dinner just before the flight. So the upgrade did not make sense.

Vienna International Airport is such an easy airport to navigate. Check-in (John had to check a bag), security, and passport control took only a few moments. I’ll review the Austrian lounge in a separate post.

Boarding commenced precisely on schedule with business class passenger and Star Alliance Gold members invited to board first.

I’ll start with the seats and the following warning: these slimline seats are very uncomfortable. By the time we reached Yerevan three hours later, I could not wait to get off. The seats do recline slightly, but the lack of padding makes for an uncomfortable flying experience on flights longer than 60-90 minutes. But that’s hardly a unique experience to Austrian. Seat pitch is 30 inches.

Notice that the only difference in business class hard product is that the middle seat is blocked:

A sticker on the aircraft fuselage indicated wi-fi internet would be available, but it did not function. There are no in-seat power ports.

First, I appreciated the pillows and blankets, both of which were better than many airlines offer in economy class. Heck, United does not even offer pillows in domestic first class except on premium transcontinental flight.

That said, it was roasting outside and the cabin was not overly cool…not exactly heavy blanket weather.

Second, I appreciated the meal, as small as it was. A vegetarian cheese pasta with cake and bread was served after takeoff. Talk about a load of carbs! Passengers were not offered a choice of meal.

Flight attendants came around before the meal and also about 90 minutes before landing with a beverage serevice.

Finally, the lavatory was very clean…these pictures are toward the end of the flight.

I appreciate that Austrian is full service in the sense that blankets, pillows, and meals are provided. But three hours really pushes the limit for this type of slimline seat. I’ll happily fly Austrian again, but ideally on a shorthaul route or on a widebody jet in business class…

I have never understood who pays for the business class when it is the same seat, and if you have status you can get within a few rows of the front of the plane in economy.

I also don’t understand why all EU countries fly planes with no real business/first on flights that are this long, (2-4 hours) and are very much international. Almost all US planes have domestic first, even if they are only going an hour or two. How did things evolve so differently in the EU??

Many executives in Europe have business class travel as a part of their contracts. Non-cash perks like company cars, per diems, and travel perks are (and have historically been) more common there because they’re not taxed the same way (if at all) as wage/salary income.

These flex systems, although offering an inferior hard product, allow European carriers to flex their cabins to accommodate far more business class fliers. I’ve seen as many as the first 12 rows flexed to biz!

@Lara S, mallthus is correct that the present business class model allows for flexibility depending upon loads. Aeroflot, Tarom, and Turkish have real business class seats.

Iberia has also started incorporating ‘real’ business class seats on short to mid-haul flights on its A319..I had it from MAD-FLR, but I think its more commonly used on routes to Tel Aviv, Moscow Etc.

Looks and reminds me a lot of DLs old J seat on their 767s..

One reason to use it is when connecting with a long haul flight. Suppose you buy a business class ticket from New York to Yerevan via Vienna. You’d get the real thing in the trans Atlantic section, then a blocked middle seat.

The seats are the same as LH. After two hours on one recently I had back pain and a numb a*se. Apparently they are now being replaced by ones that according to the LH CEO Spohr are ‘even more comfortable’. I wait in fear!

Austrian unlike the other LH group carriers also use these seats on their long haul aircraft in economy. You have been warned!

I think Europeans find US Domestic premium cabins and products as strange and confusing as we find their intro-European premium product.

In the US, we call it First Class (but it’s closer to Business Class). You get a big seat with more leg room. Generally the plane is WiFi equipped with either IFE or streaming entertainment at no charge. You only get a meal if it’s over a certain length (2-3 hours) and during meal times. You also do not get Lounge access (but lounge access is commonly available through a credit card or membership program).

In the EU, you get a coach seat with a blocked middle. The leg room is less than what is available in the US in the Economy Plus, Main Cabin Extra, etc. cabins. You get Lounge access and a meal that is generally better than what you would get on a US carrier for the same stage length. WiFi and IFE/streaming entertainment is not as common.

I absolutely prefer the US model but it is what I am used to. I get my Lounge access through my credit cards. I would prefer an MCE seat to Euro Business any day and I can book those seats at ticketing. But I’m guessing some Euro business man would find the lack of a meal and complimentary lounge access disappointing.

#6173. Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., said that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

“Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján said.

The nomination of Thumann Severs, who currently serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

Currently Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., said Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper said.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC currently focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he said Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

“The First Amendment places important limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz said. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

However, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

“Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she said. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs said she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”

Luján also asked Thumann Severs to name issues where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she said her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

Thumann Severs said that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it currently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

“Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any new Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been announced by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

#6172. To Write ‘The Brightness,’ Chad Harbach Planned a Friends Trip to Block Island

This is Write Here, a column where authors and literary luminaries tell us about the travels they took to find inspiration and create their latest books.

In this installment, author and n+1 editor Chad Harbach describes his love for Block Island, Rhode Island, and a 2016 trip that informed a keystone part of his latest novel The Brightness. In the book, a bildungsroman that tackles topics like campus politics, the discourse around sexual assault, and the anxiety of being in one’s twenties, Block Island serves as the dramatic setting for a long, eventful wedding night that alters the lives of Harbach’s characters—particularly that of Pella Affenlicht, who originally appeared in Harbach’s 2011 debut The Art of Fielding. Below, Harbach recalls gathering his own friends for a summer holiday on Block Island as an excuse to refamiliarize himself with the destination as he began to write it in fiction—and the local peafowl that nearly made it into the book.

“In the early stages of writing The Brightness, one of the first things I decided was that the book’s centerpiece, the big wedding of the character Owen, would be located on Block Island, Rhode Island. I wanted the scene—which is now this 150-page stretch of the story, when all sorts of crazy things happen over a single, almost Shakespearean night—to be on the island’s eastern shore where houses are positioned at the top of these stone cliffs. I pictured an outdoor dance floor overlooking the beach and the ocean with the moon in the distance. Essentially I wanted to write the destination wedding I desperately wanted to attend. But as I was working on it, I realized I needed to go back there to check if my memories of the place were accurate, to have it fresh in my mind.

My then-partner and I organized a trip to Block Island with a large group of friends in the summer of 2016. We rented a big house and folks came from places like New York, Philadelphia, California, and Amsterdam. It felt like a wedding in that sense—everyone gathered for this joyous celebration in a beautiful place. We didn’t do all the terrible stuff to one another that’s maybe required for the juicy plot of a novel, but we did spend eight days cooking together, playing the piano, singing songs, drinking a lot, and staying up very late.

But we couldn’t sleep in very late because, well, there were these peahens. There was a sort of farm with animals, maybe a petting zoo, near our house, and their peahens liked to come and roost in the trees on our property. Every morning at 5 a.m., after we had been up until 2 or 3 a.m., the peahens would just start. I don’t know if you’ve ever heard the squawking of peahens, but suffice to say it was awful. It’s funny: When I started doing publicity for The Brightness, an announcement mentioned that part of it is set on Block Island. I got texts from friends who were on that trip, saying, congrats, we’re so excited, the fucking peahens better be in there. I initially did have this whole bit about the peahens, but there was so much going on in the plot that I cut them—not without really trying to make it work first.

Other than the loud birds, it was a great trip. The place struck me as just as magical as it had when I first went at 19 years old, when I was in college. I had a friend whose grandparents had a house there. I’ve visited several times since, and always loved it. But this was the only time I’ve ever gone somewhere for book research, and I was able to lock in some granular details like what the downtown looks like, the shape of the buildings, the sight of the marshlands, and what it’s like to bike out to the airport.

I was also excited to find that the feel of it was exactly as I remembered. Block Island has this rugged, natural beauty—it’s a rocky, tree-filled place surrounded by ocean, where everyone just rides bikes around, and part of it is a protected nature preserve. It’s sort of the forgotten sibling of Nantucket or Martha’s Vineyard. Some people don’t even know that Block Island exists, which keeps it from changing too much, even though it was settled by Europeans in the mid-1600s. The cemetery there has the tombstones of families that date back centuries, long before the United States became a country. I think some of those same families still live on the island now. So there’s this sense of continuity and timelessness.

Even before you reach Block Island, there’s just something about climbing on to the ferry and heading out into the open water, this freedom and openness that’s very inspiring to me. I grew up in Wisconsin, on Lake Michigan, which isn’t an ocean but looks like one, and I’ve always loved that feeling of vastness and mystery that comes with a massive body of water—that literal depth. It reminds me that we as humans actually haven’t mastered everything, and there are many things in this world that are not easy for us to touch.

All of this made Block Island a helpful setting in The Brightness. What happens on this wedding night propels the characters toward life paths that are very different from what they thought they were going to have, and having the story be imbued with the island’s sense of openness, possibility, and what might be feels fitting. As a writer, that can be part of the work: tapping into that feeling or gestalt of a place. It can be very easy to do at times, and difficult at others. And, you know, sometimes it’s just hard to write. So it was a great help writing about somewhere I love visiting literally and creatively. Instead of resisting sitting down at my desk, I’d be like, I’m ready to go to Block Island. It’s this setting I could picture well, enjoy being in, and keep traveling to—even if it was just in my imagination.” —As told to Matt Ortile

#6171. Finding Unexpected Joy In Music And Hospitality From Los Angeles To Malibu

One of the beautiful things about traveling around the world is the chance to experience hospitality in different ways in different countries. I’ll never forget the hospitality I experienced In Iran or in Ukraine, but sometimes we don’t have to travel far to experience it, as I recently found out in Los Angeles.

I listen to music during the day as I work on this blog and on my other work. Some people require absolute silence to work, but I like music, specially Christian hymns. I primarily use YouTube and of course the algorithm gets to know you. There’s no music I like more than a powerful organ playing a beloved hymn. Lately, the algorithm has been suggesting a very gifted organist named Lauma Akmene, a Latvian-born musician who is the organist, conductor, and music director at St. Peter’s Episcopal Church in Salisbury, Maryland.

As I listened to her music all morning, one of her YouTube shorts noted that she would be performing a classical concert in Los Angeles, which immediately piqued my interest.

I obtained a ticket and found the concert would be held at a place called Stan’s Musical Parlor, which was actually a beautiful 1926 home in LA’s posh Lafayette Square neighborhood. Not knowing quite what to expect, I showed up and was warmly greeted by Stanley Harris himself, who I came to find out has opened his house since 1986 to showcase musical talents. Dr. Harris is a retired psychiatrist and was a longtime clinician and faculty member at the University of Southern California.

Stan has a Johannus-BachMen-Hauptwerk organ (including Hauptwerk virtual pipe organs) in his living room. Essentially, this digital organ can be set to emulate sounds from many of famous pipe organs around the world.

The concert began at 8:00 pm and was simply fabulous, with Lauma playing several classic and neo-classic works.

One of the guests mentioned that he was hosting Lauma the following evening at his home in Malibu, and invited me to attend. I had to be in Palm Springs for work that day, but I drove from Palms Springs all the way to Malibu via Pacific Coast Highway (took about three hours!) and made it just in time for the concert, another fabulous evening of food, fellowship, and great music.

Already, I’ve made friends through these two events, who I am staying in touch with, and will go to more of these concerts. Community is beautiful thing, as is hospitality, and all in my backyard, one of the many reasons I love Los Angeles and Southern California so much.

Truth be told, I almost did not go to either event. I was tired and probably could have used a couple extra hours of sleep. But I’m so glad I did go and I’m thankful to YouTube for suggesting Lauma and making these two possible in the first place.

Lauma is such a gifted organist. If you like classical music and especially sacred music, you can enjoy her work here.

#6170. Rift grows among Senate Democrats over who will lead in majority

Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

More Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

But Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete plan” that provides change.

“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”

Sanders said during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a new and bold direction.”

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”

Some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking said he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but said she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

“Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”

She urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she said, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”

Asked about his plans Monday evening, Van Hollen said, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to new members who have just come off the campaign trail.”

“What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”

Van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he said, according to a livestream of the event.

Schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he said of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she said.

Gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is currently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she said.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., said Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”

“Yes,” he said of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”

Mark Schoeff Jr., Paul M. Krawzak and Kelly Livingston contributed to this report.

#6169. 11 Best Airbnbs in Stockholm for Historic Architecture, Saunas, and Beach Access

For a break that balances the buzz of discovering a new city with a good dose of fresh air, Stockholm’s mix of lush parks and eclectic architecture is an enduring choice. The city is formed of 14 islands, meaning you’re never too far from a waterfront to amble along. It's packed with historical charm (head to Gamla Stan to see one of Europe’s oldest medieval cobbled streets), as well as stylish boutiques and museums championing everything from Abba to the world’s best-preserved 17th-century warship. While the city is home to a slew of excellent hotels, from elegant converted townhouses to the former home of Astrid Lindgren (author of the beloved Pippi Longstocking book series), you’ll want to look to Airbnb for a real home-from-home vibe.

These 11 excellent rentals throughout the city and its outskirts balance top-notch amenities with the freedom that only comes with a private booking. True to Nordic form, there’s a clutch of homes with their own sauna and steam rooms, and all have either sea or skyline views. Below, the best Airbnbs in Stockholm to book for a weekend of weaving through medieval streets, gallery hopping, and lots of cinnamon buns.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic architecture, prime location, dedicated workspace

Subverting traditional Scandi minimalist sensibilities, this cool retreat in the hip heart of Södermalm channels a moody, more underground kind of charm. On the top floor, light-flooded, open-plan living areas are packed with rich, creamy furnishings and crisp architectural lines—multiple previous guests say that this is one of the most stylish homes they’ve ever stayed in. Downstairs, two tranquil bedrooms are carved directly into the exposed natural rock, so you can sleep beneath historic vaulted ceilings after a long day skipping from sight to sight. On that note: Södermalm is an eclectic area of town, with plenty of vintage shops and wine bars, after which you can hole up in this cocooning, cave-like retreat, as though you’re stepping into your own secret—and very stylish—bunker.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Riddarholm Church, Stockholm City Museum

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Forest access, indoor fireplace, outdoor gas grill

Blink, and you might miss this off-grid, A-frame cabin, hidden among a thick swathe of pine trees. It’s worth searching for: Once you make your way through the foliage, you’ll find a truly wonderful Swedish escape for two. The glass-fronted structure invites in all of the elements, while inside, it’s time to switch off—there’s a crackling open hearth where you can grill all of your meals, and precious little noise other than the rustle of wind through the canopy. Fair warning: There’s a very rustic toilet and seasonal shower about a 30-second walk down the forest path, so if you’re not a DIY fan, perhaps look elsewhere. Nonetheless, for more adventurous sorts, the trade-off means absolute tranquility surrounded by happily grazing sheep and twinkly starry night skies—all within a hop and a skip of the capital.

Neighborhood: VärmdöThings to do nearby: Lillsved Beach, Buddharama Temple, Stora Sandön

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic warehouse, steps from the lake, wood-burning fireplace

Wood-beamed ceilings, clattering floors, a muted color scheme, and a signature bright exterior welcome you in from the cold—this former warehouse just oozes 19th-century charm the moment you round the corner. Better yet, it’s totally massive, sprawling across three roomy floors, with a prime spot perched right on the peaceful banks of Åkers canal. A snazzy and social kitchen space opens onto a central island and a fireplace, where all the family will want to gather. When it’s time to bed down, there are cozy curtained sleeping nooks and an additional attic dormitory, adding a playful, rustic vibe. You can rent canoes from host Cecile to paddle down the canal, or jump on an e-bike to explore the surrounding nature reserves. When you return, fire up the outdoor grill and gather around the dining table for a long dinner with more endless views.

Neighborhood: Norrö-StavaThings to do nearby: Prästfjärden lake, Näsudden nature reserve, Åkersbro walking trails

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Sea views, sauna, hot tub

This joyfully bobbing houseboat turns the gray blue waters of the Baltic into something akin to your own front lawn—and it does so just 15 minutes from the heady sights of central Stockholm. Panoramic floor-to-ceiling glass means you feel that you’re virtually out on the water—and, of course, you can dive straight into the lake from your bedroom deck. Dry off and hop into the private wood-fired sauna to warm up. Hop off the boat, and you can sunbathe on the jetty, cook up some local catches on the barbecue, or jump into the complimentary canoe. All in all, this is an idyllic waterside playground that active types will love.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Kringelgården bakery, Saltsjöbadens golf course, Artipelag

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sauna, beach access, pet-friendly

Expect some truly good seascape ASMR when you stay here—you’re so close to the water you can hear the waves rolling onto the shore right from the porch. Grab the kayak from the cupboard and head down to the beach to make the most of this beautiful location. It’s a short drive from the home to Stockholm’s city center, but you’re rewarded with much serenity and glorious views instead. For those seeking a secluded family stay, this is the place.

Neighborhood: TyresöThings to do nearby: Sandholmarna nature preserve, Tyresta nature reserve, Lilla beach

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wood stove, sauna, beach access

This spacious waterside cottage is not in Stockholm’s city center, but by compromising on a 30-minute commute into town, you gain something really special. The owners took the original 130-year-old structure down piece by piece, rebuilding it on their own property. It was worth the effort. Now, it lies surrounded by pine trees in a nature reserve beside a sparkling, clear lake, with the sea just a few steps further in the other direction. A large porch provides the spot for barbecue dinners and sunbathing sessions in the summer, and there are two spas within walking distance for those looking for their Scandi sweat fix—the sea-facing Skepparholmen Spa, and Japanese onsen-style Yasuragi. But you don't have to head that far, as the property has its own sauna. Stay in as long as you can muster, then cool off by jumping in the lake—something all the more satisfactory in the winter months.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Boobadet Beach, Nyckelvikens wildlife refuge, Sushi Bar Namiyama

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Rooftop views, beach access, pet-friendly

A previous guest says this flat has a New York City vibe, and we can see why—the interior space is small but stylish, with an industrial bent and views all over the coolest part of Stockholm from the balcony. It’s on the top floor of this apartment block, so the vistas can’t be beat. It’s been a winner for those on work trips, thanks to superfast WiFi and a dedicated workspace, and, unusually for Airbnb stays, you can bring your dog too.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Liljeholmsviken waterfront, Högalid Church, Skinnarviksberget

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroomWhy we love it: Steam room, in-unit washer/dryer, fully equipped kitchen

For an Airbnb stay that’s as close to checking into a luxury hotel as possible, look to this plush apartment right in the city center. The whole place is brand new, and no expense has been spared on the fittings—there are genuine oak floorboards, Italian travertine surfaces, underfloor heating, and a slew of top-notch furniture, plus little touches such as a shower seat and a gloriously powerful rainfall shower. The best bit is the steam room; there’s no better way to decompress after a long flight or a blustery autumnal walk by the river.

Neighborhood: VasastanThings to do nearby: Vanadislunden park, Odenplan plaza, Swedish Museum of Natural History

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Proximity to metro, private patio, in-unit washer/dryer

If dopamine itself could be characterized as a building, it’d be this one. The place (all 300 square feet of it) is pure joy from top to bottom—with a pink-tiled kitchen, mint-green bathroom, and cozy bedroom nook with yellow walls and blue candy-striped bedding. Cheery artworks add a final flourish. Despite its bijou size, there’s room for two more guests on the pullout bed, and there’s a patio with twinkly fairy lights to sit out on sunny afternoons with a book, a glass of wine, or both.

Neighborhood: ÄlvsjöThings to do nearby: Älvsjö Forest Nature Preserve, Herrängens Gård, Långbro park

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Beach access, sauna, kayak

Forget your average homely fisherman’s cottage—this home here, on the cusp of the lake in the city’s swish Stocksund neighborhood, marks a newer, more modern breed of lake house. It’s chic as anything you’ll find in the city, with smooth, polished concrete floors and knotty pine walls finished with a moody, cocooning interior palette. Sweeping glass windows make the most of the beautiful views that stretch over the water and right to the city as it twinkles on the other side. Grab the kayak and spend an afternoon bobbing on the lake, then stop in for a well-deserved sweat session in the private sauna.

Neighborhood: StocksundThings to do nearby: Restaurang Hemma, Svanholmsparken park, Swedish Museum of Natural History

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Wood-burning fireplace, Aesop toiletries, garden view

This traditional Swedish apartment has had a modern facelift recently. Now it pairs gorgeous original features, including imposing 10-foot-high ceilings and whitewashed floorboards, with a sleek new kitchen and selection of cool designer furniture pieces. There's also a truly cloudlike sofa just made for cozy nights in. The surrounding streets are just as cool as the interiors; this home is smack dab in SoFo—by far Stockholm’s trendiest district—so you're just one street over from a clutch of the best of the city’s bar, restaurant, and café scene.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Stockholm City Museum, Vitabergsparken park

You'll need a valid passport to enter the Cayman Islands. U.S. citizens do not need a visa for stays of up to 30 days, though you'll receive a tourist entry stamp on arrival. Make sure your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond your travel dates to be safe.

Yes, many restaurants automatically add a 15% gratuity to your bill, so check before tipping on top of that for exceptional service. Cash tips are fine, but many places also take cards.

English is the official language and is widely spoken everywhere you'll go as a visitor. You won't need a translation app.

Grand Cayman is compact and manageable by taxi, rental car, or ride-sharing services. Taxis are metered and reliable; rides typically start at  $8–15, depending on distance. If you rent a car, remember to drive on the left side of the road. Uber does not operate here, but other services are available.

The Cayman Islands are generally safe for tourists, with a strong police presence and low rates of violent crime. Standard travel precautions apply: don't leave valuables unattended, be aware of your surroundings at night, and keep a copy of your important documents separate from the originals.

November through April offers the best weather, warm and comfortable. In peak season, expect higher prices and more crowds. May through October is hurricane season, so be aware that even though direct hits are rare. If you're flexible, September and October can offer lower rates and fewer tourists, with the tradeoff of higher humidity and occasional afternoon storms.

Top-tier resorts, nature excursions and seven-mile stretches of clear water — there's much worth experiencing when visiting the Cayman Islands.

The Cayman Islands’ luxury boom in hotels, restaurants and experiences made it an easy pick for our 2027 Where to Go list. But building the right itinerary can be a challenge when there’s so much to enjoy — especially when you're trying to maximize your point earnings and fit everything into a long weekend.

What really makes the Cayman Islands work as a points destination is how every part of your trip, from flights and hotels to dining and activities, can help you earn.

That's why TPG and Chase are teaming up to bring travelers everything they need to know to make the most of their trip to the Cayman Islands. Planning and earning are easier with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees), thanks to its recently refreshed benefits, including the annual $100 Chase Travel℠ Hotel Credit, a statement credit of up to $120 back every four years for a TSA PreCheck®, Global Entry or Nexus application fee charged to the card. Cardmembers also enjoy long-standing benefits, including no foreign transaction fees and a comprehensive suite of built-in travel protections.

Here's how I spent four unforgettable days on the islands, and how you can use your Chase Sapphire Preferred card to do the same.

Getting to the Cayman Islands is easy, as there are plenty of nonstop flight options to Owen Roberts International Airport (GCM) year-round from major U.S. hubs, including:

All three airlines are Chase transfer partners, meaning you can book through the Chase Travel or transfer points to any of these airline loyalty programs.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Getting to and from the airport is one of my favorite ways to earn some extra points on a trip. With the Chase Sapphire Preferred, you can earn 5 points per dollar on Lyft* if you opt for a ride, or 3 points per dollar on gas station purchases and EV charging if you decide to drive yourself, as I did.

Either way, don't forget that your Chase Sapphire Preferred card offers a statement credit of up to $120 every four years toward a Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or Nexus application fee. If you choose Global Entry, membership also includes TSA PreCheck, making it easier to breeze through airport security.

Once you land in Grand Cayman, you will need to take a taxi or book private transportation to your resort. Hotels, resorts and condo properties are not permitted to offer complimentary or in-house airport shuttle services to arriving and departing guests to protect the local taxi and licensed public transit trade. When exiting the airport, simply locate the taxi stand directly outside the main arrivals greeting area for a ride to your hotel.

The best part of staying in Grand Cayman is that the island has no shortage of luxury hotel options in the Seven Mile Beach area, the ideal home base for island activities and excursions.

I stayed at the Kimpton Seafire Resort + Spa, which has three on-site restaurants and bars, a Forbes Five-Star spa (trust me, book the massage) and daily yoga and fitness classes overlooking the ocean. The sprawling pool connects directly to Seven Mile Beach, and the hotel regularly hosts events ranging from mixology classes to live Caribbean music, so there is always something to do.

Other TPG-recommended properties include:

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Cardmembers can book hotels through Chase Travel and receive up to $100 in statement credits each account anniversary year on eligible hotel stays. The cherry on top? After the first $100 in hotel purchases that qualify for the credit, you'll earn 5 points per dollar on additional hotel purchases made through Chase Travel with your Sapphire Preferred card.

All these recommended properties are part of a wave of luxury hotels elevating the Caribbean escape. Keep an eye out for additional resorts opening in 2027 and beyond, including the highly anticipated Grand Hyatt Grand Cayman Resort & Spa.

Once you check in and freshen up, head downstairs at Kimpton Seafire to dine at Ave. The Mediterranean-inspired menu has plenty to choose from, and I can say the local snapper ($38) and the Mediterranean orzo salad ($22) were excellent — and don’t skip the creamy mashed potatoes ($9).

The cocktails were as beautiful as the sunset you'll watch from their outdoor patio. I sipped a colorful mocktail called the Butterfly Lemonade ($12), made with butterfly pea flower, ginger, rosemary, orange, cinnamon, lemon and soda, while my husband enjoyed the Ponoma, which features Beefeater gin, Dolin dry, grapefruit and hibiscus cordial, lemon and ginger ale. It was a perfect ending to day one.

Spend day two on one of Cayman Island’s most popular and iconic excursions: a boat tour to Stingray City. The famous shallow sandbars on the North Sound sit in water that can only be described as Gatorade blue, where visitors can stand, swim and interact with dozens of friendly, wild southern stingrays. If you don’t feel like getting up close and personal with the rays, you are welcome to soak up the sun and enjoy the views from the boat.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Activities and tours booked through Chase Travel, such as a boat excursion to Stingray City, earn 5 points per dollar when you pay with your Preferred Card.

For a rooftop sunset dinner, make a reservation at Pom Pom at the neighboring Hotel Indigo, where you can enjoy Caribbean small plates and cocktails with some of the best views Grand Cayman has to offer. Since Hotel Indigo and the Kimpton Seafire are IHG sister properties, you can just take a quick three-minute golf cart ride to get there, no taxi required.

After a long day in the sun, I sipped on the Raspberry & Chicha Tereré ($13), an alcohol-free refresher that blends yerba mate, raspberry, and purple corn. For food, our server recommended the Picanha ($39), a 10-oz. sirloin cap with a Brazilian vinaigrette and lava salt, and Pollo Anticuchos ($30), chicken skewers with Peruvian chilies puré and chimichurri that had a little kick without being too spicy. For dessert, do not skip the Quatro Leches ($15) cake; it was sweet, light and absolutely delicious. Needless to say, it was one of my favorite meals of the whole trip.

Wake up bright and early and take a taxi to Cayman Crystal Caves, an underground cave system that's part geology lesson, part adventure, and it’s safe for all ages. The caves are accessible through guided tours that last about an hour and a half, and take you through chambers filled with stalactites and stalagmites that formed over millennia.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Transportation expenses such as taxi rides can earn 2 points per dollar with the Chase Sapphire Preferred card, helping you earn bonus points even when you're exploring beyond your hotel or resort.

If you have time, visit the Queen Elizabeth II Botanical Gardens before heading back to the resort. It has 65 acres of maintained grounds with orchid gardens and woodland trails. You'll wind through native plant collections, endemic species and tropical pathways, home to endangered Grand Cayman Blue Iguanas and other Caribbean-native animals. I’d budget about 90 minutes to wander.

For sunset dinner on the beach, head over to Bonny Moon Beach Club. It’s a two-minute walk from the Kimpton, and the restaurant offers seating under their outdoor canopy or directly on the sand. You can’t go wrong with anything on the menu either: flatbreads, ceviches and hummus will all make for delicious accompaniments to another perfect view of the sun setting over the water.

After a few days full of adventure and sightseeing, I prefer to slow it down on my last full day with a little R&R, and that, of course, includes a trip to the spa. Book a morning treatment at The Spa at Seafire, as I did, and enjoy the Artisan’s Touch massage ($250) or a facial that incorporates locally inspired ingredients and techniques to really lean into the Caribbean vibes. (Ask for Donna if she is available!)

And of course, take advantage of the included amenities, such as the spa garden, steam room, cold plunge and hot tub.

In the afternoon, take it easy with a poolside lunch, then head on over to the beach to unwind on a lounger and go for a calming swim in the Caribbean's clear waters.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: One of my favorite multipliers on the card focuses on dining. You’ll earn 3 points per dollar on dining, whether it’s happy hour at Tillie's or breakfast at Ave.

For your final night, make your last dinner count at Cocoloba. The beachfront Mexican-inspired restaurant is elevated enough to feel like a celebration, but since it's located at the Kimpton Seafire, you can enjoy the meal and easily head back up to your room to pack and get proper rest before your flight home the next day.

After four days spent swimming with stingrays, exploring underground crystal caves and enjoying the Caribbean, leaving was definitely the hardest part. Thankfully, my Chase Sapphire Preferred card helped make the trip home easier. The card's application fee credit for Global Entry helped cover the cost of enrollment, and the program's expedited arrival process meant minimal wait times when we landed. Instead of standing in long lines, we had extra time to enjoy our layover before the final leg of our journey.

Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Back home, my grocery delivery was waiting for me. The Chase Sapphire Preferred can earn 3 points per dollar on online grocery purchases to help make the reset from vacation a little easier.

The growing number of hotels bookable with points in the Cayman Islands means your points stretch further when you visit. Plus, when you're making the most of everything the islands have to offer, the Chase Sapphire Preferred card makes it easy to earn along the way so you can easily redeem when you’re ready to come back and visit again.

*Valid through Sept. 30, 2027; does not apply to Wait & Save, bike or scooter rides; activation required.

#6167. Alaska Cuts Four Routes

Alaska Airlines will drop four destinations from its network in Portland, Oregon.

The carrier confirmed it will end service from Portland to Baltimore, St. Louis, New Orleans, and Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

Three of the connections launched only months ago. Portland-Jackson Hole came online in June, and service to Baltimore and St. Louis started in May.

“As we add new routes to our network, we constantly assess existing routes to ensure we’re using our aircraft in the markets our guests want most,” the carrier said in a statement provided to AirlineGeeks. “As part of that process, we’ve made the decision to discontinue service between Portland and Baltimore, Jackson Hole, St. Louis, and New Orleans. We remain committed to Portland and will continue to invest in opportunities that strengthen our network there, including adding service in markets where we see the greatest opportunities for our guests.”

Alaska serves over 60 destinations from Portland, and recently opened a new lounge there.

#6166. Columbia Coupon Codes & Deals: 15% Off

The right gear can make or break your trip, especially when you’re dealing with the wilderness. Ensuring that you have the best footwear, weather protection, and bags to make it from point A to point B can mean the difference between a fun hike with friends and a sullen drive home. Whether it’s your first foray into the great outdoors or you’re an old hand on the trails, Columbia’s gear is a fan favorite for a reason.

As a frequent camper and hiker, my family and I have our fair share of Columbia products, mainly a few different fleece zip-ups and a trusty backpack that functions just as seamlessly on national park hikes as it does cross-country flights. Thankfully, whether you’re trying out a new product or interested in repurchasing a favorite, there are some great ways to spend less on top Columbia items. Read on for some of the best promo codes, deals, and savings across the brand. In the market for even more outdoor gear? Take a glance at our Salomon promo codes, North Face discounts, and Patagonia coupons to get the most bang for your buck.

If you're new to the brand, or haven't bought Columbia gear straight from the source yet, you'll want to join the free Columbia Greater Rewards program. Those who sign up will receive a 15% off coupon code to use on their first order. Once you're a member, you'll benefit from free shipping year-round—on all orders with no minimums—and early access to any new gear. You’ll also be able to earn points when you purchase products online or in-store, which you’ll be able to redeem for rewards. For every $100 spent (equivalent to 1,000 points), you'll receive $5 to use on a future purchase. You’ll also be able to score a 20% off coupon annually on your birthday.

Those who regularly hit the trails or set up camp can upgrade to Titanium status by spending $300 at Columbia annually, and get additional perks like double points on shoe purchases, a first look at all sales and gear, and access to a dedicated customer help line.

Columbia shoppers don’t have to wait for Black Friday deals—members can already score early access to the sale and take up to 50% off all their favorite gear. Early access to these budget-saving prices is only available for Greater Rewards members, and products have to be purchased online on the brand’s website; in-person shopping is excluded. But for orders of $150 or more, guests can take advantage of free shipping within the 48 contiguous US states. From winter coats that keep the chill at bay, like the women’s Karis Gale II long jacket, to casual layers like the women’s Holly Hideaway waffle tunic, there’s plenty to score at excellent prices.

Personally, I’m looking to stock up on basics like the women’s MW Fair Isle thermal socks, which are 50% off, and a pair of comfortable walking shoes for my next beachy trip, like the women’s Konos Hiker 2-Strap sandal. You can also shop winter boots, blankets, hats, and water bottles, in addition to coats, socks, and layers. Whether you’re looking for some new gear, a holiday gift for friends, or to nab a new pair of polarized sunglasses, there’s plenty to shop while supplies last.

Another easy way to spend less on your next outdoor gear purchase: Sign up to receive emails or text messages on upcoming deals, new gear, and exclusive offers, and score a one-time coupon to use on any purchase of $100 or more. Those who sign up for emails will get $10 off their $100 purchase, but if you’re willing to sign up for both emails and text messages, your savings will bump up to $20 off. Keep in mind this coupon expires 30 days after you sign up, so it’s best to have the product that you want to purchase in mind before you make the jump. Military members, first responders, teachers, and students can all benefit from an additional 10% off at Columbia with a valid ID. To register and receive this discount, log in directly to ID.me and verify your ID. Unfortunately, the discount is not applicable to Columbia Greater Rewards, but there are still plenty of great products you can use it on, like full-price athletic skorts and camping gear.

Heading on a multi-day backpacking trek or an international vacation and making a bunch of big purchases? Columbia has partnered with Klarna, so travelers can shop now and pay over time—meaning you don’t have to put your cart through a tournament bracket to decide which products get voted off the island. #6165. Republicans tap Moreno and Jack to lead Senate and House campaign arms

Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

House and Senate Republicans picked their new campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack with leading the GOP campaign arms for the 2028 election cycle.

In their new positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.

Republicans returned to Capitol Hill this week still reeling from their losses but resisted calls to delay Tuesday’s leadership elections. In the Senate, South Dakota’s John Thune was reelected Republican leader without any opposition, while Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan defeated Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise in a closed-door, secret-ballot election to lead House Republicans next year.

Moreno will succeed South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

“Republicans must enter this next election clear-eyed: the road ahead back to a Republican Senate majority will by no means be easy but the fight has never been so important,” the Ohio senator said in a statement.

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill, Moreno described his new role as “a hell of a job.” He said Republicans would be “absolute savages” on ending government corruption and continuing “to work for the American people.”

“I suspect the best tailwind we’ll have is that the Democrats will learn all the wrong lessons,” he told reporters.

Moreno, a close ally of President Donald Trump, is currently serving his first term. He first ran for Senate during the 2022 cycle but dropped out of a crowded GOP primary eventually won by JD Vance. Two years later, buoyed by an endorsement from Trump, he won a contested primary for the state’s other Senate seat and went on to oust Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown that fall.

Brown is poised to return to the Senate after defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week in a special election for the remaining Senate term of Vice President Vance. While Ohio has swung heavily toward Republicans over the past decade, Democrats scored big wins in the Buckeye State last week, winning several statewide offices and flipping three seats in the U.S. House.

But assuming he runs again for a full term, Brown will be on the ballot in 2028, setting up what’s likely to be a tense home-state fight.

In an apparent reference to the returning Brown, Moreno offered some Washington advice Tuesday: “Make sure you rent. Do not buy.”

The 2028 Senate map gives Republican pickup opportunities in a handful of swing states, including Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania. The party will also be defending battleground seats in Alaska, Iowa, North Carolina and Wisconsin. Also on the Senate ballot are races for Republican-held seats in Kansas and South Carolina, where Democrats scored surprise wins last week.

On the House side, Jack defeated Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym III to become the next chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. He takes office after one of the worst elections for the GOP in recent decades and will succeed outgoing NRCC Chair Richard Hudson, who lost his own North Carolina seat last week.

House Republicans face the tough task of cutting into Democrats’ 40-plus-seat majority next cycle. But the party will have a slew of pickup opportunities, given the sheer number of seats Democrats won in historically red territory this year.

Like Moreno, Jack was first elected to Congress 2024, leveraging a close relationship with Trump to win an open seat outside Atlanta. He previously was White House director of political affairs during Trump’s first term and was a senior adviser to the president’s 2024 campaign. Over the past two years, he served as the NRCC’s recruitment chair.

Savannah Behrmann contributed to this report.

#6164. Mullin: Wave of Tech Failures May Be Linked to AI

Artificial intelligence could be playing a role in the cascade of high-profile technology failures seen over the last week, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Monday.

Mullin told FOX News’ Sean Hannity that he spoke with someone in the tech industry, “one guy who is very smart with tech,” who identified AI as a possible culprit.

“He said, ‘I believe that it’s the SI, because the programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is,'” he said.

The individual suggested that the technology’s ability to move fast and fix itself created “ripple effects” that overwhelmed older conventional systems. The secretary said that theory “kind of makes sense to me.”

The Trump administration uses the term “super intelligence,” or SI, in place of AI.

Mullin said his source did not want to be identified but ruled out at least one famous personality from the tech sector.

Multiple large, U.S.-based networks have crashed over the past week, including the FAA’s air traffic control communications system, United’s internal applications, Microsoft’s business services, and software used by banks such as JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo.

Mullin said there is no indication from the intelligence and cybersecurity communities that the outages are part of a cyberattack.

The FAA has blamed Friday’s nationwide ground stop on a faulty or improperly installed router, which flooded other routers with data and ultimately crashed the system.
