#6163. The Best Places to Go in Central and South America 2027

This is my fourth year leading our guide to the Best Places to Go in Central and South America, and each time I’m in awe of the final result—our list for 2027 is no exception. We’re talking about a region where the Pacific, the Atlantic, and the Caribbean converge; where the Andes reach for the Amazon; and where strings of puffy volcanoes and postcard-worthy islands stud the map like jewels. Within it all there are thriving cities where cultures ancient and modern collide head-on, and small towns that are timeless in a way that feels increasingly rare.

It may be a fool’s errand to distill all this wonder into a list of just 10 destinations. But the places below, as singular or more broadly representative as they may be, are the region’s answer to how we are traveling right now. For example, a pioneering set of travel specialists are ready to bring you to eco-lodges that are tucked in the untamed jungle of Guyana for wildlife sightings and citizen science experiences that will broaden your understanding of the only (official) English-speaking country in South America. If you’re looking for a sport to pick up, Preá on Brazil’s northeast coast has an open invitation on kitesurfing, the wind-driven sport this fishing village has long been known for—and the reason a set of quietly luxurious boutique hotels have been cropping up within driving distance of the rolling sand dunes of Jericoacoara National Park. If wine is what moves you, then Chile’s Central Valley should be your next stop: A slew of new culinary experiences and interesting bottles from up-and-coming winemakers make this Santiago-adjacent region the trip to take in 2027. There’s also next-gen wellness in Costa Rica, quintessential expedition cruises in Ecuador, offseason trekking in Argentina, and so much more.

Get ready to max out that PTO. These are the Best Places to Go in Central and South America in 2027. —Megan Spurrell

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: new jungle stays, ancestral wellness experiences, and a next-level approach to ecotourism

In the Central Highlands of Costa Rica, Finca Madre Tierra is part of a new generation of properties redefining ecotourism.

Tucked in the Monteverde Cloud Forest, Hotel Belmar's Artista Villages offers 10 bungalows in a reforestation site.

Half a century ago Costa Rica helped pioneer a new model of travel in the Monteverde Cloud Forest that would come to be known as ecotourism. Today the free-spirited residents of Monteverde, three hours northwest of the capital, San José, are once again redefining responsible travel—yet now the goal extends beyond minimizing tourism’s footprint to actively restoring ecosystems, supporting local communities, and forging deeper connections between visitor and place. That ethos is embodied by Artista Villas, a collection of 10 swish bungalows in a reforestation site at Hotel Belmar. Guests at the carbon-neutral property, which opened in June, engage with the surrounding jungle using in-room art kits, meet visiting artists and filmmakers at the property’s Cervecería Belmar, forest bathe in the mountain at Artista-owned Savia nature reserve, and learn about the source of their meals at Finca Madre Tierra. Calling this new form of regenerative travel ecotourism feels too small to capture its weight.

As conventional foreign-owned resorts proliferate along the nearby Gulf of Papagayo, Monteverde and the surrounding highlands continue to chart a different course. In March 2027 the working ranch and private reserve Hacienda Montezuma, located beneath the Tenorio Volcano (and normally reserved for exclusive buyouts), will launch the first in a series of wellness retreats bookable for up to 15 people. These will feature local practitioners leading equine therapy, meditation, and forest walks—all rooted in ancestral traditions. The region is also transitioning to a deforestation-free coffee model that is reshaping how one of Costa Rica's most important crops is both grown and experienced by visitors on educational tours. —Mark Johanson

Go for: chef-led experiences, new Cachapoal Valley bungalows, and up-and-coming wine scenes

In Chile's best winemaking regions, there's plenty of old and new. Case in point: Chile’s most extravagant wine hotel, VIK, expanded in 2026 with eight glass-mirrored bungalows and an art-filled wellness center, with five cabins set to open next in an oak forest on the property.

Chile’s central wine valleys have long been defined by their vines—emerald rows sprawling along riverbanks, blanketing a terrain reminiscent of the Mediterranean, yet hemmed between towering Andes and a thrashing Pacific. Recently, dynamic chefs from Santiago have begun adding their touch to the region, crafting new culinary tours and elevating the work of emerging bodegas and wineries. Kurt Schmidt is among them. He first rose to fame crafting nine-course tasting menus at Santiago’s 99 Restaurante, built around the traditional foodways of Chilean viticultural regions. In 2027 he’ll be teaming up with the rural tourism cooperative Ruta de los Abastos (“The Supply Route”) on menu-to-territory day tours that will begin at 99 and expand out to wine valleys like Huasco, Maule, and Aconcagua, where Schmidt has spent years building relationships with vintners, cheesemakers, foragers, and fisherfolk (later multiday itineraries are in the works). Conveniently, Santiago lies just south of the Maipo Valley, which is famed for bold Cabernet Sauvignons and also home to the striking new Centro del Vino from Concha y Toro, Latin America’s largest wine producer. The 129,000-square-foot facility features contemporary art installations, barrel-side tasting rooms, and an interactive wine museum, plus access to manicured gardens and (for an additional fee) the 19th-century mansion of founder Don Melchor.

If you have days to spare, consider heading three hours south to the Cachapoal Valley. Here, Chile’s most extravagant wine hotel, VIK, expanded in 2026 with eight glass-mirrored bungalows and an art-filled wellness center. Five cabins are next, set to open in an oak forest on the property, where winemaker Cristián Vallejo ages natural wine in clay amphorae. Continuing south, you can explore the next generation of experimental and low-intervention vino emerging from the neighboring Maule and Itata valleys, where Millennial and Gen Z winemakers are injecting fresh energy into one of South America's oldest regions at bodegas like González Bastías and Carter Mollenhauer. Add it all up and it makes for an epic wine country road trip.

As if that weren’t enough to keep you busy, know that excellent vino isn’t the only reason to dedicate your big vacation to Chile this year. Once you wrap up in Santiago, consider hopping over to Rapa Nui (Easter Island) for some extreme set-jetting. This remote Chilean territory in the Southeastern Pacific is the backdrop of Academy Award winner Martin McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, and it’s sure to become a rising star on more travelers’ itineraries this year. —Mark Johanson

Go for: new conservation-minded cruises, stargazing experiences, and an endless parade of wildlife

In 2027 National Geographic–Lindblad Expeditions will celebrate 60 years since Lars-Eric Lindblad introduced travelers to the Galápagos on the first nonscientific civilian expedition voyage, establishing the islands as a premier destination for conservation-minded exploration.

The Galápagos Islands, an archipelago of 13 major isles and over 100 rocks and inlets off Ecuador’s coast, have long attracted travelers seeking solitude and wildlife: endemic giant tortoises and marine iguanas, native scalloped hammerhead sharks, and blue-footed boobies, for starters. Nearly 97% of the Galápagos’ land area is a single national park. Visitor access remains tightly managed, making the destination one of the rare places where travelers can experience wildlife on nature’s terms (and, as scientists are learning, occasionally encounter new species, like the deep-sea Microeledone galapagensis, or blue octopus). In 2027 National Geographic–Lindblad Expeditions will celebrate 60 years since Lars-Eric Lindblad introduced travelers to the Galápagos on the first nonscientific civilian expedition voyage, establishing the islands as a premier destination for conservation-minded exploration. The brand doubled its Galápagos fleet in 2025 by adding the 16-guest catamaran Delfina and the 48-guest Gemini. In January 2027 the brand will launch Ultimate Galápagos, a 13-day itinerary aboard the 96-passenger Endeavour II that visits 11 islands including remote Genovesa, known for its red-footed booby colonies. Elsewhere, Natural Habitat Adventures’ Galápagos Tortoise Camp just transitioned to 100% solar power and introduced the Galápagos’ first fully electric panga (a small skiff for excursions)—part of trips booked aboard the brand’s Petrel luxury catamaran—reducing emissions for wildlife excursions and setting a new benchmark for sustainable travel in the destination. —Hannah Selinger

Go for: volcano trekking, peak birdwatching, price points that range from shoestring to big spender

Guatemala, beloved for its artisan heritage, birdwatching, and volcano trekking up peaks like the Volcán de Fuego (pictured), will continue to draw a wide range of travelers in 2027.

Long a backpacking destination on the Central America 101 route known as the Gringo Trail, Guatemala is an increasingly popular destination for a generation of young travelers seeking slower, more enriching tourism that won’t break the bank. INGUAT, the Guatemala Institute of Tourism, says that arrival numbers support the TikTok thesis—and are only projected to increase. Some of the appeal is timeless: Guatemalan day-to-day life is deeply steeped in ancient heritage and culture. Sprawling artisan markets like Nim Po’t in Antigua offer easy access to hand-carved and painted wood animal masks, for example, but deeper dives are offered by Antigua-based textile studio Luna Zorro, which organizes craft retreats throughout the country. The brand’s recently opened La Valiente (February 2026) is a two-bedroom guesthouse in the heart of the city, and almost everything at the property—from the bedding to ceramics—is artisan-made by local creators. The country’s natural beauty is also an evergreen draw, but as younger generations embrace the mores—and aesthetics—of hiking (and even birdwatching), trails like the rigorous two-day Acatenango trek are list-toppers in the central highland region that is ripe with some of the 780 species recorded in Guatemala. Many choose to continue to the Tikal National Park in the northeast, where 3,000-year-old ruins of the Maya city sit amid a lush green jungle setting. At the park’s recently reopened Conservation and Research Center, visitors can observe the behind-the-scenes preservation process of ruins and artifacts, only now visible to the public. It all makes for welcome news that Guatemala is getting even easier to access: Frontier is offering daily, seasonal, nonstop service from Los Angeles to Guatemala City from December 17 until January 4, if you need a last-minute holiday getaway, and United Airlines has a permanent direct route from Houston. —Anna Zou

Go for: untamed rainforest, immersive eco-lodges, and easier-than-ever access

Guyana still remains 85% forested, with sites like the impressive Kaieteur Falls—among the world's strongest single-drop waterfalls—awaiting travelers.

Guyana, South America’s only country with English as its official language, celebrated six decades of nationhood this May. Yet from a small plane bound for Kaieteur Falls, one of the most powerful single-drop waterfalls in the world, the lush rainforest below appears several geological eras older. Perhaps it’s no wonder; an impressive 85% of this country remains forested.

Most travelers start in the coastal city of Georgetown, where the country’s Caribbean identity is tangible in the annual Mashramani carnival (every February), vibrant Stabroek Market, and Gothic St. George’s Anglican Cathedral, which is made of wood. But journeys quickly turn toward the rainforest and savanna, with Kaieteur as their most dramatic introduction. At the falls, the Potaro River drops 741 feet from a sandstone ledge—more than four times Niagara’s height—yet just over 8,000 people see it each year, usually on a day flight from Georgetown. A fuller interior journey requires a separate, multiday circuit through Iwokrama International Centre for Rainforest Conservation and Development (IIC), a nearly million-acre reserve managed alongside 20 Indigenous communities, and into the North Rupununi, a landscape of savanna, wetlands, and river villages where Indigenous-led conservation becomes part of the itinerary. For in-the-know travelers, right now—when a host of new expeditions and accommodations have risen to meet vanguard voyage interest—is the time to go.

On that circuit, three conservation-linked stays give travelers a direct role in the work. Atta Rainforest Lodge is the base for Iwokrama’s canopy walkway, suspended 100 feet above the forest floor and managed by the reserve in partnership with Makushi communities and local tourism operators. Further into the North Rupununi, road and river lead to Rewa Eco-Lodge, operated by Rewa Village, where anglers help measure and tag arapaima before release. Another tributary leads to Yupukari’s Caiman House, a village-run guesthouse and research station where visitors help researchers study black caiman after dark. The community also raises yellow-spotted Amazon river turtles for release. Reaching these stays still requires small planes and long road-and-river transfers, though one important link is easing: In August 2026, Jags Aviation added a 19-seat turboprop service four days a week between Georgetown’s Eugene F. Correia International Airport and Lethem.

Back in Georgetown, the arrival of international hotel brands marks a new era at the start and finish of any trip. The 152-room AC Hotel opened in December 2025, with the 172-room Four Points by Sheraton following in April 2026. A Hilton resort is due on the seafront in 2028. And there are more reasons to linger in 2027: From October 8 to October 17, the capital will also host Carifesta XVI, which will return the Caribbean Festival of Arts to its 1972 birthplace, promising a cultural counterpart to the wilderness of the interior. —Paul Jebara

Go for: new off-season expeditions, and a slate of fresh lodges

For the first time in 2026, tour company Hielo & Aventura offered its popular ice hiking excursion atop the Perito Moreno Glacier—in winter.

Los Glaciares National Park, with its toothy granite spires, windswept steppe, and glaciers that crack and roar as they calve into milky-blue lakes, has long been the crown jewel of Argentine Patagonia. Yet its main gateway town, El Calafate, hasn’t seen a new luxury hotel in over two decades. That changes in December 2026 with Explora El Calafate, an all-inclusive 20-key lodge snaking across a Patagonian estancia near Lake Argentino. The hotel’s design leans into soothing earth tones—with giant windows framing distant glaciers—while menus highlight Patagonian lamb, trout, and wine. Guides take guests on 30 different adventures out to remote wildlands like the ice fields of Brazo Sur or the bird sanctuary of Laguna Nimez. Explora will simultaneously open a second property just across the Chilean border in its private Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve, further linking the two destinations by building out a binational circuit.

Meanwhile, southern Patagonia is shedding its reputation as a summer-only destination. Awasi Patagonia, near Torres del Paine, will now remain open through the 2027 winter season—prime time for puma safaris—while ecotourism operator Chile Nativo extols the virtue of the offseason with its Winter W Trek, tracing the iconic route past Paine Grande and the Grey Glacier in the region’s quieter season. The momentum is even greater in Los Glaciares. In 2026 park concessionaire Hielo & Aventura, responding to greater off-season demand that can help disperse the annual tourist traffic, operated its popular ice hiking excursion atop the Perito Moreno Glacier during the winter for the first time. Unlike most Patagonian mountain towns, El Calafate doesn’t shut down when crowds depart, which means there are still hot chocolates to be had after a day on the ice. —Mark Johanson

Go for: a buyout villa in jaguar country, and groundbreaking conservation efforts

Caiman’s new private villa, Cordilheira, has seven bungalows with buyout options for larger groups, offering a new way to stay in this wildlife-rich corner of Brazil.

For flora and fauna lovers headed to South America, the Amazon has long been the marquee trip. But further south, where the waters of the Amazon trickle down into the world’s largest tropical wetland, something different awaits. The Pantanal stretches across 42 million acres in Brazil, Bolivia, and Paraguay. In comparison to the Amazon, it’s a bit more arid, with strong cowboy culture, and the foliage is sparser, making this a great place to spot jaguars in the wild. This is in no small part thanks to important conservation work that has taken place over decades. At the upscale Caiman Pantanal, a trailblazing safari stay in the Brazilian Pantanal, jaguar rescue group Onçafari has an on-site location, allowing guests at the all-inclusive property to explore 131,000 acres of land with the big cat experts who have meticulously tagged and tracked dozens of them. Caiman’s new private villa, Cordilheira, was unveiled in June 2026. It brings together seven bungalows (private infinity pools included) that fit up to 16 people, making it possible for families and groups to have a buyout experience as they spend days tracking jaguars—and tapirs, and giant anteaters, and capybaras—before evenings filled with Brazilian barbecue and folk music under the stars. Operators like Natural Habitat Adventures can continue the journey northbound to destinations like Porto Jofre, where cat sightings happen by boat on the river, and jaguars can be seen chasing caimans at the water’s edge. The conservation work required to protect this rare natural landscape and its fauna is ongoing, but new projects like the Jaguar Rivers Initiative, announced in fall 2025, prove the only way is forward. This new coalition, which connects the aforementioned Onçafari with Kristine Tompkins’s Fundación Rewilding Argentina, Nativa in Bolivia, and Fundación Moisés Bertoni in Paraguay, hopes to better link and restore various jaguar habitats. The goal is, of course, ecological first and foremost—but if the preservation work in Pantanal has taught us anything so far, it’s that great conservation can lead to great wildlife experiences. —Megan Spurrell

Go for: uncrowded surf spots, a noteworthy beach hideaway, and plenty of seafood

Opened in February 2026, resort Inkaterra Cabo Blanco overlooks the Pacific Ocean on a coastline frequented by Marilyn Monroe and Ernest Hemingway.

The seaside towns and villages of Peru's northern shore are known for their seafood dishes, such as picante de mariscos and raw-fish tiraditos.

On Peru’s northern coast, life moves slowly in the seaside towns and fishing villages that have long drawn a quiet trickle of visitors including surfers chasing mythical waves, Limeños lured by closer-to-the-equator sun and tranquility, and culinary-minded travelers who know that nowhere else does seafood quite like this part of the country. In the past few years, an increasingly stylish crop of Airbnbs have popped up—like Kahu Beach House in Los Órganos, where modern design uses endemic natural materials and where fantastic surf breaks are visible from your breakfast table. The more recent resort opening of Inkaterra Cabo Blanco in February 2026 has shone an even brighter spotlight: On the same stretch of sand where Marilyn Monroe and Ernest Hemingway vacationed in the 1950s, this contemporary beachside stay with just 13 rooms is an elegant approach to the destination’s barefoot ease, refined coastal dining, and experiences that range from a day on the water with a local fishing collective to surfing and kitesurfing lessons just steps from the private plunge pools. As for the region’s culinary offerings? You won’t have to look hard. This sun-baked stretch of coast is where carne seca dries on clotheslines and makes its way into seco de chavela (a pounded beef and plantain dish bursting with chile), and where Peruvian classics like conchas a la parmesana (scallops baked with cheese) are remixed using conchas negras, a unique shellfish found in the mangroves of Tumbes, near the border with Ecuador. Hearty dishes like picante de mariscos, a seafood stew, sit side by side with chilled raw-fish tiraditos that fly close to the sun in their spice. —Megan Spurrell

Go for: kitesurfing for pros—and newbies—in a fishing village now home to quietly luxurious stays

With the charm of a fishing village and powerful winds, Preá has become an ideal kitesurfing destination.

From spa treatments to horseback riding and yoga Preá's hotel scene brings a bevy of activities to travelers.

Preá has the unmistakable charm of a Brazilian fishing village—a seemingly endless shoreline, a sandy-street village center, and beachfront restaurants serving fresh-caught seafood—with one major difference: wind, and lots of it. From July through early January, this sleepy town catches some of the world’s most consistently powerful gusts, the kind kitesurfers cross oceans for. Now, with the sport growing in popularity, beginners are starting to come too, bringing with them an exciting new energy. Kitesurfing has become so popular among Brazil’s well-heeled travelers that Marco Dalpozzo, a partner at the pioneering pousada Rancho do Peixe, dubbed the sport “the new golf, the new tennis, the new skiing.” Learning takes some commitment: First-timers start on the sand before progressing into the water, with a full beginner course happening over several days. Yet new kitesurfing locations are making it easier than ever for newcomers to join the scene.

While the famed Jericoacoara next door is known for its lively nightlife and parties, Preá’s new crop of high-end boutique hotels and villas offers a more exclusive take on barefoot luxury. Think ocean-facing rooms, intimate private villas, and seaside bungalows paired with their own kite schools, full-service spas, and feet-in-the-sand restaurants. Whether you’re up for braving the wind or not, there is plenty else to do in terms of both adventure and restorative wellness.

Preá offers easy access to the landscapes that made neighboring Jericoacoara famous. Set off by buggy or quad to explore the region’s enormous sand dunes and freshwater lagoons that naturally occur between them, or visit the otherworldly Jericoacoara National Park. Back in Preá, book a treatment at L’Occitane spa at the Preabeach Boutique Hotel, take advantage of the yoga offerings at Hotel Kabana, or horseback ride along the shore. By sunset, everyone gathers on the beach to watch the last kiters streak across the water as what looks like a giant ball of fire slips into the ocean. Later, dinner can range from candlelit seaside dining to charming restaurants like Casinha in the rustic village center, where flip-flops are acceptable attire.

The wind is bringing in major investments too. Grupo Carnaúba is building what it envisions as the wind sports equivalent to an Alpine ski resort. Its members-only Carnaúba Wind House, opened in 2024, offers bungalow stays with a kite center, beach club, restaurant, and freshwater lagoon, while the larger Vila Carnaúba development is adding more luxury residences and beach tennis facilities. The biggest arrival yet comes in 2028, when Anantara opens its first property in the Americas: A beachfront resort complete with its own signature spa and dedicated kitesurfing school. —Carla Vianna

Go for: cheffy restaurant openings, a revitalized downtown, and a lineup of literary festivals

Bachour by Mata (above) is pastry chef Antonio Bachour's first Latin American pastry shop—and it joins a wave of buzzy culinary openings that have made this city an increasingly hot food destination.

São Paulo is a city for those with an appetite—for business, culture, and, of course, food. Brazil’s largest and most frenetic metropolis is home to some of Brazil’s most extraordinary architectural landmarks, from Lina Bo Bardi’s museum of art (MASP) to Paulo Mendes da Rocha’s reimagined Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo. Meanwhile, the restaurant landscape has never been more exciting: São Paulo is now home to the only two restaurants in the Southern Hemisphere recently awarded three Michelin stars: Tuju and Evvai.

That momentum is reshaping the city well beyond its established dining districts: Near Avenida Paulista, the Mata São Paulo hospitality complex has gathered some of the city’s buzziest names, including Mata Città, Korean barbecue spot Lavva, and pastry chef Antonio Bachour, who opened his first Latin American pastry shop Bachour by Mata here, all in one place. More is on the way, including a new boteco, Á Brasileira, from Janaína Torres (named the World’s Best Female Chef in 2024 by World’s 50 Best). Her beloved Bar da Dona Onça, on the ground floor of Oscar Niemeyer’s sinuous Copan building, has itself gained new neighbors, including seafood-focused Brisa do Barú and Tem Umami!, an ice cream shop with a near-permanent line out the door. Together with an observation deck, the new arrivals are turning the 1,160-apartment Modernist landmark into one of downtown’s liveliest destinations.

Also inside the Copan is Livraria Megafauna, part of a new wave of independent bookstores bringing literary life back to São Paulo’s streets. Its Poesia no Centro poetry festival, returning in April 2027, has already become a fixture on the city’s cultural calendar; meanwhile the growing Feira do Livro, organized by literary magazine Quatro Cinco Um, is expected to draw around 100,000 people to the Praça Charles Miller in May 2027, and it will nearly double the space devoted to its mostly independent publishers.

That literary boom is part of a broader cultural surge, with major events like SP-Arte in April and the Bienal de São Paulo—Latin America’s largest visual arts event—returning to Ibirapuera Park in September. The expansion of Museu de Arte de São Paulo Assis Chateaubriand, the city’s landmark art museum, only adds to the momentum: Its newest building, opened in March 2025, increased exhibition space by more than 60% and made room for new shows and works from the collection previously kept out of public view. —Rafael Tonon

#6162. A total solar eclipse, the real-life Tatooine and crowd-free Roman ruins: The ultimate 7-day Tunisia road trip

American citizens do not need a visa to visit Tunisia for stays of 90 days or less, just a valid passport with at least six months’ validity and one blank page.

Tipping is appreciated but not expected, unlike in many neighboring countries such as Egypt. I generally added 10% to restaurant bills and rounded up taxi fares. For my tours, I tipped between 20 and 50 dinars, depending on the length and whether there was a separate driver.

Tunisia is essentially bilingual, with most people speaking Arabic and French fluently. In most tourist destinations and hotels, people spoke English, but the French I remembered from high school did help me in a few situations.

Ride-hailing apps like Uber are not available in Tunisia. Taxis are available, but ask for the fare upfront or confirm the meter is turned on before getting in. I pre-booked airport transfers through my hotels to avoid negotiating prices on the spot.

For my road trip, I found it easy to rent and drive a car throughout Tunisia. There is a major highway with toll booths running north to south through the country. In more rural parts of the south, roads are still well maintained — just watch out for sneaky speed bumps. All my hotels featured easy parking, but keep in mind that hotels inside medinas may not be accessible by car or might require navigating very narrow streets. Driving behavior is more erratic in Tunis, but generally, I found the rest of the country easy to drive in.

To visit mosques, you’ll need to cover your knees and shoulders — as well as hair if you’re a woman — but coverings are provided free of charge at most. To adapt to the heat and sun, wear loose layers of light-colored linen and be sure to bring a hat.

The U.S. Department of State lists Tunisia as a Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution, which contains areas with a higher security risk, the same as Turkey and Egypt. Save for a few curious stares from men and one overzealous self-appointed medina guide who demanded a tip, I felt perfectly safe as a solo female traveler. It is best to avoid wandering around medinas after dark since most shops and restaurants are closed anyway. I felt most comfortable with pre-arranged guides, but more because they knew exactly where to go, and I didn’t have to navigate things solo.

For the most comfortable weather with a low chance of rain, visit Tunisia between March and May or between October and November. If you do decide to visit for the Aug. 2, 2027 solar eclipse, keep in mind it can get up to 120 degrees Fahrenheit in the middle of the day out in the desert. During my visit in August, I also experienced rolling blackouts and bottled water shortages.

Tunisia is about to have a big year. On the morning of Aug. 2, 2027, a total solar eclipse will cut a path across the central part of the North African nation, bringing several minutes of darkness to sites like the ancient Roman amphitheater in El Jem, the Great Mosque of Kairouan and the dramatic Sahara Desert dunes and canyons surrounding Tozeur.

The latter will also draw “Star Wars” fans to many of the Tatooine filming locations to mark the franchise’s 50th anniversary of the movie’s release in 2027. The capital of Tunis isn’t in the path of totality, but any trip in 2027 should also include a stop in the picturesque cliffside village of Sidi Bou Said, which UNESCO recently added to its World Heritage list, joining other culturally significant sites like the Medina of Tunis and the Archaeological Site of Carthage.

This 7-day itinerary covers a tour of Tunisia’s most important cultural and historic landmarks in a road trip from Tunis to Tozeur and back, plus tips for where to be during the 2027 eclipse and how to maximize the perks and benefits of the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) along the way.

Currently, there are no nonstop flights between the United States and Tunisia, so you’ll need to plan for at least one layover before connecting to Tunis-Carthage International Airport (TUN), the country’s largest airport.

I flew to TUN on Air France via Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), since I’m loyal to the SkyTeam alliance and it offered the most frequent connections. However, if you’re loyal to another airline alliance, you can also find connections to TUN on Lufthansa via Frankfurt, ITA via Rome, Royal Air Maroc via Casablanca and Turkish Airlines via Istanbul.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: When booking flights, check the Chase Travel℠ portal to see what routes and airlines are available to book using the Points Boost feature. I found several business-class fares offering the maximum Points Boost value of 2 cents per point. I ultimately transferred 142,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Air France-KLM Flying Blue after finding an amazing round-trip business-class fare directly on the Air France website, yielding a value of 5.83 cents per mile.

I landed in Tunis around 5 p.m. after a red-eye flight from New York and a relaxed connection in Paris.

A pre-arranged car transfer whisked me to the Four Seasons Hotel Tunis, a luxury beachfront resort in the suburb of Gammarth, about 30 minutes from the airport. Upon arrival, staff greeted me warmly and took me directly to my upgraded Deluxe Sea-View Room for an in-room check-in. The spacious room had a balcony overlooking the Mediterranean, a walk-in closet and a marble bathroom with a separate tub and a shower.

After a quick rinse, I wandered down to Blu, the hotel’s alfresco poolside restaurant, where I enjoyed a refreshing salad of a soft local cheese, tomatoes, onions and peppers served with a glass of Tunisian rosé. Since it was my first day in the country, the friendly staff made sure I tried some spicy Tunisian harissa, a smoky chili paste drizzled in olive oil that I sopped up with fluffy squares of focaccia.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Book the Four Seasons Hotel Tunis through The Edit to use one of the twice-annual, up-to-$250 credits toward prepaid hotel stays of two or more nights reserved through Chase Travel. By booking through The Edit, I also received other perks like complimentary hotel breakfast for two and up to $100 property credit, which I used for meals but could have used toward spa treatments like the ceremonial hammam experience, which comes out to approximately $100.

Since I only had one full day in Tunis, I headed out bright and early for a private tour of the capital’s major sites, booked through Chase Travel with Didon Tours. My guide, Baligh, and a private driver picked me up for a full 8-hour day that included lunch and fascinating storytelling about the city’s ancient and modern history and politics.

To beat the cruise groups and midday heat, we visited the ancient ruins of Carthage first, taking in the views from Byrsa Hill before heading down to the circular Punic port and the massive seaside complex of the Baths of Antoninus.

From there, we drove to the charming blue-and-white village of Sidi Bou Said, Tunisia’s newest UNESCO World Heritage site, for fresh juice and almond cakes at Cafe des Delices and iconic views of the beach below. While we didn’t have much time to browse the cliffside town’s shops, I did pick up some handmade souvenirs at the ceramic store at 16 Rue Habib Thameur.

For lunch, we stopped in the coastal suburb of Le Goulette at Restaurant La Victoire for a traditional Tunisian meal of brick à l’oeuf, a deep-fried pastry stuffed with egg, tuna and onion and a freshly grilled dorade fish served with rice and carrots.

Next, we turned inland toward the western side of the city to visit the Bardo Museum, set in a former palace and home to the world’s largest collection of Roman mosaics. (Don’t miss the mosaic of the Roman poet Virgil, flanked by the muses of history and tragedy, as it’s considered to be the Mona Lisa of Tunisia.)

Finally, we hit the medina of Tunis, where we visited the courtyard of the Zitouna Mosque and made a quick pass through the souk's meandering lanes before returning to the hotel for a much-deserved swim in the indoor pool and a nap before a quiet room-service dinner.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Earn 8 points per dollar spent on Chase Travel purchases, including activities and tours like the one I booked. Those with more time can add another day in Tunis and split this itinerary into two for a more relaxed pace in each location.

Around midday, I returned to the airport to pick up a rental car from Avis and set the GPS to drive two hours south to Kairouan, a UNESCO-recognized city famous for its picturesque medina and Great Mosque, which dates to the 9th century AD. While Kairouan is considered one of the holy cities of Islam, film buffs may recognize it from “Raiders of the Lost Ark,” where it stood in for 1930s Cairo. It lies along the northern boundary of the 2027 solar eclipse’s path of totality.

La Kasbah Hotel, booked via Chase Travel, provided a soft landing with its private parking lot, pool and strong air conditioning. The shops and sites in the medina tend to close in the late afternoon, so if you arrive after then, plan on a quiet night in the hotel, cooling off in the pool or lounging on woven rugs in its vintage café, drinking mint tea.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Pay for car rentals with Chase Sapphire Reserve to receive primary auto rental coverage (just be sure to decline the agency's collision insurance). Though I didn’t end up needing it, I had peace of mind knowing I was covered for up to $75,000 of theft or collision damage to the rental car.

Having arrived the previous afternoon after the mosque closed, I went first thing the next morning to admire the column-lined courtyard and three-tiered minaret before the tour groups arrived. The ticket to the mosque also included admission to the nearby Sidi Abid el Ghariani Mausoleum, built in the Moorish style with black and white marble arches. A few doors down, I stopped by the former home of the governor of Kairouan, an ornately decorated mansion that now serves as a rug shop. While I wasn’t in the market for a carpet, I enjoyed the architecture and left with a handwoven scarf for 40 dinars ($14).

After checking out, I hit the road again for the 4.5-hour drive south to Tozeur, a city in the heart of the Sahara Desert. Though I drove straight through, making brief stops at gas stations along the way, it’s also possible to break up the drive with stops at either the well-preserved archaeological site of Sbeitla or the Roman baths of Gafsa.

Just be mindful of timing: I wouldn’t recommend driving at night. Though the roads are well-maintained, speed bumps are common and harder to spot after dark.

Once in Tozeur, I checked into Dar Saida Beya, a traditional Tunisian guesthouse, booked through Chase Travel. After a long drive, I had a quiet evening to walk around and explore the nearby old town center.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Though the upscale Mora Sahara Tozeur resort west of town isn’t bookable via Chase Travel currently, it’s still possible to earn 4 points per dollar spent on direct hotel bookings made with the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

The Atlas Mountains meet the salt flats and sands of the Sahara Desert in Tozeur, creating an otherworldly landscape that inspired many film directors. Most notably, the canyons and dunes around Tozeur served as the filming location for the desert planet of Tatooine in the “Star Wars” movies. The epic sci-fi series is celebrating the 50th anniversary of its release in 2027, and fans can experience the eclipse from here, since Tozeur falls along the southern boundary of the path of totality.

I booked a 7-hour tour with Attractive Discoveries via Chase Travel to see everything the area had to offer. Before diving into the area’s cinematic legacy, my driver and guide, Firas, began the day at Chebika Oasis, where a 45-minute hike wound through the ruins of a former Berber village and down to the oasis and its waterfall.

Our next stop was the Grand Canyon of Tunisia, Mides Canyon, roughly a mile from the Algerian border and featured in films like “The English Patient.” During the 30-minute hike along the dry riverbed, I spotted no fewer than six falcons diving in and out of the cliff face while hunting.

To avoid the worst heat of the day, the tour included a break from 1 to 5 p.m., during which we stopped to pick some dates from my guide’s family’s oasis of palm trees. I also tried a makloub sandwich filled with chicken, cheese and harissa and took a short nap.

At 5 p.m. on the dot, Firas picked me up again in his 4x4 to head out into the desert to watch the sunset over the dunes. Along our drive, we spotted a herd of camels, stopped to climb the Ong Jmal or “Camel’s Neck” rock formation and did some adrenaline-inducing 4x4 driving. We arrived at the remaining film sets that served as the desert trading post of Mos Espa in “The Phantom Menace” just before sunset.

To cap off the day, we drank fresh mint tea with almonds — a local treat — and watched the sun set behind the dunes before heading back into town.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Put the card's up to $300 annual credit to work on travel purchases like the tour I booked. The credit is applied automatically to eligible purchases each account anniversary year.

The biggest Star Wars fans may want to stay another day to visit other nearby filming locations, such as Sidi Bouhlel Canyon and the Lars family homestead exterior near the town of Nefta.

Since I had another 4.5-hour drive ahead of me that day, I left around 11 a.m. to drive back north to the city of El Jem via Chott el Djerid. Before heading off across the massive salt lake, I filled up my gas tank and packed snacks for the long drive since there aren’t many places to stop in the first couple of hours.

Built about 1,800 years ago, the Roman amphitheater of El Jem is roughly 70% the size of Rome’s amphitheater but has significantly fewer crowds and offers wide-open access to each level — even the underground level where animals were kept before they fought gladiators.

After checking into Hotel Julius, booked through Chase Travel, I dropped my bags and took the five-minute walk to the amphitheater before it closed. The 20 dinar ($7) ticket includes entrance to both the amphitheater and the nearby El Jem Archaeological Museum on the same day. Since I arrived a little later in the afternoon, I went to the museum first thing the next morning and justified the extra $7 by spending a leisurely morning taking in the incredibly detailed mosaics without being rushed.

El Jem falls within the path of totality for the 2027 solar eclipse, so history buffs may want to make this city their home base for the celestial event.

Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Tunisia is still a predominantly cash-based society, so it may be hard to find restaurants that accept cards. I couldn’t earn 3 points per dollar spent on dining worldwide with my Chase Sapphire Reserve in El Jem, but the two fricassee (fried dough buns stuffed with egg, tuna, potato and harissa) I ordered at a street food stall on the way back from the amphitheater only cost 7 cents total (yes, really), so I wasn’t worried about missing out on too many points.

After checking out the museum, I loaded up my rental car one last time for the two-hour drive back to Tunis. Those with more time and desire to sit on the beach than I did could easily add a day or two in the coastal town of Hammamet, which sits about two-thirds of the way back to Tunis from El Jem.

Once I handed off my rental car keys at the airport, I met the taxi driver I had prearranged with my final hotel, Dar Ben Gacem, a traditional guesthouse in the Tunis medina. Since my tour of Tunis at the beginning of the trip only included a brief visit to the medina, I was glad to have the rest of the afternoon and evening to poke around the shops and alleys of the historic city center and do some final souvenir shopping before flying home the next day.

Keep in mind that most stalls in the medina are open from around 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with more closed on Fridays and Sundays, so plan your visit accordingly. (Plus, many restaurants are closed for dinner on Sunday nights as well.)

Though some flights depart in the evening, I opted to take a connecting flight back to Paris in the morning and stay an extra night to avoid a rushed final day.

During my week-long road trip, I explored Tunisia’s ancient ruins, UNESCO-recognized Islamic architecture and otherworldly desert landscapes, many of which lie in the path of totality of the 2027 solar eclipse. Booking through Chase Travel maximized my Ultimate Rewards earnings, while the card benefits helped offset travel expenses along the way, like the $300 annual travel credit on tours, The Edit perks and $250 statement credit at the Four Seasons and primary rental car coverage through Avis. When I returned to New York, I was glad I had enrolled in Global Entry before my trip. The Sapphire Reserve's $120 Global Entry application fee statement credit helped offset the cost, and the program made reentering the U.S. much easier.

#6161. Independents decide the election, again!

A group of new senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer’s office in Washington on Monday. The large class of incoming Democratic senators was propelled by votes from independents, Winston writes. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

According to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

Independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also shows that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they showed up.

Looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

For example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

Despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

Overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

Clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

In the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

According to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top issue concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent said it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

The president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent said his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

Trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic issues and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

Neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls showed that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

Independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

At a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent said the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

Democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

David Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy issues, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

#6160. Avelo Airlines Launches 16 New Routes In 4 Weeks: See Full List Now

Newish airlines tend to grow strongly, benefiting from the revenue, unit cost, market share, and competitive advantages of doing so. For example, five-year-old Breeze Airways' passenger traffic grew by 47% in the 12 months to August. In distinct contrast, Avelo Airlines' passenger numbers fell by 15%.

Avelo has been struggling recently as it seeks to find what works. As such, it has cut many routes, including its entire international operation, and removed multiple served airports from its map. However, the airline, whose fleet consists of 17 Boeing 737-700s and 737-800s, will launch 16 new routes in November and December. Still, compared to the same two months in 2025, 30+ routes have been removed.

Analysis of the airline's schedule submission to Cirium Diio has been explored. This compared the budget operator's network between January 2025 and October 2026 with what is set to operate in November 2026. The process found that the following ten routes will launch. This includes a return to the Caribbean. However, as the two routes will be to Aguadilla, Puerto Rico, they'll be domestic. Aguadilla is a brand-new destination for Avelo.

Half of the entries will be from McKinney (DTX), where Avelo's latest base just opened. Located around 34 miles (54 km) north of downtown Dallas, McKinney's passenger terminal opened on November 11. Not surprisingly, that was exactly when the ultra-low-cost carrier Avelo began flying from the airport. In doing so, the carrier now serves three airports in the Lone Star State: Dallas/Fort Worth, McKinney, and Houston Intercontinental.

McKinney is near Dallas, Concord is near Charlotte, and Lakeland is between Orlando and Tampa

Initially, Avelo had one aircraft based at McKinney. However, that'll jump to two this month and, eventually, three. When a trio of aircraft are stationed there, nearly a third of the budget carrier's fleet will be there, which perhaps illustrates the challenges that it has faced.

Simple Flying's Live Flight Tracker shows that the N801XT and N803XT, both of which are 737-800s, will be there this week, although the specific airframes may change in the future. Generally, each aircraft has four legs per day. For example, on November 19, the 20.8-year-old N803XT, which is ex-Turkish Airlines, will fly McKinney-Orlando-McKinney-Las Vegas-McKinney.

As part of the announcement, Allegiant will pull out of Chicago Midway. Find out more now!

They will all be from McKinney and, like the five mentioned earlier, will be brand-new markets. Significantly, it'll be the first time that Avelo has flown to Denver, albeit only with one route and four weekly departures. It'll mark Avelo's return to Colorado after last flying there in September 2024 from Burbank to Colorado Springs.

Previously, the airline also flew from Burbank to Grand Junction and from Burbank and Las Vegas to Fort Collins. The new route contributes to Avelo having a record number of flights to Atlanta, the world's busiest airport for passengers but not for flights

However, context is needed. Only three markets will exist: Lakeland, McKinney, and Tweed New Haven. Previously, Avelo flew there from Wilmington, Delaware. Things are not this simple, as it appears that Lakeland-Atlanta service will end in early January 2027. No flights are scheduled beyond there, but that might change.

US Department of Transportation (DOT) information currently extends to August 2026. In the 12 months to that summer month, Avelo transported nearly 2.3 million round-trip passengers. Compared to the prior 12 months, traffic fell by 15%. While not a like-for-like comparison, Breeze grew by 47%.

Avelo's average load factor is 77.7%. While that is low compared to many budget operators around the world, it is relatively normal for US airlines. As the number of seats for sale fell by 16%, the smaller reduction in traffic (-15%) means that the load factor improved to the highest level since the 12 months to August 2023. What is not known is how fares changed.

#6159. Aer Lingus to Introduce First Premium Economy Cabin

Aer Lingus is moving to upgrade the widebody aircraft operating its transatlantic network.

The carrier said Wednesday that it will introduce its first-ever Premium Economy cabin on 10 refurbished Airbus A330s. The aircraft will also get upgraded Business Class seats – now enclosed as suites – and an improved Economy section.

“[This] is a transformation of the entire experience across our A330 fleet, elevating Business Class, Economy, and, for the first time in Aer Lingus history, introducing Premium Economy,” CEO Lynne Embleton said in a news release. “We want to give our customers greater choice, comfort, and connectivity while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus.”

The upgraded Business Class will have 28 Collins Elevation suites in a 1-2-1 configuration, giving each passenger direct aisle access. Each seat will have a fully flat bed, a closing door, enhanced bedding, and “well-being amenities.” A self-service snack and refreshment bar will also be available.

The carrier will also roll out new Economy seats with more personal space and six-way adjustable leather headrests.

New interior elements will tie the three cabins together, officials said. Plans call for mood lighting, artwork reflecting Irish landscapes, and custom fabrics in colors inspired by the sea.

All seats will have larger 4K high-definition entertainment screens, Bluetooth headphone connectivity, USB-C charging ports, and access to Starlink wireless internet. Starlink is already available across all of Aer Lingus’ transatlantic routes.

The first of the overhauled A330s will reenter service in October 2027, flying between Dublin and New York-JFK. The new cabin experience will become available on additional North American routes as work on the remaining A330s is completed.

Aer Lingus serves a total of 20 destinations across the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, including Boston, Newark, New Jersey, Miami, Los Angeles, Toronto, and Cancún.

#6158. Where to go in 2027

Learn how to get started earning and redeeming rewards so you can make the most of your everyday spending.

See how far your points, miles and dollars go in TPG's first loyalty report.

See how TPG ranks the top US airlines for 2026.

Curated annually by TPG’s team of travel experts, this year’s Where to Go list highlights particularly exciting moments happening across the globe in 2027, including hotly anticipated and fabulous new hotels, milestone museum openings, travel-worthy celestial events, new UNESCO designations, new flight routes, major sporting events and so much more. And for 2027, we’ve pulled out all the stops: Below, you can explore our new interactive map displaying the 22 destinations that earned a spot on our list.

Now more than ever, exploring new and familiar destinations fosters curiosity, connectedness, and, perhaps most importantly, compassion. It’s time to put those hard-earned points and miles toward your dream trip — and we’ve got just the ticket.

Epic celestial events and ancient landmarks with no galaxy far, far away required.

Caribbean luxury that rewards every dollar you spend.

Best in July through August + December through March

New sightseeing trains and upscale points hotels make Japan’s stunning northern island even more alluring in 2027.

For those who want to experience Hokkaido’s beautiful countryside by train, Hokkaido Railway Company will debut two scenic tourist trains in 2027: the Red Star luxury train in February, when the region is blanketed in Hokkaido’s signature fluffy snow, and the Blue Star premium class train in June, just in time for Hokkaido’s lavender season.

And for skiers and snowboarders who are looking to experience Hokkaido’s incredible winter sports scene, Moxy Niseko will debut in late 2026, just in time for the start of ski season. Other exciting Niseko openings to look forward to in the coming years include Six Senses Niseko and an Aman property. In nearby Sapporo, new and forthcoming points hotels are plentiful, too: 2025 saw the opening of the InterContinental Sapporo, and both Hyatt Centric and Fairmont are planned for 2027 into 2028. -⁠Ellie Nan Storck

World-class dining and hotels to help fans refuel between Women’s World Cup matches.

One of the most accessible host cities of the Women’s World Cup is also among the most captivating. Beyond the pitch, visitors can experience the city’s dining renaissance, the long-awaited Museum of Image and Sound and the one of the oldest national history museums in the Americas, recently reopened after a 2018 fire. Plus, Rio (and nearby Maricá) is the midst of a luxury hotel boom, with exciting points properties opening over the coming years. December will bring the opening of Accor’s Sofitel Rio de Janeiro Ipanema, and over the next few years, Marriott will debut an eco-luxe Ritz Carlton Reserve and an all-inclusive JW Marriott in Maricá. -⁠Rachel Craft

Best in March through May + October through November

A perennial favorite is experiencing a luxury hotel boom.

Mexico’s massive capital never lacked excellent hotel options, but a recent slate of renovations and openings has us more excited than ever to revisit the city. The St. Regis Mexico City completed a multimillion dollar renovation with Frida Kahlo-inspired design elements in Sept. 2026. Hyatt loyalists can look forward to the February opening of the colorful new Standard Hotel in the Tabacalera neighborhood, followed by the April debut of the luxe Park Hyatt in Polanco. Other upcoming projects to look forward to include a Mama Shelter (part of the ALL Accor hotel loyalty program) in the heart of Roma Norte, set to open by the end of 2026, as well as Pendry Mexico City and Rosewood Mexico City, both planned for 2027. -⁠Lyndsey Matthews

The perfect mix of new luxury hotels, a distinct wine scene and endless opportunities to get outside.

In the Texas Hill Country, charming towns steeped in German culture are surrounded by award-winning wineries, idyllic swimming holes and Main Streets packed with restaurants, shops and some of the friendliest people in the Lone Star State. Near Fredericksburg, the epicenter of the Hill Country’s must-visit charm, Waldorf Astoria is opening its first Texas property, while Aman has plans for a secluded ranch retreat of its own. Add mouthwatering barbecue, legendary live music, popular rivers to float and an expanding Austin-Bergstrom International Airport (AUS), and there are more reasons than ever to head for the hills. -⁠Tanner Saunders

Rich in natural beauty, this coastal California town is ready to step into the spotlight.

Wellness travelers, adventure travelers and everyone in between will fall for this sleepy coastal enclave along the northern California coast. Unwind at Marriott Bonvoy’s newest adventure lodge after exploring the recently opened Great Redwood Trail or sampling the latest additions to the town’s renowned sustainable food and wine scene. And thanks to nonstop flights from Alaska Airlines and Southwest and $20 million in roadwork funding, Mendocino is easier than ever to reach. -⁠Rachel Craft

Experience a quieter side of India in one of the world’s lushest biodiversity hotspots

Like many of the best places, it can take a lot of time and effort to get to Coorg, a hill station in India’s verdant, biodiverse Western Ghats. But it is well worth it to see this little-visited region rife with endemic wildlife including elephants, leopards and myriad avian species. Spend your days sampling world-class coffee at the area’s many plantations, hiking the misty mountain trails and recentering yourself with immersive multiday Ayurvedic wellness programs at the stunning new Leela Coorg Forest Sanctuary. -⁠Eric Rosen

In anticipation of hosting the EXPO 2027, the Serbian capital is undergoing a major glow-up

From May 15 to Aug.15, the Serbian capital will host a specialized world exposition with 140-plus countries gathering to showcase innovations in architecture and design. In anticipation of the event, Belgrade is debuting several major projects of its own, including a Nikola Tesla Museum designed by Zaha Hadid Architects. The former main railway station will become the new permanent home of the Historical Museum of Serbia, while the Museum of the City of Belgrade and the Museum of Natural History Belgrade will also open in new facilities. Finally, the Aeronautical Museum of Belgrade will also complete a modernization project in 2027. To accommodate the influx of visitors, the city already opened a St. Regis in 2024, while the InterContinental Belgrade is accepting reservations from next March, with a Ritz-Carlton also anticipated to open, too. -⁠Lyndsey Matthews

Best in May through June, September through October

A pair of new destination-worthy hotels, both bookable with points.

Hyatt and Marriott will both debut luxury properties in Detroit come 2027. Hilton’s new hotel, the NoMad Detroit, will open inside the historic Michigan Grand Central Station, a once-abandoned Beaux-Arts landmark restored by Ford. Later in the year, the Marriott Edition will open as part of a ground-up development, bringing downtown Detroit its first five-star hotel. -⁠Carly Helfand

A new film festival is just one facet of this art-meets-outdoors jewel.

Between hosting its first Sundance Film Festival and celebrating 50 years of the iconic Pearl Street Mall, Colorado’s trendy cultural hub is going all out. Visitors can also look forward to new dining concepts from Michelin-recognized chefs, new interactive art labs and easy access to new Rocky Mountain hiking trails. An hour away, Denver International Airport (DEN) is expanding to accommodate increased traffic from United, Southwest and even Delta. -⁠Rachel Craft

Jungle-covered islands and seas teeming with marine life beckon explorers beyond the bright lights of Bali.

Cruise companies are lining up new expeditions to explore the Indonesian archipelago’s untouched corners, including a seven-day sailing aboard Uniworld’s Aqua Blu that will stop in Komodo National Park and the Spice Islands, Ponant’s team-up with Smithsonian Journeys on a 15-day jaunt around the Maluku islands among other ports of call and specialized dive-focused sailings in wild West Papua, reef-rich Raja Ampat and untamed Borneo from Swan Hellenic and Noble Caledonia. It’s the best way to experience regions of the Indonesian archipelago most folks never see. -⁠Eric Rosen

Australia’s first Michelin Guide, new luxury hotels and experiences, nonstop access from the U.S. and an extraordinary mix of world-class wine, wildlife and wilderness make 2027 South Australia’s moment on the global stage.

Australia’s first Michelin Guide and United’s nonstop San Francisco-Adelaide flight are putting South Australia within easier reach — and on the global culinary map, too. A significant transformation of Adelaide Central Market, Australia’s first Treehouse Hotel and new luxury stays are adding fresh reasons to visit, alongside the Barossa and McLaren Vale wine regions and the wildlife and rugged beauty of Kangaroo Island. -⁠Tanner Saunders

Best in April through June, September through October

Natural wonders and a burgeoning culture scene without the crowds.

Though Kazakhstan first made a name for itself as a nature travel destination, this Eurasian country wants the world to know there’s more to it than its glorious landscapes. Travelers can enjoy a new art museum and immersive ethno-village in the cultural capital of Almaty, check into new hotels in the Burabay resort region or combine natural and cultural wonders at the newly inscribed Mangystau Rock Mosques UNESCO World Heritage Site. With plans to launch the first-ever direct flight from the U.S. in 2027, this hidden gem may not stay hidden for long. -⁠Rachel Craft

Best in May through June, September through October

Two iconic cultural institutions, back and better than ever.

The Pergamon Museum will reopen in June after a multi-year renovation, debuting a fully redesigned Museum of Islamic Art and making the Pergamon Altar accessible for the first time in more than a decade. Later in the year, the Bauhaus Archive will reopen after extensive renovations with a new annex building. With nonstop options from the U.S. on United, Delta and Lufthansa — and strong Hilton and Marriott footprints downtown — early points bookings are a smart play for visiting Berlin in 2027. -⁠Carly Helfand

Best in April through June, September through November

Experience a slower type of journey that has captivated travelers for over 1,000 years.

Special events will be taking place at waystations along this ancient pilgrimage trail throughout the Holy Year of 2027. Among the highlights are braving the wine battle in Haro at the end of June, or attending St. James’s Feast Day on July 25 in Santiago de Compostela, where you can see the famous swinging of the Botafumeiro silver incense burner and attend an awe-inspiring mass in the Praza do Obradoiro. Aside from a full calendar of culinary festivals and lively concerts in Santiago, you can take in quieter stretches of the trail among the forested peaks of Cantabria and the vineyards of Rioja. -⁠Eric Rosen

Astrotourism investments and a highly anticipated points hotel transformation.

Dramatic coastal landscapes, the new Atlantic Canada UNESCO Tourism Corridor and the re-opening of the transformed The Algonquin Resort St. Andrews by-the-Sea, Autograph Collection resort make a compelling case for a 2027 visit to New Brunswick. Specifically, we’re excited to check out the Bay of Fundy Dark Sky Corridor that’s set to open in 2027 — a 137-mile stretch that could be the densest cluster of dark-sky and observatory areas on the planet. A stargazer’s dream come true. -⁠Madison Blancaflor

A burgeoning wine scene, an exciting UNESCO designation and outdoor attractions aplenty give one of BC’s prettiest regions a well deserved moment in the spotlight

With plenty of sunny days and a generally milder climate than the rest of British Columbia, the Okanagan Valley is becoming an increasingly compelling alternative to larger wine regions; oenophiles can look forward to sipping wines from smaller producers (small but mighty; there are over 200) in a community-forward and breathtaking lakeside setting.

Those in search of a city getaway should head to Kelowna, the valley’s largest metropolis set along the breezy shorelines of Okanagan Lake, where a major culinary moment is afoot. Recently designated Canada’s first UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy — a designation that honors not only the city’s agricultural innovation and culinary creativity, but the traditional foodways and land stewardship of the indigenous Syilx people — Kelowna offers a fast-growing restaurant scene (many with a sustainable, farm-to-table focus) and its own array of impressive wineries. -⁠Ellie Nan Storck

Travelers can look forward to fully restored access to Denali Park Road for the first time in six years

With more access now than ever, thanks to both recently expanded Alaska Airlines routes to nearby Fairbanks International Airport (FAI) and the very exciting full reopening of Denali Park Road for the summer season, 2027 is the year to plan an epic trip to Denali National Park. And the fun doesn’t stop there — Holland America, celebrating 80 years of Alaskan exploration, will complete a massive transformation of Holland America Denali Lodge, debuting 72 new guest rooms, updated public spaces and refreshed dining programs. Beyond the park, the Alaska Railroad — which celebrated its centennial in 2023 — is a great way travelers can experience a legendary scenic trip between Anchorage, Talkeetna, Denali and Fairbanks. -⁠Ellie Nan Storck

Expanded access from the U.S. and newly awarded Michelin key hotel recognition.

Delta is adding a new nonstop route from L.A. to Manila and Philippine Airlines is joining the oneworld alliance, making a trip to the gorgeous islands of The Philippines easier than ever in 2027. Head to the islands early in the year for milder temperatures, vibrant festivals and the chance to ethically swim with majestic whale sharks in Donsol, Sorsogon. Nature lovers and beach loungers can also enjoy luxury properties like the Raffles Makati and the forthcoming Mandarin Oriental Makati, Manila (opening in December) or use points to book the brand new AC Hotel by Marriott Manila. -⁠Madison Blancaflor

Best in June through September, January through March

These lush African islands are ready for their moment in the sun.

Thanks to its pristine tropical forests and rare wildlife species, in 2025 São Tomé and Principe became the first country in the world whose entire territory, both land and sea, was designated as a UNESCO biosphere reserve. This past year, the country scored a second UNESCO designation for its historical roças, or colonial agricultural estates, making São Tomé and Principe ripe for discovery. Even better — you can use your Star Alliance points and miles to fly direct from Lisbon on TAP and Hilton points can set you up for a beachy stay at the luxurious Sundy Praia – Principe Collection. -⁠Eric Rosen

Best in April through May, September through October

For travelers ready to venture beyond familiar South American tourism destinations and experience a different side of the continent.

Travelers who have already visited Peru, Brazil, Argentina and other South American hot spots can find something different in the continent’s less-visited interior. Don’t go expecting a long list of world-famous sights or extensive tourism infrastructure. Instead, go for a quieter, slower-paced trip shaped by Indigenous Guaraní culture and landscapes ranging from the vast Chaco lowlands to the biodiverse remnants of the Atlantic Forest along the Paraná River. New attractions are adding reasons to visit: MUVA Museo Viedma, a museum exploring Paraguay’s Guaraní-Jesuit heritage through murals by artist Manuel Viedma, opened in Misiones in May 2026, and Asunción’s Museo de Ciencias plans to open a planetarium in 2028. -⁠Mackenzie Roche

#6157. White House warns Democrats against aggressive oversight

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.

The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to issue subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

The letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter says.

Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse," Garcia said. "The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.

"It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.

Last week, President Donald Trump himself said that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

He also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

And Trump last year publicly called for longtime critic Sen. Adam B. Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

Garcia and other Democrats have signaled they intend to pursue oversight aggressively in the new Congress. After Democrats won the House majority last week, Garcia put out an all-caps statement urging administration officials to “LAWYER UP” ahead of the new year.

Garcia, as well as other likely incoming chairs such as House Judiciary ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; Homeland Security ranking member Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., have hinted at broad inquiries ranging from the handling of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to immigration enforcement and more.

Raskin told reporters last week that he thought Democratic oversight efforts could dovetail with the party’s broader effort to address affordability issues, including by addressing the Iran war, allegations of corruption within the Trump administration and more.

“We're going to get all the information that we need in order to restore the rule of law in American constitutional democracy,” Raskin said.

The letter also echoes a previous fight the administration pitched with the House in the first Trump administration, where officials resisted in court allowing former White House Counsel Don McGahn to testify to the House Judiciary Committee for years.
