#6143. Buy Hilton Honors Points With 120% Bonus By November 21: Worth It?

Through November 21, 2026, Hilton Honors is offering a buy points promotion, which is the program’s best-ever bonus on purchasing points! While Hilton Honors ordinarily offers up to a 100% bonus on purchased points, this time around the program is offering up to a 120% bonus, which is a cost of 0.45 cents per point. This could represent a great value for hotel redemptions, especially with an immediate use in mind, as members can purchase up to 528,000 points in one transaction.

As always, I only recommend buying points with a short term use in mind, and if you understand the mechanics of how award redemptions with a program work, including what redemption costs are like.

Link: Buy Hilton Honors points with this promotion with a 120% bonus

Between 12AM ET on October 7 and 11:59PM ET on November 21, 2026, Hilton Honors is offering a bonus on purchased points. Different Hilton Honors members may be targeted for different bonuses, so you’ll want to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for. It would appear that the best offer is for up to a 120% bonus, and that’s structured as follows:

Hilton Honors ordinarily charges one cent per purchased point, including all taxes and fees. That’s before any discounts or bonuses. If you’re eligible for the 120% bonus and maxed out the offer, you’d receive a total of 528,000 points at a cost of $2,400, which is a rate of 0.45 cents per Hilton Honors point.

Ordinarily, Hilton Honors lets members buy up to 160,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased by 50%, to 240,000 points. With a 120% bonus, that means you could purchase up to 528,000 points.

The purchase of Hilton Honors points is non-refundable, and points purchased don’t count toward elite status. Purchased points will post within 48 hours of finalizing the purchase (though in my experience, much faster than that).

While Hilton Honors has a strict limit on how many points you can buy, note that there are ways to acquire more points than that limit without violating the rules.

Hilton lets members combine points across accounts at no cost, so in reality you could acquire substantially more points by simply buying them across accounts and then consolidating them. Hilton Honors lets members transfer up to 500,000 points, and receive up to two million points, per calendar year. Each member can make up to six transfers to other members per calendar year, and new Hilton Honors members can only transfer or receive points a minimum of 30 days after enrollment.

Hilton also allows points pooling, whereby Hilton Honors members can combine points with up to 10 other members, with the same limitations.

When Hilton Honors offer a promotion on purchased points, it’s most common to see a 100% bonus (the equivalent of a 50% discount). So this 120% bonus is the best-ever promotion we’ve seen from the program, so that’s awesome.

Below is a chart with some of the recent buy points promotions we saw from the Hilton Honors program, before this one.

Hilton Honors point purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with a Hilton credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s Hilton spending.

I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

There’s potentially huge value to be had buying Hilton Honors points. Hilton Honors sells points at a reasonable cost, has lots of aspirational properties, has good redemptions with a fifth night free opportunity, and elite status is also easy to earn with the program. Hilton’s partnership with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) is also awesome, and offers great redemption opportunities.

However, people shouldn’t blindly buy Hilton Honors points, as there are also lots of redemptions where you won’t come out ahead. As I see it, the biggest value with buying Hilton Honors is for aspirational redemptions at expensive properties. Let me give some examples, based on current redemption rates.

For example, take the Waldorf Astoria Maldives, which is bookable for 250,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $1,125. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be $3,400, so that’s like two-thirds off. That’s pretty amazing!

As another example, take the Waldorf Astoria Los Cabos, which is bookable for 250,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $1,125. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be close to $2,200, so that’s like half off.

Above I mentioned the Hilton Honors partnership with SLH, so let me give an example there. RiverView Ranch Retreat is located in Montana, and is bookable for 220,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $990. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be over $3,800 (the screenshot below is for two nights, since that’s the minimum stay), so that’s close to three-fourths off.

Now, while the above are all examples of what a good deal it can be to buy Hilton Honors points, let me of course acknowledge that these are all top-end properties. Unfortunately I find that for your run of the mill Hilton properties, including many limited service hotels, the value just isn’t there in the same way.

For example, take the Hilton Garden Inn Tampa, which is bookable for 45,000 points per night. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $203. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be under $180, so there’s absolutely no reason to buy points, only to redeem them for less value than what you paid. You’ll find that to be pretty common, which is why I always recommend crunching the numbers before making a purchase.

Hilton Honors doesn’t have a published award chart, but rather the program has dynamic award pricing. This means that the cost of a standard free night award can vary depending on the day of the week, time of year, etc.

As a general rule of thumb, Hilton Honors free night awards start at 10,000 points per night, and go up to 250,000 points per night (which is a shame, because up until last year, properties maxed out at 150,000 points per night).

Sometimes you’ll see award costs that are way higher than these amounts. In those situations it’s because there’s not a standard room available, so higher pricing kicks in for premium rooms. That’s generally not nearly as good of a use of Hilton Honors points, and you’ll find that some awards even cost one million or more points per night. Obviously that’s a lousy value.

If you have Hilton Honors elite status (which is easy to earn, as I’ll outline below), you receive a fifth night free on award redemptions. This is a way to stretch your points even further, and whenever possible, I’d recommend making your Hilton Honors award stays in increments of five nights.

To take advantage of this, just log into your Hilton Honors elite account, and go through the process of making an award booking for five nights. When you get to the booking page, you should notice that the cost of the fifth night is automatically deducted.

Let me give an example how much value this can add. Say you want to book five nights at the Waldorf Astoria Seychelles Platte Island. At a rate of 150,000 points per night, you’d pay a total of 600,000 points for five nights, which averages out to 120,000 points per night. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, that’s like the equivalent of paying $540 per night. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be over $1,800 per night, so that represents absolutely massive savings.

One thing I love about the program is how easy it is to earn elite status with credit cards, including both Hilton Honors™ Gold Status and Hilton Honors™ Diamond Status. These tiers offer perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, hotel credits, and more. For example:

Hilton Honors points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 24 months. Eligible account activity includes earning or redeeming points, so buying points would even reset the expiration of your points.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Hilton Honors points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. As you can see, the pricing here is potentially better than what I value these points, and there are lots of ways to get outsized value with this promotion.

Hilton Honors doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, and all standard rooms are available for award redemptions. So this is about as good of a policy as you’ll find with any hotel group when it comes to award room availability.

There are lots of ways to earn Hilton Honors points, beyond just staying at Hilton properties or buying the points directly. You can easily earn points by using Hilton Honors’ co-branded credit cards, which also offer great welcome bonuses. These cards include the following:

You can also transfer points from Amex Membership Rewards to Hilton Honors (at a 1:2 ratio), and from Bilt Rewards to Hilton Honors (at a 1:1 ratio). I wouldn’t consider either of those redemptions to represent a good deal. That’s simply because I value Hilton Honors points at 0.5 cents each, while I value those points currencies at 1.7 cents each, so the math just doesn’t work out.

Hilton Honors is currently offering a best-ever bonus on purchased points, whereby members can receive up to a 120% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire points for 0.45 cents each. In the past we’ve generally seen bonuses of up to 100%, so this is a better offer than ever before. In fairness, Hilton Honors points have also been devalued a bit over time. With a short term use in mind, there are plenty of situations where this could represent a good deal.

Do you plan on buying Hilton Honors points with a bonus?

#6142. Transfer Chase Points To Virgin Atlantic Flying Club With 40% Bonus: Worth It?

The Chase Ultimate Rewards program is currently offering a bonus for points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While I’d only transfer points with a specific use in mind, there’s huge value to be had here, as a 40% transfer bonus is massive.

Between November 16 and December 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when transferring Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

This promotion is being offered on Chase’s end (in the United States), and is hard coded into the transfer ratio, meaning you should see the bonus at the time that you make the transfer. You can take advantage of this offer an unlimited number of times. Transfers from Chase to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club are generally instant.

We see a bonus like this to Virgin Atlantic a few times per year. We last saw a transfer bonus over the summer, so it hasn’t been a long gap at all. Past transfer bonuses have been in the range of 25-40%, so this is at the very top end of that spectrum.

There are several great cards earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points, and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Virgin Atlantic is a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic (with steep carrier imposed surcharges), there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta, as well as more broadly on SkyTeam airlines.

Nowadays Flying Club has dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. What’s exciting is that on the low end, redemption rates are very attractive, and it’s possible to fly Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and United Kingdom for under 30,000 points, in some situations. And that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 45,000-47,500 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with. Then when you consider the 40% transfer bonus, that means you could be paying significantly fewer Chase points. First class can also be a good deal.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Through December 30, 2026, you can receive a 40% bonus when you transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. This is more of a niche program, but with a specific use in mind, there’s a lot of value to be had.

With the 40% bonus, you can potentially get some incredible redemption values for travel on Virgin Atlantic, including in Upper Class. There’s also significant value to be had if redeeming on partners, whether it’s on a SkyTeam partner, or on one of Virgin Atlantic’s non-SkyTeam partner airlines.

Some pretty significant changes are coming for Hyatt loyalists in 2027.

After introducing a five-tier award chart and annual category changes this May, we weren't sure what to expect with this announcement — but the good news is that the updates are largely positive, save for a few changes that might frustrate higher-tier members.

"We’re shaping the future of World of Hyatt around what our members value most. After a year of listening, one thing is clear: members want more distinctive benefits, more freedom to use their awards, and the opportunity to choose awards that matter most to them,” said Laurie Blair, senior vice president, global marketing and loyalty, Hyatt. “We’re continuing to deliver more of what members want, with the ability to combine valuable awards, earn Tier Qualifying Nights faster, and choose more of the experiences they love. Together, these new options make every milestone a chance to personalize the journey ahead."

From a newly minted Delta partnership (with exciting double-dipping benefits) and more flexibility with awards and earnings, here is what we know about the changes, which will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Related: Complete guide to the World of Hyatt loyalty program

For years, Hyatt has allowed members to redeem one award per stay. If you wanted to use a Category 1-7 certificate, you couldn't also use a Suite Upgrade Award. If you gifted Category 1-4 certificates to friends or family members, they couldn't also use Guest of Honor awards to receive your Globalist benefits.

Starting Jan. 1, members will be able to stack Free Night Awards, Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards and Free Parking Awards (more on this in a bit) on the same reservation. This is a fantastic improvement that addresses a key frustration for many loyal members, who currently must carefully pick which award makes the most sense on a given stay.

In addition, all awards will now be available for 365 days from the date of issuance.

This is great news for the free-night certificates you earn through Hyatt's Milestone Rewards, which were previously valid for only six months. Next year, you'll have twice as much time to use them.

However, this will negatively impact Suite Upgrade Awards.

Today, you can select these upgrades starting at 40 nights, and when you do, they're valid through the end of the year plus an additional 14 months. Now, they'll have a shorter window of validity — potentially much shorter.

For example, if you reached 40 nights on Aug. 1, 2026, and immediately picked a Suite Upgrade Award, it'll expire Feb. 28, 2028 — giving you 19 months to use it. If you hit that same threshold on July 15, 2027, and again picked an upgrade immediately, it'll only be valid through July 14, 2028.

You'll still have up to 90 days to select each milestone reward, so come 2027, you may want to wait until the end of that window to commit to an upgrade award if you don't have an immediate use for it.

Related: How to redeem Hyatt points for free nights and more

One of the biggest changes within this update to the World of Hyatt program is the flexibility of Milestone Rewards — and the rewards themselves. Starting in January, Milestone Rewards will now begin at 10 qualifying nights or 20,000 Base Points, with additional milestones every 10 qualifying nights, up to 150 nights per calendar year.

Additionally, the company has added a handful of new awards, including the following:

Here is a full breakdown of your choices starting Jan. 1, 2027:

In addition to the new options, you'll have additional flexibility at certain milestones.

For example, the 30-night milestone is currently a Category 1-4 certificate plus a choice of other options. Now, you can choose between that award or 10,000 bonus points, plus a second choice among five options. And at 60 nights, rather than the one-size-fits-all approach, with the same four rewards for every member, you now get to pick three of the four.

Unfortunately, there are three (potentially) negative changes to flag here:

Losing free parking on award stays is a notable loss, as is the reduction in Suite Upgrade Awards. That said, just how impactful these are will depend on your individual stay habits.

In September, Delta and Hyatt announced an upcoming partnership, and we've finally learned about the details — and yes, elite SkyMiles and World of Hyatt members will be able to "double-dip" with their hotel stay and flight earnings.

As noted by TPG writer Sean Cudahy, there are two primary things to keep in mind about the Delta-Hyatt partnership:

When Delta SkyMiles and World of Hyatt members link their accounts, they'll be able to access the new Delta Milestone Rewards detailed above starting in 2027. These rewards start at 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 Base Points and include eCertificates, Delta Sky Club passes and even opportunities to earn Medallion Status.

Finally, World of Hyatt will also debut an updated booking flow through its app and website that will make it easier to tailor your trip to your needs and rewards. Right now, the "Pay My Way" options are fairly limited — essentially just cash or points. The new flow will give much more flexibility.

"Members can select, gift and redeem eligible awards online or in the World of Hyatt app, while an enhanced Pay My Way experience will let members tailor payment for each night using awards, points, cash or Points + Cash," the company shared in the press release.

Overall, we're calling these changes a net positive. The ability to combine awards on a single stay is the standout here, and it's great to have the extra time to use many awards that currently have a very limited window. The new Delta-Hyatt tie-up is also exciting, with reciprocal earning opportunities for elite members of each program. Finally, it's great to see an expanded list of Milestone Rewards and additional flexibility in customizing them.

That said, there are some notable drawbacks here, especially the loss of free parking on award stays for Globalists — though it's nice to have a transition period through February 2028 before that takes effect for existing Globalists.

As a reminder, these new perks won't launch until Jan. 1, 2027, so it's status quo until then.

The World of Hyatt program is making several changes that'll impact its most frequent guests starting in 2027. Between the long-awaited benefit of being able to combine awards, a slew of new Milestone Rewards and some shiny new partner perks with Delta, Hyatt is adding a lot of new potential value for members. Of course, it's not all positive — but many of us here at TPG are excited about what's to come.

What do you think about these program updates? Feel free to sound off in the comments section below!

#6140. House Dems target Trump family, JD Vance in sweeping new investigation push

White House counsel Will Scharf joins 'Fox News Sunday' to address incoming Democratic investigations targeting the Trump administration. Scharf warns that the Department of Justice will push back aggressively if lawmakers use their oversight powers to threaten or intimidate administration staffers.

The likely next chairman of the House Oversight Committee is officially taking the first steps to launch a wide array of investigations before Democrats take control in the new Congress.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is sending document preservation letters to 12 figures in President Donald Trump's orbit on Wednesday morning, including Vice President JD Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

House Oversight Committee Democrats are looking to investigate the Trump family's business deals, alleged misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the federal government's handling of Jeffrey Epstein's case, they said in a release.

Garcia said the probes "will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans."

THE TOP TRUMP OFFICIALS DEMOCRATS ADMIT ARE ON THEIR HIT LIST FOR INVESTIGATIONS IN THE NEW CONGRESS

Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump look on as President Donald Trump and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen announce a U.S.-EU trade deal after a meeting at Trump Turnberry Golf Club on July 27, 2025, in Turnberry, Scotland. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The California Democrat is all but guaranteed to hold the Oversight gavel in the next Congress and has already signaled that he intends to kick off the new year with an aggressive investigation schedule.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

His committee will also be key to any potential impeachment efforts House Democrats take on in the next term.

Other investigatory targets include former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, former DHS senior advisor Corey Lewandowski, former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William K. Marshall III and Trust for the National Mall CEO Catherine Townsend.

"Oversight Democrats have been investigating the potential corruption, self-dealing, and abuses of power that have funneled billions of dollars to the Trump family as Americans struggle with rising costs," letters to the president's two eldest sons read.

"While the Trump Administration’s failed policies have made life increasingly unaffordable for the public, you have engaged in business pursuits that appear to have allowed you to personally profit from your father’s presidency on a massive scale and at the expense of the American people."

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., gives remarks to media outside the House Democratic Caucus meeting in the Longworth House Office Building on Nov. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

The letter to Miller reads in part, "Oversight Democrats have heard directly from the victims of the lawless conduct of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign and from whistleblowers appalled by agency behavior. There must be accountability for those responsible for orchestrating, carrying out, and covering up these abuses, at all levels of the agency."

DEMS PIVOT FROM ‘AFFORDABILITY’ PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS

Democrats have positioned their investigative efforts as accountability measures long-sought by the American public. But Republicans have argued that it shows Democrats are more interested in political retribution than working on solutions to lower issues like the high cost of living that millions of Americans are dealing with.

Trump and his family have long denied any wrongdoing when it comes to their business interests.

And while Miller and Noem did face bipartisan criticism over the administration's crackdown on illegal immigration, the majority of Republicans have lined up behind the White House and maintained that it is what Americans voted for.

White House chief of staff Stephen Miller addresses the audience during opening remarks at the Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism at the State Department on July 16, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

A White House official told Fox News Digital of the letters, "Democrats have made it abundantly clear their intentions are to use congressional investigations to threaten, prosecute, and intimidate government officials through baseless political attacks, slander, and outright falsehoods. We are ready to engage with Congress on investigations that serve a legitimate legislative purpose, but will not be intimidated by baseless political investigations. Ranking Minority Democrats’ do not have the authority to conduct oversight and demand the Administration turn over records."

And White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said, "As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

It's not immediately clear whether the investigatory targets will comply with House Democrats' demands to preserve documents and communications.

Republicans selected House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, as their leader in the new Congress and de facto top spokesman against Democrats' partisan activity.

Garcia's counterpart on the House Oversight Committee remains to be seen, but both Reps. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, and Pat Fallon, R-Texas, have expressed interest in the role.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

#6139. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”

#6138. Atmos Rewards Upgrade Certificates: How Do They Work, Are They Worth It?

Atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. The program has four elite tiers — Silver, Gold, Platinum, and Titanium — and somehow I’m actually going to end the year as a top tier member, it looks like, without having once stepped foot on an Alaska or Hawaiian flight.

As I’ve worked my way through the elite ranks, I’ve become eligible for the milestone perks program, whereby you can select perks when passing various elite thresholds. Along those lines, At the higher tiers, one of the choices becomes upgrade certificates, so I’d like to talk about those a bit, as I’m trying to decide whether or not I should select these.

I’m intrigued by Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, given the increasingly global route network of Alaska and Hawaiian. At the same time, the execution of this upgrade program definitely leaves a lot to be desired, including the lack of confirmable upgrade availability.

I have to make a selection soon, so I’d like to talk through the Alaska and Hawaiian upgrade certificate program, and then get some feedback from Atmos Rewards loyalists. The last time I was focused on upgrade certificates at the airline was when Alaska Mileage Plan had Gold Guest Upgrades as the upgrade currency, and MVP Gold was the top tier status… those were the days!

Atmos Rewards issues upgrade certificates as part of the Atmos Rewards milestone perks program. This can be unlocked based on how many status points you earn over the course of a calendar year. Let me emphasize that these upgrade certificates are intended for confirming upgrades in advance, and they’re separate from the complimentary space available upgrades offered.

Specifically, Atmos Rewards members could earn upgrade certificates at the following thresholds:

Titanium status requires 135,000 status points, and I expect to end the year with roughly that many status points. That means I could select up to eight upgrade certificates. However, that would come at the opportunity cost of 70,000 bonus points, for example. Of course I could also mix and match, like selecting four upgrade certificates and 50,000 bonus points.

Now let’s talk a bit about the rules for redeeming Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, at least on paper. Upgrades are valid across the Alaska and Hawaiian route networks, and fall into one of two categories:

Upgrade certificates can be shared with others, but of course can’t be bartered or sold. One other interesting quirk is that if you cancel or change an itinerary that was upgraded, the certificate will be forfeited. However, a replacement upgrade certificate code can be requested through customer care. Let’s cover the details of upgrades based on the region.

When it comes to upgrading within North America, an Atmos Rewards upgrade certificate can be confirmed at the time of booking, as long as the “U” fare class is available. If it’s not available, the upgrade will be waitlisted.

To cover the very basics, the upgrade certificate is valid for one-way travel (with no connections longer than four hours), for tickets issued by and flown on Alaska and Hawaiian. Tickets purchased in Y, B, H, K, M, L, V, S, or N fare classes, are eligible for upgrades using certificates, while tickets purchased in Q, O, G, or X fare classes, are not eligible.

To search if a flight is upgrade eligible, select “Upgrade Certificate” in the dropdown in the “Upgrade type” section, during the booking process.

Then on the search results page, you should be looking for two things:

When it comes to upgrading outside of North America, Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates have completely different rules, both for better and worse. First, it’s worth understanding that an upgrade requires either one or two upgrade certificates, depending on the route, per the below chart.

When it comes to using Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates on global (non-North America) flights, there are both pros and cons:

I have to say, the execution of this perk is odd. Keep in mind that Atmos Rewards has a one-of-a-kind upgrade perk for top tier Titanium members, whereby they receive space available upgrades globally on the day of departure. So what’s odd is that if you’re a Titanium member you’re eligible for a complimentary upgrade close to departure, but having applied an upgrade certificate previously gives you no priority. You’d think they’d prioritize members who requested an upgrade, but I suspect it’s a technology limitation of some sort.

I’d like to address the question of whether Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates are worth it both broadly, and more specifically to my situation.

I hear all the time from Atmos Rewards members who are frustrated by the lack of confirmable upgrade space. And indeed, compared to back in the day, upgrade space that can be confirmed is incredibly limited. At the same time, that’s true across airlines nowadays, given how much better airlines have become at actually selling their first class seats, rather than filling them with those upgrading.

For example, looking at the route between my home airport of Miami (MIA) and Seattle (SEA) as far out as the schedule opens, I don’t see a single date that has confirmable upgrade space. Now, you’ll sometimes find confirmable upgrade space up and down the West Coast, especially during off peak times, so I don’t want to suggest it’s impossible to find a confirmable upgrade.

But just broadly speaking, confirmable upgrades with “U” class available for transcontinental and Hawaii flights are exceedingly rare, and it’s like winning the lottery. So it’s really hard to get excited about that.

In theory, I of course love the idea of being able to upgrade a long haul flight with upgrade certificates. The catch is that an upgrade clearing at most 72 hours before departure really limits flexibility. I suppose you could always apply an upgrade, hope it clears, and then cancel your ticket if it doesn’t, but this would be a last minute scramble.

To me, that’s just too risky. It’s not that I’d be unwilling to fly economy on a long haul flight, but by strategically using points, it’s really not necessary in a vast majority of situations, at least based on my own travel patterns.

The thing is, it’s also important to view Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates in terms of the opportunity cost of selecting them.

For example, as I mentioned above, at 55,000 status points I can select two upgrade certificates or 5,000 bonus points. At an opportunity cost of 2,500 points per upgrade certificate, I think it might be worth selecting upgrade certificates. Based on my latest points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, so the opportunity cost per upgrade is $37.50. That’s a rate at which I’d probably be happy to gamble, because if the upgrades expire, it’s not the end of the world.

Meanwhile at 95,000 status points, the opportunity cost becomes 7,500 bonus points per upgrade, so that’s a value of $112.50 per upgrade. Then at 125,000 status points, the opportunity cost becomes 12,500 bonus points per upgrade, so that’s a value of $187.50. That’s the point at which I’m definitely more inclined to take the “sure thing,” rather than take my chances with an upgrade.

Atmos Rewards lets members select upgrade certificates as part of the milestone perks program. This always comes at an opportunity cost, and is a better value at some tiers than others.

Upgrade certificates can be used on Alaska and Hawaiian flights globally, with most one-ways requiring one upgrade certificate, though some global routes requiring two upgrade certificates. While upgrades within North America can be confirmed at the time of booking (pending upgrade availability), global upgrades can only be confirmed at most 72 hours before departure.

The big issue with upgrades is the lack of availability. Alaska is just really bad about making confirmed upgrades available, and upgrades clearing at most 72 hours before departure on global flights is less than ideal.

What do you make of the value of Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates?

I haven't been able to use any upgrade certificates yet. I recently booked SEA-PSP RT for March and on at least one of the flights, it looked like no F seats at all had been sold yet--but there were no seats available in U. I am still learning the mechanics of how to apply the certs after purchase so they may work out but my guess is they will be useless.

They're not a sure thing, but as a Gold, I've still managed to clear SFO-JFK, though sometimes after booking only and after monitoring for availability. To me, the main frustrations are: lack of waitlisting (this is coming in 2027 but will probably hurt lower tier elites like me), and fare class minimums (I do not want to pay for a higher fare class for the *chance* of upgrading if there is no availability to confirm). In some ways, the long haul process works better for me since there is no fare class minimum

Don't forget that they've announced that next year they will be cutting the certs at 55k in half and they will introduce waitlisting for all certificates. They didn't announce this via an email blast or any sort of convenient way but rather it's on their website under 2027 updates, which I check obsessively.

I chose 4 certs (2 certs 2x) at the 55k threshold earlier this year, mainly to see if they could be usable for me. Their value did work out when I decided to look up flights to Alaska for Summer 2027, when the schedule opened. A confirmable upgrade was available on my PHX-ANC and ANC-PHX flights, and I immediately used them to upgrade to F on both flights. Considering that's a 6+ hour flight (and $400 difference) each way, I would say I've gotten value for those certs. For the other 2, right now I have a PHX-SEA-LHR flight booked in Jan and will try my luck to snag a J upgrade using those. It's a backup flight to my AA J PHX-LAX-LHR flight, so if it doesn't clear by the morning of my flight, I will cancel, and hope to use those certs another time before they expire in July. I am looking forward to AS adding the ability to apply an upgrade cert to a flight that doesn't yet have U space available in 2027, so you don't have to constantly check for a seat to open. It'll hopefully make it easier (and probably a bit harder because others can do the same) to use the certs.

The certs are hard to use domestically. Close in bookings on open flights in off season travel for anything but a 1-2 hr flight is the only hope. The intl process which they kept from Hawaiian is weird and I agree it should be linked to the DOD waitlist for titaniums. I have not had the intl form process work yet but another coming up soon.

#6137. The New Changes That Could Make The US Air Force's C-17 Globemasters Become Fighters Instead Of Transport Aircraft

Bluebearwing | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

The United States Air Force is exploring a concept that could fundamentally change how it generates long-range strike capabilities by turning conventional cargo aircraft into formidable missile-launching platforms. Known initially as Rapid Dragon and now progressing under the Dragon Cart initiative, the program uses specially configured pallets to deploy multiple air-launched cruise missiles from aircraft such as the Lockheed Martin C-130J Super Hercules and Boeing C-17 Globemaster III.

Rather than developing entirely new combat aircraft, the concept leverages the existing air mobility fleet to provide commanders with additional precision-strike capacity. With growing demand for affordable, mass-produced munitions and the need to expand the US military's weapons stockpile, this approach could give the Air Force a significant advantage in future high-intensity conflicts.

In 2019, the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) initiated experiments that could, if successful, transform conventional transport aircraft such as the C-17 and C-130 into dual-use aircraft with immense firepower. Once deployed, these cargo haulers will be able to carry significant numbers of rapidly producible cruise missiles and saturate a battlespace, augmenting strike aircraft and heavy bombers.

The AFRL noted that the program has brought together more than "30 stakeholders, including Air Force Major Commands, the Test and Evaluation Enterprise, Program Offices, Mission Planners, other Services, Foreign Partners & Allies, and Industry to develop and demonstrate the capability through modeling, simulation, analysis, demonstration, and flight tests."

The project began as Rapid Dragon and is now known as Dragon Cart. The project tested the possibility of loading palletized munitions, such as JASSM-ER cruise missiles, into C-130s and C-17s. Air & Space Forces Magazine states that the "Rapid Dragon program performed several tests on the C-130 and C-17, including a live-fire test at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, in December 2021." AFRL has also stated that Rapid Dragon has employed the palletized munitions concept on three separate continents, including the EUCOM and INDOPACOM theaters.

According to CENTCOM Citadel, a C-130J Super Hercules can carry two pallets, each containing six missile tubes, enabling the aircraft to deploy up to 12 air-launched cruise missiles. Meanwhile, the C-17 Globemaster III, with a maximum payload capacity of 170,900 lb (77,519 kg), could theoretically accommodate five nine-missile pallets carrying up to 45 JASSMs. This substantial weapons payload could temporarily transform the cargo aircraft into a formidable standoff strike platform.

The US Air Force Research Laboratory is at the cutting edge of weapons and general technology development for the US military and partner states.

As demonstrated by Operation Epic Fury, during which US strike aircraft deployed approximately 1,100 JASSMs, from an estimated inventory of 4,400, the need for affordable mass in this category of munitions has become increasingly apparent. Further, the ability to deploy these weapons flexibly would allow US commanders to strike targets without placing additional demands on bomber, fighter, and strike aircraft crews.

Due to the need for an expanded stockpile of missiles, particularly more affordable varieties, Dragon Cart dovetails with the Air Force's investment in its Family of Affordable Mass Missiles (FAMM) program. This initiative is designed to expand the service's munitions stockpile with comparatively inexpensive, less exquisite air-to-ground missiles. To this point, Air&Space Forces Magazine reports that just last July, the "Pentagon announced framework agreements for multiyear deals with three companies to produce and develop two versions of FAMM weapons—FAMM-Lugged, for fighter aircraft, and FAMM-Palletized, for airlifters."

As part of this plan, the Air Force has requested $355 million in its FY2027 budget to procure 1,000 weapons under the broader FAMM program. Its five-year budget projections call for the purchase of 28,000 missiles for $12.6 billion, as detailed by Defence Industry Europe.

The massive buildup of precision missiles will be supported by companies such as Anduril, whose Barracuda cruise missile recently received certification as the Air Force's first large-scale production munition compliant with open systems architecture. This certification provides a clear path forward for the new weapon, which offers commanders greater flexibility, as technicians can swap out payloads and reconfigure other features depending on mission requirements.

Under the FAMM program, Air&Space Forces Magazine states that "Anduril, CoAspire, and Zone 5 Technologies were selected. The agreements call for the three companies to produce 8,000 missiles annually once production ramps up. That timeline targets 5,300 missiles in 2028, rising to 8,000 by 2031." Anduril is slated to deliver its first Barracuda missiles to the Pentagon in early 2027.

Comparing France's exquisite omnirole jet to the leading fighters.

With the missiles getting ever closer to delivery and the capability already within the Air Force's grasp, the service is planning to field this new weapon system in 2027, according to Defence Blog. Regarding the impending deployment of the missile delivery system, General Kenneth S. Wilsbach, US Air Force Chief of Staff, stated: “As you might gather, capabilities like FAMM-P blur the distinction between our combat air forces and mobility air force mission sets. That’s a cultural shift we need to be prepared for, and I need every mobility Airman in the room to embrace that change.”

Regarding this blurring of the line between combat and air mobility, this new weapons capability could potentially turn suitably equipped C-130s and C-17s into platforms capable of striking targets across a given theater. Between its active-duty, Air National Guard, and Reserve units, the Air Force operates 428 C-130s and 222 C-17s. That's a substantial number of potential missile-launching platforms. Another consideration is that any adversary will now have to devote resources and plan for the possibility that cargo aircraft operating in the area could be carrying a devastating payload of cruise missiles, placing high-value targets under potential threat.

Manufactured with a longer fuselage, C-130J-30 for combat delivery

Special Operations; aerial and ground refueling (US Air Force-only variant)

Search and rescue support missions; aerial and ground refueling (US Air Force-only variant)

Search and rescue/maritime support missions (US Coast Guard–only variant)

Civil-certified multipurpose air freighter

If the aircraft are called upon to strike hostile military sites, the missile pallets are loaded like standard cargo through the aircraft's Cargo Handling System and secured in place using pallet locks and a restraint system. Once over the designated launch area, the crew pushes the pallet or pallets out through the rear cargo door, much like any other airdropped load. Once clear of the aircraft, the pallet deploys a parachute, allowing the missiles to be released into the air. Their engines then activate, and the missiles maneuver toward their designated targets.

One of the program's greatest advantages is that, during contingency operations or high-intensity conflicts, the Air Force could support ground operations and provide substantial follow-on strikes without placing additional demands on its dedicated strike aircraft and heavy bomber crews. Further, using cargo aircraft as precision-strike platforms could provide commanders with highly accurate firepower against multiple targets, offering considerable value in support of ground operations.

Over 2,700 C-130-family aircraft have been produced so far, with production expected to run into the 2030s.

Despite the advantages of converting transport aircraft into missile-launching platforms, the concept is not without operational challenges. The C-130J Super Hercules and C-17 Globemaster III were designed primarily for air mobility, not penetrating heavily defended airspace. Consequently, these aircraft would need to operate at considerable standoff distances from hostile air defense systems, relying on the extended range of their cruise missiles to engage targets without entering contested airspace. This places greater importance on missile range, accuracy, and mission planning.

Further, deploying palletized munitions requires coordination between aircraft crews, mission planners, intelligence personnel, and weapons operators. Although the Cargo Handling System allows missile pallets to be loaded using conventional cargo procedures, aircraft must accommodate specialized release equipment, parachute deployment, and systems to coordinate missile launches. Additionally, cargo aircraft assigned to strike missions would temporarily be unavailable for traditional responsibilities, potentially placing additional demands on an already heavily tasked air mobility fleet.

Another consideration is the availability of suitable weapons and the ability to integrate different missile systems across multiple aircraft platforms. Rapid Dragon and the broader Dragon Cart initiative aim to make this process more flexible through palletized configurations and modular weapons architectures. However, individual aircraft and missile combinations still require testing, integration, and operational certification. The Air Force also has to ensure sufficient missile inventories are available to support conventional strike operations and expanded palletized weapons deployment. These considerations will determine how effectively the concept transitions from experimental demonstrations into a dependable component of US long-range strike capabilities.

The Rapid Dragon concept represents a significant shift in how the US Air Force could generate and deploy long-range strike capabilities. By adapting existing cargo aircraft to launch palletized cruise missiles, the service could substantially expand its available weapons-delivery platforms without relying exclusively on traditional bombers and fighter aircraft. The transition toward Dragon Cart, alongside the development of affordable, mass-produced munitions such as Anduril's Barracuda, further demonstrates the growing importance of flexible weapons deployment.

Although operational challenges involving aircraft availability, weapons integration, and survivability remain, the potential benefits are considerable. With hundreds of C-130s and C-17s across its active-duty, Air National Guard, and Reserve fleets, the Air Force has a substantial transportation infrastructure that could serve an additional combat role. Ultimately, Dragon Cart could reshape how the US generates strike capacity in future conflicts.

#6136. Wow: Lufthansa Adds Premium Business Seats On Some Short Haul A320 Flights!

Lufthansa has just announced plans to introduce “real” business class seats on some of its narrow body planes, and that’s a really exciting development, given the typical business class standard on narrow body aircraft in Europe!

Interestingly, this is a concept that was initially trialed on Lufthansa Group low cost subsidiary Eurowings, and we knew at the time it was being used as a test for a more widespread implementation across the airline group. I’m delighted to see this become more widespread, and I hope this is just the start of a bigger trend.

Lufthansa has revealed that it will expand its premium offering on short and medium haul routes. With the introduction of the new Premium Business Seat, passengers will get more personal space than they’re used to on short haul aircraft.

Historically, business class on Airbus A320-family aircraft has consisted of standard economy seats with a blocked middle. So that means with the 3-3 layout, four seats were only sold per row. What’s happening is that the first three rows on some aircraft are being replaced with two rows of recliner seats, meaning the per-seat footprint is around 50% bigger than in standard business class.

At launch, the new Lufthansa Premium Business Seat will be available on six Airbus A320 aircraft (and these planes will also be equipped with Starlink). The seat will feature significantly more space, with nearly one meter of legroom, plus extra recline. This doesn’t replace the standard business class product, but instead, is an upsell option.

This new product is now available for sale for flights as of March 1, 2027, on routes between Frankfurt (FRA) and Athens (ATH), Cairo (CAI), and Nice (NCE). However, the first plane with the seats will already be in service as of December 16, 2026, and as of February 2027, it’ll be deployed on the above routes (but tickets are only on sale as of March as of now).

If a flight has this product available, you’ll see the “Premium Business Seat” designator during the booking process.

The process of actually booking a Premium Business Seat is essentially an upgrade cost on top of the standard business class fare. For example, looking at a Frankfurt to Athens route, I see an upgrade cost of €139, which frankly seems quite reasonable for a flight of this length.

Lufthansa is for the time being describing this as a commercial test, with the aim of examining demand for additional comfort on these routes, and the results will form the basis for deciding whether to expand the offering.

You’ll see many people refer to short haul business class in Europe as a “scam” (I don’t agree, but people say that), and they’re shocked to find economy seats with blocked middles. Admittedly product standards differ vastly around the globe.

The reason that airlines in Europe can get away with this product is threefold:

Keep in mind that most of the network carriers in Europe don’t make much money on short haul flights (or even lose a lot of money), given high costs and fierce competition from ultra low cost carriers.

With that in mind, I think Lufthansa is going about this exactly right:

I’d love to see more airlines introduce something similar. In particular, Air France, as Europe’s most premium airline, seems best positioned to do this, and could do it with very little opportunity cost. Why?

Honestly, if I were Air France, I’d just introduce this throughout the A220 fleet, and it would be a major point of differentiation, competitively. No airline could do it as efficiently as Air France, and every A220 flight has at least two rows of business class, so the opportunity cost is minimal.

Lufthansa will be introducing “real” business class seats on a subfleet of its Airbus A320s. As of the spring of 2027, expect these planes to be flying from Frankfurt to Athens, Cairo, and Nice. This Premium Business Seat concept will complement the existing business class, and will be available as a buy-up for business class passengers.

I’m very happy to finally see some more comfort on flights within Europe, and I imagine this will prove successful. If it doesn’t, I suspect it would be due to a lack of people knowing about this, rather than there not actually being demand.

What do you make of the Lufthansa Premium Business Seat concept?

#6135. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

JSX, the boutique semi-private flight operator, is launching a new daily route between New York City and Dallas, the company announced this week.

The new service will fly to Dallas Love Field (DAL) starting on Feb. 17, with one daily flight in each direction.

JSX did not immediately disclose which airport in New York it plans to fly from. JSX typically flies to New York’s Teterboro Airport (TEB) and Westchester County Airport (HPN), although various restrictions set by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey mean that JSX cannot publicly promote TEB as a destination.

Those restrictions limit JSX to only selling those New York flights to members of its free Club JSX program, which offers rewards and has no minimum spending or flying requirements. When logged into that platform, the new route is currently bookable from TEB.

Club JSX: Earn rewards and fly in comfort with JSX’s new loyalty program

The carrier will use its Embraer E145 aircraft on the route, which can seat up to 30 passengers in a 1-1 configuration. Introductory fares start at $799 one-way.

"New York City and Dallas are two of America's most influential business and cultural centers, and we believe traveling between them should be as seamless as the opportunities that connect them,” Alex Wilcox, CEO of JSX, said in a statement. "With this new daily service, we're bringing the simplicity, comfort, and convenience of JSX to one of the country's most important travel corridors."

The new flight to Dallas is JSX second New York City expansion in as many weeks; the carrier announced new flights between New York and Boston earlier this month. The Dallas route is the company's fifth route from New York — aside from Boston, JSX flies from New York to Fort Lauderdale Executive Airport (FXE); Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport (OPF); Naples Airport (APF); and President Donald J. Trump International Airport (DJT), formerly known as Palm Beach International, all in Florida.

JSX operates out of 30 airports across the U.S. and Mexico and functions as a public charter service, rather than a formal "airline." This lets the carrier's flights work more like private ones — although anyone can buy a ticket, the flights use posh private Fixed-Base Operators (FBOs) instead of public airport terminals. That allows passengers to venture from curb to seat in just 20 minutes.

More: JSX eyes more turboprops and new mountain routes after strong passenger response

The flight experience itself is equally luxurious with no middle seats, lots of legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, complimentary snacks and drinks and checked luggage that’s returned right at the side of the plane. The carrier has a fleet of 56 ERJ-family jets and 4 ATR 42-600 turboprop aircraft. Overall, the service pitches the idea of private jet convenience for a fraction of the cost.

JSX passengers used to bypass security screening, like passengers on most private flights. In 2025, the carrier implemented its own in-house screening process to address security concerns.

#6133. New Resy Rewards Program Offers 4x Bonus Amex Points For Dining Out

Resy has just launched the Resy Rewards program, which lets American Express card members in the United States earn an extra 4x points per dollar spent at participating Resy restaurants, on top of their credit card rewards. As you’d expect, it’s not quite that straightforward, but I’d still consider this to be pretty exciting!

American Express owns both Resy and Tock (which is now being integrated into Resy), as part of its larger “lifestyle” play for attracting card members. So along with that, Resy is leaning more into the rewards program side of things, with the new Resy Rewards program offering an extra 4x Amex points per dollar spent at eligible Resy restaurants.

Resy Rewards is first launching in New York City, where users will see a new “Rewards” tab within the Resy iOS app, where they can browse and book eligible restaurants. Restaurants participating in the Resy Rewards launch include Carne Mare, Le Crocodile, Hearth, Kiko, OPTO, Le Pavillon, and more. In 2027, Resy Rewards plans to expand to additional U.S. cities, and select Tock venues will become eligible to participate in the program.

So, how exactly does Resy Rewards work? Card members need to enroll a US-based Membership Rewards program eligible card in Resy Rewards, then book a Resy Rewards reservation through the “Rewards” tab in the Resy iOS app, and then pay the bill for the dining experience with the enrolled card. So this requires a little more jumping through hoops than just using an Amex card Resy credit, for example.

These rewards are in addition to whatever the standard rewards are on an Amex card. For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) ordinarily earns 4x points at restaurants globally, so if you dined at a restaurant eligible for Resy Rewards, you could be earning 8x points per dollar spent, which is pretty awesome.

Here’s how Pablo Rivero, CEO of Resy and SVP of American Express Global Dining, describes this:

“For the first time, we’re bringing American Express’s industry-leading Rewards program into the Resy iOS app and connecting two things our Card Members value deeply: great dining experiences and meaningful rewards. As we’ve seen with the success of the Resy Credit, rewarding diners while driving demand and revenue to Resy restaurants is a win on both sides of the table.”

I’m delighted to see Amex introduce an opportunity to earn points for dining out, beyond the bonus categories already offered on some of the issuer’s most popular cards. For the time being, this is rather niche, given that it’s limited to select restaurants in New York City, but the expectation is that it will expand more broadly in 2027 (though it remains to be seen how broadly).

Essentially think of this as being similar to a dining rewards program, as the idea is that restaurants have to opt-in to participate in this, with the hope being that this drums up business for them (and presumably they pay Amex and Resy something extra in exchange for that).

Furthermore, you do have to specifically reserve your reservation through Resy to qualify for this, so if you don’t have a reservation made through the “Rewards” tab on Resy, then you won’t earn bonus points.

I’m happy to see this, as earning 8x points on dining when paying with the Amex Gold Card is quite a great deal. Then again, so much of my dining out is through InKind, which is my favorite dining rewards program, given the excellent selection of restaurants the program has in Miami, and it’s tough to compete with the rewards offered by the program.

The new Resy Rewards program offers bonus Amex points when you make a reservation at an eligible restaurant and then pay with your eligible Amex card. The idea is that you can earn an extra 4x points per dollar spent on purchases at eligible restaurants, which is pretty awesome.

The catch is that this is initially launching in New York City, only “eligible” restaurants qualify, and you need to reserve through Resy and then pay with the same linked card in order to earn the bonus points. It’s nice to see this launch, and I look forward to it expanding to more markets.
