#6132. Here's How Much Larger The Boeing 737 MAX 7 Is Over The Jet It Directly Replaces

Wirestock Creators | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

The Boeing 737 MAX 7 finally received airworthiness certification from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on August 3, allowing it to enter production and succeed the legacy 737-700 Next Generation. Aside from being a modernized replacement with better fuel efficiency and superior technology throughout the airframe, the MAX 7 is quite a bit larger than its predecessor. It is essentially the direct result of specific requests from the type's best customer, Southwest Airlines.

Although the MAX 7 first flew in March 2018, its rollout stalled following the 737 MAX groundings. Southwest Airlines holds roughly 237 to 264 firm orders for the Boeing 737 MAX 7, accounting for nearly 90% of the model's entire order book. Since Southwest operates an all-737 fleet and is the world's largest 737 customer, Boeing essentially custom-built the MAX 7's stretched dimensions to keep Southwest from defecting to Airbus.

Adding two rows of seats lowers the cost per seat-mile, making the jet far more profitable on high-frequency domestic routes than a direct size-for-size replacement would have been. Those make the plane six feet longer than the 737-700 NG, while its wingspan is nearly identical, but it weighs over 20,000 lb (10,000 kg) more. It boasts the longest range in the entire 737 MAX lineup as a result of its shorter, lighter airframe using the wing, fuselage center, and gear of the larger 737 MAX 8.

Boeing initially marketed the 737 MAX 7 as a direct, one-for-one replacement for the 737-700, keeping nearly identical length, seat capacity, and layout. However, the heavier CFM LEAP-1B engines added dead-weight drag without increasing passenger capacity. As the launch customer whose massive, single-fleet 737 commitment gave it overwhelming leverage, Southwest was not impressed and threatened defection to the clean-sheet Bombardier CSeries, now the Airbus A220-300. SWA has even joined WestJet in demanding lower seat-mile costs from the smallest member of the 737 MAX line.

In response, Boeing scrapped the original blueprint it debuted at the 2016 Farnborough International Airshow and stretched the fuselage by 76 inches (1.93 meters), adding 30 inches (0.76 meters) forward of the wing box and 46 inches (1.17 meters) aft. That increased the MAX 7's two-class capacity to 153 passengers. Paired with twin LEAP-1B turbofans and larger fuel tanks, the heavier airframe stretched its unrefueled range out to 3,850 nautical miles (7,130 kilometers).

The new cabin gave Southwest a dozen additional revenue-generating seats on every flight without adding cockpit crew. Stretching the fuselage brought the jet's seat-mile costs down to competitive levels. While the 175-seat MAX 8 is Southwest's workhorse on major trunk routes, it is too large to fly profitably multiple times a day on thinner point-to-point routes or off-peak business schedules. Getting Boeing to stretch the MAX 7 gave Southwest A220-level capacity while keeping a 100% 737 fleet.

Certification delays for the 737 MAX 7 left launch customer Southwest Airlines unable to build reliable schedules around its order book of roughly 300 jets meant to replace aging 737-700s. To keep new aircraft arriving, Southwest converted large blocks of slots into 175-seat 737 MAX 8s, creating network imbalances as the larger jets flew half-empty on thinner routes while 25-year-old 737-700s required costly structural overhauls.

During these delays, Airbus saw an opportunity and made a strong pitch for the clean-sheet A220-300. The A220-300 is built with carbon-fiber composite wings, aluminum-lithium fuselage panels, and Pratt & Whitney geared turbofans. Its operating empty weight is about 81,790 pounds (37,100 kilograms), about 17,600 pounds (7,983 kilograms) lighter than Boeing's all-metal MAX 7. This results in a significantly lower trip fuel burn on 130-seat missions.

Despite the A220-300's clean-sheet fuel efficiency, Southwest and Boeing resolved to preserve the carrier's 50-year single-fleet business model. Breaking its all-737 discipline to introduce an Airbus jet would have forced Southwest to build separate pilot training pipelines, split spare-parts inventories, and sacrifice the operational flexibility to swap aircraft seamlessly during weather disruptions.

Boeing optimized the extended MAX 7 to use raw gross weight, range, and seating density to offset the structural advantage of the A220. The MAX 7 provided equivalent seat-mile economics while maintaining uniformity for all pilots, mechanics, and gate crew on a single aircraft family by carrying up to 12 more passengers in high-density single-class layouts and traveling 400 nautical miles (741 kilometers) farther than the A220-300.

What's behind the hold-up, and how does it impact the airline’s future?

Following its August FAA certification and planned March 2027 passenger debut, the MAX 7 takes over missions from Southwest's nearly 290 retiring 737-700s. Its smaller size relative to the MAX 8 means Southwest can offer multiple daily flights between mid-sized cities without having to cut ticket prices just to fill the plane. The 150-seat-count cabin also lets the airline fly with three flight attendants instead of four, saving on crew costs while still carrying more passengers than its predecessor.

Already numbering over 340 jets in Southwest's active fleet, the MAX 8 is found flying high-demand routes between major focus cities such as Dallas, Denver, Las Vegas, Chicago Midway, and Baltimore. With 175 seats, it delivers the lowest cost per seat-mile in the fleet and maximizes revenue at slot-controlled or congested airports where adding extra daily flights is not possible. Notably, the MAX 7 also handles tough flying conditions better than its bigger sibling.

Pairing the lighter body of the MAX 7 with the MAX 8's wings, engines, and fuel tanks gives it extra climbing power and range. That makes it a great plane for serving fields with short runways or high-altitude airports, or for long trips to Hawaii and the Caribbean, where a heavier MAX 8 might have to leave passengers or bags behind to take off with enough fuel.

Southwest's latest interline deal opens connections to Paris, Tahiti and the Indian Ocean while strengthening French bee's US reach.

Southwest’s recent transition from a traditional low-cost carrier into a more conventional, legacy-style airline was distinctly marked by ending its 54-year open-seating policy in January. SWA has since added extra-legroom sections, introduced checked bag fees, and is now planning airport lounges. This paradigm shift in the identity of the airline directly shapes how the MAX 7 fits into its network.

Flying a heavier jet changes the economics of Southwest's schedule. Because airports base landing fees on aircraft weight, the 22,500-pound (10,206-kilogram) jump over the 737-700 makes short, cheap regional hops less profitable. To offset those higher airport charges, Southwest has to put the MAX 7 on longer routes where its fuel-saving engines and higher-priced extra-legroom seats earn enough to cover the extra weight.

The trade-off of the MAX 7's design gives Southwest the cabin space, amenities, and long-haul capability to compete with Delta, United, and American Airlines of the 'Big Three.' The stretched cabin allows the airline to carve out a dedicated extra-legroom section without sacrificing total seat count or adding a fourth flight attendant.

The MAX 7 gives Southwest the right-sized tool to attract higher-spending business and leisure flyers. Still, even after Boeing hands over the first jets in late 2026, Southwest needs roughly three months of ferry flights, maintenance checks, and FAA-monitored proving runs before carrying paying passengers in March 2027.

They'll all take off in time for Thanksgiving. Find out more here!

Following extensive test flights across the western United States, the Federal Aviation Administration granted final certification for Boeing to begin full production of the MAX 7 in August. Roughly 30 completed MAX 7 jets are finally preparing to depart long-term storage to enter service since earning FAA approval. Technicians are now unwrapping those stored jets and installing the anti-ice upgrades ahead of deliveries to Southwest, setting the stage for passenger flights in early 2027.

The Max 7s have been waiting at the main plant as Boeing spent years clearing out the massive 'shadow factory' of hundreds of grounded MAX 8s and MAX 9s in Moses Lake, Washington. At the same time, mechanics are reworking the parked inventory; Boeing has been overhauling its manufacturing footprint to build new MAX 7s alongside the rest of the MAX family. Newly built MAX 7s are scheduled to start rolling off the Renton line for Southwest in February 2027.

To break years-long supply-chain bottlenecks as it ramps up toward a target of 47 MAX jets per month, Boeing activated a fourth 737 assembly line dubbed the North Line. Yet, getting the MAX 7 has also turned the spotlight in Renton directly toward the largest member of the family, the 737 MAX 10. Southwest anchors the MAX 7 order book with more than 300 orders through 2031, but major carriers like United, Delta, and WestJet are counting on the 230-seat MAX 10 to rival the Airbus A321neo on high-capacity routes around the globe.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Yet the stretched flagship remains stuck in regulatory limbo over flight management software flaws, unique telescoping landing gear, and strict cockpit alerting rules. Until the FAA signs off on those final design changes, airlines across North America are left waiting to see if Boeing can break the last remaining logjam in the MAX lineup and finally close out its troubled narrowbody certification saga.

#6131. Delta SkyMiles & World Of Hyatt Partnership Live: Dual Earning, Milestone Rewards, & Linking Accounts

In September 2026, Delta SkyMiles and World of Hyatt unveiled plans to launch a new, long term strategic partnership. This announcement came just shortly after American AAdvantage and World of Hyatt announced that they will be ending their partnership.

At the time, we didn’t actually have any details as to what the partnership would entail, but that has now changed, as additional information has been revealed. Parts of the partnership are even now live, and members can already link their accounts.

Delta and Hyatt are launching a new loyalty program collaboration, which comes with a “shared ambition to create additional value, recognition and engagement opportunities across more of the travel journey.” This includes reciprocal opportunities to earn rewards, and also reciprocal opportunities to select perks with the partner brand.

Here’s how Laurie Blair, Hyatt’s SVP of Global Marketing and Loyalty, describes this:

“World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles were each built to make travel more meaningful and rewarding, which makes this collaboration feel meant to be. By connecting the Delta flight and Hyatt stay, we are helping members get more from the journeys they are already taking while opening the door to new experiences, destinations and memories. It is an exciting next step in our commitment to caring for members throughout the full travel journey, from takeoff to check out.”

Here’s how Dwight James, Delta’s SVP of Customer Engagement & Loyalty, describes this:

“At Delta, we know loyalty is something we earn by delivering meaningful value and experiences that make our Members want to keep choosing us. Our relationship with World of Hyatt gives us another way to do that by recognizing and rewarding Members across more of their travel, while creating new ways to earn, engage and experience both brands.”

Effective immediately (as of November 17, 2026), elite members of both loyalty programs can earn simultaneously with the new “Dual Earn” benefit. Members must link their accounts, and can then earn additional rewards.

World of Hyatt members can earn bonus points on eligible Delta flights (which includes Delta Comfort, Delta Premium Select, Delta First Class, and Delta One), as follows:

Delta SkyMiles members can earn bonus miles on eligible Hyatt stays (which includes qualifying room rates, qualifying incidental spend, and qualifying non-stay charges at participating Hyatt properties, eligible Mr & Mrs Smith spend booked through Hyatt, and eligible spend at The Venetian booked through Hyatt):

As of 2027, eligible elite members of both World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles will gain access to new milestone reward choices, giving people more ways to earn, and more flexibility in how they use their loyalty benefits. This would apply to World of Hyatt Milestone Rewards, and Delta SkyMiles Choice Benefits.

As of January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will be able to choose Delta awards as they reach qualifying Milestone Rewards thresholds. The first Delta award choice will become available at 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 base points, with additional choices as members progress through the program, including:

As of February 1, 2027, Delta SkyMiles members will be able to choose Hyatt awards as they reach qualifying Choice Benefits thresholds. Members will be able to select free night awards, as follows:

To celebrate the start of this partnership, Hyatt and Delta are offering limited time offers for members who link their accounts.

First, from November 17 through December 31, 2026, linked members can register to earn one additional World of Hyatt elite night after completing their first qualifying Hyatt stay during the offer period. Taking advantage of this should be a no-brainer.

Next, from January 4 through February 15, 2027, linked members can:

Basically, Hyatt has dumped American in favor of Delta. Admittedly the partnership between American and Hyatt had already been scaled back over time. The two programs used to offer a dual accrual opportunity as well, but that was eventually cut.

After all, companies only want to offer perks like that if they’re driving incremental business, and I imagine at some point it’s hard to justify that expense, when you feel like there’s not much upside left:

Now the Delta and Hyatt partnership is starting out in a similar way to how the American one did, with one major exception. On the dual accrual front, SkyMiles elite members are lucky, as they earn rewards on all qualifying Hyatt spending. Meanwhile World of Hyatt members only earn rewards when booking premium tickets, which is a bit disappointing. And here I was thinking that all seats on Delta aircraft are premium!!

I do have to say, as much as I’m a World of Hyatt loyalist, the program has certainly become less differentiated over time. While Delta can argue all it wants about how premium it is, SkyMiles simply isn’t as good of a loyalty program as AAdvantage. So perhaps this swap reflects the direction Hyatt is trying to head on loyalty… I dunno.

Delta and Hyatt have launched an exclusive new partnership, which explains why American and Hyatt cut ties. The partnership is now live, and it includes dual points accrual opportunities, reciprocal milestone perks, and some limited time opportunities.

At a minimum, it’s definitely worth linking accounts. And if you’re a World of Hyatt member with a stay planned before the end of the year, be sure to register for an extra elite night, as there’s no reason not to take advantage of that.

#6129. Earning World Of Hyatt Elite Nights & Status With Credit Cards: Worth It?

Chase and Hyatt have two co-branded credit cards — the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more). I’d consider these to be among the more lucrative hotel credit cards out there, particularly the personal version of the card.

One of the awesome things about Hyatt’s two credit cards is that they can earn you elite nights, making it easier to qualify for status in the World of Hyatt program. In this post, I’d like to get into the nitty-gritty of how earning Hyatt elite status with credit cards works, and discuss whether it’s worth it.

Chase and Hyatt have both the World of Hyatt Credit Card (a personal card) and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (a business card). Both cards have valuable benefits, though I think the personal card is considerably more compelling than the business card. Let me start by just briefly recapping the perks of the two cards.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card has a $95 annual fee and offers:

This means that you’re getting five elite nights toward status and a Category 1-4 free night award every year just for having the card. To me that more than justifies the annual fee, by a long shot (I consistently get $250+ of value out of the free night certificate alone). That doesn’t even factor in the incremental perks you can get for spending on the card.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card has a $199 annual fee and offers:

The business version of the card isn’t quite as rewarding as the personal version of the card, especially if you’re not a big spender. However, for businesses that spend quite a bit on credit cards, this can be the best card for earning elite status.

Both the World of Hyatt Credit Card and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offer the ability to earn elite nights. However, the ways in which you earn elite nights differ between the two cards, so let’s go over those details.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers qualifying nights toward Hyatt status in two ways. First of all, the World of Hyatt Card offers five elite nights annually just for having the card. There’s no spending required to earn these five elite nights, and you receive them for each calendar year in which you have the card, including the year in which you open the card.

Beyond that, the World of Hyatt Card offers two elite nights for every $5,000 spent on the card (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,500 of spending). There’s no limit to how many elite nights you can earn this way, and the elite nights earned through spending on this card aren’t in any way tied to the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $2,500 on the card in 2026 and then spend $2,500 on the card in 2027, you’d earn two elite nights at that point.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offers five elite nights for every $10,000 spent on the card in a calendar year (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,000 of spending). On this card, the spending counter resets at the beginning of the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $8,000 on the card in 2026, you’d still have to spend a full $10,000 in 2027 to earn five elite nights.

As you can see, this card offers elite nights for spending at an accelerated rate, though unlike the personal card, it doesn’t offer the five elite nights annually just for having the card.

How soon do elite nights post from the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card?

While the above covers the basics, I’d like to now analyze the overall value proposition of earning World of Hyatt elite status by spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, including addressing some of the most common questions and scenarios that come up.

With Hyatt, not all elite perks are tied directly to having status, but rather some require earning a certain number of elite nights in a year, known as the Milestone Rewards program. The Milestone Rewards program is how you earn perks like suite upgrade awards, club access awards, Guest of Honor awards, and more.

Hyatt elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards would count toward Milestone Rewards the same as any hotel stays would, which adds further value to credit card spending.

One of the perks of both Hyatt credit cards is that you receive Discoverist status for as long as you have the card. Discoverist status ordinarily requires 10 elite qualifying nights or 25,000 base points per year. As a reminder, here are World of Hyatt’s elite thresholds:

One common point of confusion is that people assume these cards really come with up to 15 elite nights per year. They assume you already get Discoverist status, and that any elite nights are on top of that. Note that while these cards offer Discoverist status, you don’t get the elite nights that correspond to that.

This means that if you have a Hyatt credit card, you’ll receive Discoverist status on an ongoing basis (and five elite nights every year if you have the personal card), but you’ll still need to qualify for Explorist or Globalist status based on the full criteria.

Hyatt’s lifetime Globalist status is based on earning one million base points in the program. World of Hyatt members earn five base points per dollar spent on Hyatt stays, meaning you essentially have to spend $200,000 at Hyatts to earn lifetime Globalist status.

Credit card spending, and any elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards, won’t count toward lifetime Globalist status. That’s because the qualification criteria is based solely on base points, and not based on elite qualifying nights (in which case it would count).

World of Hyatt Globalist is my favorite top tier hotel status, and what I love is that Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards make it easier to earn that. Let’s look at the best strategy for earning Globalist status with the card. Hyatt Globalist status ordinarily requires earning 60 qualifying nights in a year. So how much would you have to spend on a Hyatt credit card to earn that status?

On the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you’d need to spend $140,000 to earn Globalist status:

Meanwhile on the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you’d need to spend $120,000 to earn Globalist status:

As you can see, the personal credit card offers more elite nights upfront, while the business credit card offers elite nights at a faster pace for spending (assuming you can reach the thresholds).

When you’re analyzing the value of spending your way toward status, don’t forget that even beyond the general status perks, the Milestone Rewards perks could really add up. For example, if you make it to 60 elite nights, you could select five suite upgrade awards and four club access awards, and would also receive a Category 1-7 free night award, a Category 1-4 free night award, and three Guest of Honor awards.

Then on the personal version of the card, you also receive an additional Category 1-4 free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a year. The value of all of those perks really adds up.

Hyatt counts award nights toward status, and just for having the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you get a free night every year, plus the opportunity to earn a further three free nights for spending $15,000, earning Explorist status, and earning Globalist status.

On top of that, presumably you want to earn Globalist status because you actually intend to stay at Hyatts with some frequency. Hotel status is worthless if you don’t actually stay at that brand.

To be realistic, let’s assume that long term you’re earning 30 elite nights per year through actual stays. There are so many great Globalist benefits to use (like suite upgrade awards and free night awards), so if you’re staying at Hyatts less than that I question whether Globalist is worth it for you.

If you earned 30 of the required 60 elite nights through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following:

Given all the incremental perks you’re picking up with Milestone Rewards, I’d say the math could really check out.

When deciding if it makes sense to spend money on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, consider the opportunity cost of the spending. For easy math purposes, I tend to consider the opportunity cost of credit card spending to be around 3.4%.

That’s because based on my valuation of miles & points, most transferable points currencies are worth 1.7 cents each, and you have some cards offering 2x points per dollar spent. Meanwhile I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

If we were to theoretically assume you’re spending $60,000 on a Hyatt credit card per year (give or take) in order to earn Globalist status, what’s the opportunity cost of that spending? By my math, you’re looking at an opportunity cost of up to 2% (the spread between a 3.4% return and 1.4% return). That’s around $1,200, if you value things the way that I do. But that’s not factoring in the value of all the other perks mentioned above:

For many, I think the above perks could more than justify the difference in return on spending otherwise.

There are many things to love about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, though the ability to get a fast track toward status is probably my favorite perk. I absolutely love Hyatt Globalist status, and credit cards have historically helped me requalify for status. If you’re a Hyatt loyalist and don’t yet have the hotel group’s co-branded credit cards, they’re seriously worth considering.

Alaska Airlines will add four new destinations across the U.S. to its map.

But the additions come at a cost: The carrier has discontinued four recently added routes from its hub at Portland International Airport (PDX) in Oregon.

As airline executives say, every route has to earn its place financially in a carrier’s network.

As for the four new destinations, Alaska will serve each of those with one daily flight from its Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) base. The additions are:

The carrier will also add a new nonstop from SEA to Guadalajara International Airport (GDL) in Mexico. Alaska will offer three weekly flights on Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays with a 737-800 from March 18, 2027 through Aug. 9, 2027.

Alaska currently serves GDL from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Jose Mineta International Airport (SJC) in California's Bay Area, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

The Seattle growth comes as Alaska builds its intercontinental offerings from the Pacific Northwest city. After launching its first long-haul flights in 2025 after its merger with Hawaiian Airlines, Alaska is building out a network of at least 15 intercontinental routes from SEA by 2030.

Next year, Alaska will offer nine long-haul routes from SEA with the addition of Athens International Airport (ATH), Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), Kansai Airport (KIX) in Osaka, Japan, and Faaʼa International Airport (PPT) in Tahiti.

Alaska plans to grow its schedule by about 4% year-over-year in 2027, with the majority in long-haul international additions.

PDX, Alaska’s wunderkind hub of recent years, is losing four recently added routes. The airline will not resume seasonal service in 2027 to:

Alaska continues to serve all four destinations from one of its other hubs.

PDX remains one of Alaska’s fastest-growing hubs as the airline shifts connections to the Oregon city. The carrier's seats at the airport are set to increase 12% in the first half of 2027 compared to this year after a 17% increase during the same period in 2026, Cirium schedules show.

"Portland is a story of focused smart growth that improves utility, strengthens the local franchise and captures the right traffic flows," Andrew Harrison, the chief commercial officer at Alaska, said in September. "[PDX] proves that Seattle and Portland are stronger together, allowing us to serve more customers, connect more traffic and improve the efficiency of our Pacific Northwest network."

As part of its PDX growth, Alaska Airlines opened a new, $18 million lounge at the airport in June.

#6127. Dem governor’s tale of mourning fellow serviceman ripped apart after soldier's wife gives brutal fact check

Fox News Digital spoke to Retired Lt. Col. Jamie Gottschling who pushed back against Moore’s claims that he "led paratroopers in combat" in Afghanistan.

Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore – widely believed to be seriously weighing a presidential run in 2028 – is facing controversy yet again over his characterization of his military record, this time facing allegations he embellished his relationship with a fallen soldier and used an impossible timeline to tell an emotional story in his memoir.

The issue stems from a Baltimore Sun report over the weekend highlighting a passage in Moore's 2015 book, "The Work: Searching for a Life That Matters," where he told the story of breaking into tears at his grandfather's funeral when hearing about the death of his friend Tobias "Toby" Meister.

"Inside that casket, I also saw Toby," Moore wrote in his book, adding that he cried for his grandfather, Toby and other fallen soldiers.

MARYLAND GOV WES MOORE IN HOT SEAT AFTER REPORT QUESTIONS CLAIM ABOUT GRANDFATHER AND KKK

Gov. Wes Moore (D-Md.) appears on "Meet the Press" in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 7, 2025. (Shannon Finney/NBC via Getty Images)

However, Moore's grandfather's funeral was on Dec. 17, 2005. Meister was killed in a roadside bombing 11 days later, on Dec. 28, 2005.

Moore did not learn about Meister's death until January of the next year, when he returned to Afghanistan, the Baltimore Sun reported.

After Meister's death, his wife Alicia told the outlet that many of his friends from the military have reached out to her over the years and kept his memory alive with their son, who was just over a year old when his father was killed.

A group of soldiers patrols in Afghanistan. (Getty Images Creatives)

"I’ve never heard from him," his wife, Alicia, told the outlet. "I’ve never personally heard from him," she added. "I don’t know who [Moore] is. I don’t recall my late husband ever talking about him."

WES MOORE CONFRONTED ON REPORTED MISREPRESENTATIONS ABOUT MISSING OXFORD THESIS, STORY ABOUT GREAT-GRANDFATHER

Days after the Baltimore Sun reached out to Moore's office for comment, Alicia Meister said she heard from Moore.

"It was good," she told the outlet. "He paid his respects and apologized for not reaching out sooner."

She added, "I do wish, though, that my late husband would be removed from the situation completely. I just don’t like that he has been brought in the middle of it."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Moore spokesperson Ammar Moussa pushed back.

"Governor Moore is deeply proud of his military service. He raised his hand to serve his country at 17, left his civilian career, and deployed to one of the most dangerous regions in Afghanistan, where he served with distinction and earned the praise of his superiors and fellow service members," Moussa said.

"A Republican swiftboat campaign orchestrated by Sinclair executive chairman David Smith reached a new, despicable low. Smith—a right-wing billionaire ally of Donald Trump—is now exploiting grieving families and fellow service members for a political hit job. The facts are clear and confirmed by the Governor’s fellow service members: Governor Moore knew and worked with First Sgt. Toby Meister in Afghanistan, and this shameless attempt to drag a grieving Gold Star family into the political mud is a disgrace."

Moussa also accused Sinclair of lying about Moore's response in the article and calling it a "bad-faith approach" that is "typical of an organization run by a right-wing billionaire who is using his media empire to try and intimidate the Governor into silence."

1st Lt. Anthony Del Signore, a Marine who served alongside Moore in Afghanistan, has also defended Moore against recent criticism.

"Questioning his combat record isn't just a political attack on him—it diminishes the very real dangers all of us faced out on those roads. Wes did his job, took the risks, and served honorably," he said. "Turning our deployment into a partisan hit job is an insult to everyone who wore the uniform."

Moore previously acknowledged the conflicting timeline in interviews with the Baltimore Banner in June, attributing the inaccuracy to poor editing and the effects of stress, grief and time on his memory.

Chelsea Clinton and Gov. Wes Moore speak onstage during the Clinton Global Initiative 2026 Annual Meeting at New York Hilton Midtown on Sept. 22, 2026, in New York City. (JP Yim/Getty Images for Clinton Global Initiative)

The report comes on the heels of a Baltimore Sun story earlier this month in which his former Army supervisor questioned the governor's claim that he led soldiers in combat, a story told in the same book.

In an investigative deep dive into Moore's military service, the Baltimore Sun spoke with retired Army Lt. Col. James A. "Jamie" Gottschling, who served with Moore in Afghanistan in 2005 and 2006. What Gottschling described was Moore's patriotic service and dutiful fulfillment of his role, but exaggerations — and in some cases falsehoods — about incidents that occurred overseas.

Sgt. Matthew Taylor from Orlando, Florida, 1st Lt. Wes Brockbank from Seattle, Washington, and Cpl. Matthew Moebes from Decatur, Alabama, with the U.S. Army's 4th Squadron 2nd Cavalry Regiment, walk through a village during a joint patrol with Afghan National Army soldiers near Kandahar, Afghanistan, on March 2, 2014. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

Del Signore pushed back on that criticism as well, saying in a statement, "I’ve heard the comments from Major Gottschling claiming this didn't happen and that Wes didn't go outside the wire. I can tell you that this 100% happened because I was there."

"Wes and I were outside the wire an average amount of the time, we traveled a decent amount, and we'd be gone for a week at a time traveling around the region. It is not surprising that Major Gottschling doesn't think this happened because he was not in the chain of command that would have been reported to, and he wasn't in charge of the convoy."

Additionally, a New York Times exposé found in 2024 that Moore for years claimed to be the recipient of a Bronze Star when he had not been awarded one at the time. He included the Bronze Star claim on his resumé when applying for a White House fellowship in 2006. In 2024, he received the award after then-Sen. Laphonza Butler, D-Calif., urged the Army to give him one.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

#6126. Why The World's Debut Boeing 747 Was Built In Half The Time Of Other Aircraft Of Its Size In 1968

The Boeing 747 has earned its title as one of the most iconic airliners ever built for several reasons. It was the first widebody aircraft, easily distinguishable by a humped second deck, a key enabler in opening up aviation to the masses, and it enjoyed roughly fifty years of production. But equally as impressive as the Queen of the Skies itself is how it came about.

Boeing took the 747 from the drawing board to rollout remarkably quickly. That is, notably faster than the Airbus A380 program took to churn out its first model after officially launching, and quicker than both Boeing and Airbus took with their latest widebodies. What is more, Boeing pulled it off decades ago in the late 1960s.

Just 29 months separated the 747 project’s official launch and the rollout of the first model. Boeing announced on April 13, 1966, that it would build the 490-seat passenger transport that would come to be known as the 747. Exactly two years, five months, and 17 days later, on September 30, 1968, the first 747-100 ceremoniously rolled off the production line at a new purpose-built assembly plant in Everett, Washington.

Less than five months later, on February 9, 1969, the aircraft took off for its maiden flight. Test pilots Jack Waddell and Brien Wygle, accompanied by flight engineer Jess Wallick, took the controls, and the jumbo jet passed the major test with flying colors, paving the way for its introduction into service just under a year later in January 1970.

All told, that saw the Queen of the Skies go from a mere concept to carrying passengers in under four years. While that is no doubt a rapid turnaround by today’s standards, the reasons behind the pace are plentiful and clear-cut.

Behind it all was keen interest from Pan American World Airways, which had set out to source a jet two and a half times larger than the existing Boeing 707 against the backdrop of an increasingly busy market. Though the industry was mulling whether supersonic flight would come to dominate in the years ahead, there remained appeal for a huge, versatile airliner that could handle cargo operations rather than passenger services in the future, if needed.

As it turned out, Boeing had already looked into something similar, having lost out in a 1965 military transport design competition to the Lockheed C-5 Galaxy. Although the 747 was ultimately largely built from scratch, research into high-bypass engine technology and the thinking behind the 747’s distinctive hump can be traced back to the military project bid. As such, when Pan Am head Juan Trippe and then-Boeing president William Allen met that same year for initial discussions about the 747, something of a basis was already there.

It was Trippe himself who is said to have pushed so heavily for the 747. He had spent years beforehand attempting to open up aviation to the masses, overseeing the introduction of the world’s first economy fare in 1958, for instance. Given that an ambitious project like the 747 would only aid in reaching that goal, Trippe reportedly told Allen in 1965: “If you’ll build it, I’ll buy it.” By April 1966, the commitment was solidified through a $525 million deal — worth almost $5.5 billion today — for 25 of the new jumbo jets. This set an ambitious deadline of 1969 for the first delivery, though.

The 747 transcended aviation and became an iconic silhouette.

Nonetheless, Boeing did not waste any time in dwelling on the task at hand. After signing the contract with Pan Am, the design team of just a few hundred workers conceptualizing and writing up requirements for the 747 ballooned to 4,500 almost instantaneously. These workers, who would later become part of a group known as The Incredibles, were led by Joe Sutter, who would similarly earn the title of the Father of the 747 over time.

Sutter himself enjoyed a 40-year-long career at Boeing, although he recalled in a 2013 interview fearing for his job as he and his team rushed to get the 747 ready. Without public backing, Boeing found itself racking up debt on the back of the project, leaving Sutter under pressure to cut jobs. Instead, he requested hundreds more engineers. “I figured that was the day I lost my job at Boeing,” he said, “but I went to work the next day, and nobody said anything, so I kept working."

According to Boeing, some 50,000 employees ultimately ended up working on the jumbo jet over the course of its development cycle. Armed with an eye-watering 75,000 drawings, physical assembly of the first model got underway in September 1967, a year prior to its initial presentation to the world and only 16 months before the first flight. All of this, of course, required a specialized facility for production to actually be carried out.

Such a factory did not exist when Boeing first unveiled plans for the 747, so it had to be built almost in conjunction with the first model. Among the battles Sutter fought in his bid to steer the project to a timely conclusion was one over where his team would be based. Faced with the proposal of being sent to California, Sutter argued against it and insisted his engineers stay close to where those who would eventually build the aircraft would work.

This turned out to be Everett, which was far from Boeing’s first choice to house the 747 program initially, but prevailed on similar fears that key personnel would not relocate in great numbers to a new facility elsewhere. Regardless of where the 747 would be built, a new building would have to be constructed to accommodate such a vast aircraft and all the equipment needed to build it.

Under the tight deadline set by the deal with Pan Am, Boeing set about clearing forest and then building the facility in 1967. Work began just before assembly of the first 747 started, but the two efforts overlapped, meaning the prototype was under construction in an incomplete factory for a period. When the former was eventually completed, it took the crown as the largest building in the world by volume — a title it retains to this day and a reflection of the mammoth undertaking by Boeing to get the project off the ground.

The original designs for the Boeing 747 were made with a different purpose in mind. Find out how the 747 came to be as we know it today.

Naturally, such an effort required vast financial backing, and it took a monumental amount of risk on Boeing’s part to get the first 747 successfully turned around at such a pace. Boeing had secured $525 million — or $21 million per aircraft — under its deal with Pan Am. This covered barely half of the program's total $1 billion costas it transpired; however, adjusted for inflation, it would exceed $10 billion today.

As a result, Boeing faced financial pressure and was forced to turn to the banks, which explains Sutter being asked to cut engineers midway through the program. He said in 2013 that “it was a big gamble,” adding, “I think the only reason that it happened is that Bill Allen was a forward-seeking guy, and Juan Trippe from Pan Am also had that characteristic.”

Despite racking up debt, the gamble paid off, and the 747 was a resounding success. Not only did the first model get built and delivered on time, but the factory Boeing built for the jumbo jet has enjoyed decades of service since. Some 1,574 747s rolled out of the site over the life of the program, culminating in the delivery of a final 747-8 Freighter variant to Atlas Air in 2023. Notably, this saw production of the 747 end just a year before that of its primary challenger, the A380, despite its initial introduction decades earlier.

The A380 is an impressive feat of engineering in its own right. The industry moved in a different direction, and while Boeing hit a sweet spot with the 747, the appetite for huge quad jets was by no means as strong as it was at the A380’s commercial entry in 2007. All told, this saw the 254th and final A380 completed in 2021.

Airbus grappled with a string of delays between officially launching the A380 in December 2000, unveiling a prototype in January 2005, and then making the initial delivery to Singapore Airlines in 2007. How severely these impacted the A380’s long-term success is up for debate. Either way, the A380’s stretched timeline offers some context for how impressive Boeing’s effort was in getting the 747 up and running so quickly.

And it is not just the A380. Boeing itself took three years and six months to show off its first 777 after launching the program in October 1990. Its 787, despite going from concept to prototype in three years and three months, then took an additional two years and five months to first take off in December 2009. As for Airbus, the A350 and its answer to the clean-sheet 787 went from launch to initial rollout in six years and five months. Similarly, the 777X project took more than five years after launching in 2013 to produce a prototype, with certification still not secured today.

#6125. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night."

Trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over."

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly."

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”

#6124. Tulum Is Losing Airlines Fast: Why The Hyped New Airport Is Failing

In late 2023, we saw the opening of the Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport (TQO), in Tulum, Mexico. For those not familiar, Tulum is located on the eastern coast of the Yucatan Peninsula, and for years, it was a growing tourist destination.

While it could previously be accessed via Cancun International Airport (CUN), the hope was that by opening a new international airport, visitor numbers would expand massively. Unfortunately what has actually happened is exactly the opposite, as airline after airline has pulled out. What exactly is going on here? I think it makes for an interesting story, and thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this.

In 2023, we saw airline after airline announce flights to Tulum. Among US carriers, we saw American, Delta, JetBlue, and United, all launch flights to Tulum, while Spirit announced flights, but never launched them.

That was only a small part of the overall international service to the airport, as we also saw flights to Tulum on Air Canada, Air Transat, Avianca, Copa, Discover, and WestJet, along with flights on domestic carriers like Aeromexico, Mexicana de Aviacion, Viva, and Volaris.

Less than three years after the airport opened, where do things stand? When it comes to international year-round service, we’ve now gone from service to 12 airports, to service to four airports, which is an absolutely massive reduction:

Just to put this into numbers, in the first half of 2026, the airport saw a 33.2% reduction in passengers. June 2026 was the worst month to date, with a 44.8% drop, as there were just 47,600 passengers, compared to 86,200 passengers the year prior.

It goes without saying that for a newly built airport, this is rather catastrophic, and not what you hope to see.

In some ways, it feels like the whole concept behind Tulum Airport was sort of unnecessary. That’s also easily explained by the fact that the airport was well over a decade in the making, so while I can see how it might’ve seemed like a good idea at some point, tourism trends do evolve over time.

The reality is that there was a point where Tulum was cool, edgy, and a bit off the beaten path, compared to… whatever it is now. But when it comes to the struggles that airlines have had with flying to Tulum, it seems like the problems have been endless:

It’ll be interesting to see if Tulum can reverse any of these trends, and regain visitors…

A few years ago Tulum Airport opened to some fanfare, as a good number of airlines rushed to add service there. Unfortunately the excitement didn’t last long, as the airport has gone from a dozen year-round international routes, to just four.

This reduction in demand particularly evident from the United States, as soon there will just be nonstop service on American and Delta, and even that will be with reduced frequencies and routes.

Tulum Airport is facing endless challenges, not the least of which is a decline in visitors to Mexico from the United States, combined with increasing competition for those fewer visitors. Mexico just isn’t a value destination in the way that it used to be in places like Cancun, Tulum, Los Cabos, etc., and that’s understandably impacting demand.

I’m curious if Tulum can find a way to turn things around, but it’s not a good situation.

What do you make of the Tulum Airport demand problem?

#6123. Delta CEO: “Customers Are Not Choosing Airlines Based On Wi-Fi”

I’ve gotta be honest, I don’t envy the situation that Delta CEO Ed Bastian is in. Unlike most other carriers in the United States, Delta hasn’t opted for SpaceX Starlink Wi-Fi, and has instead gone with Amazon Leo.

In theory that’s fine, except Amazon Leo is years behind Starlink, and just faced a new setback, due to a rocket failure. Elon Musk has also repeatedly publicly ridiculed Bastian, regarding what Bastian reportedly said about Musk to employees.

There’s now an interesting update, as Bastian made some comments about the carrier’s Wi-Fi choice, and overall customer preferences. It sure is amazing how narratives can change, based on what’s convenient…

This week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum 2026, Delta’s CEO was asked about the carrier’s decision not to choose Starlink, plus the public spat with Musk. Here’s what Bastian had to say about this:

“We’ve been the leader in Wi-Fi, and in free and fast Wi-Fi, and we’ve been at it for five years. I’ve got a long history with Elon on that. We’ve looked at Starlink, we actually helped them started in aviation, we gave them our planes to use during COVID, when we weren’t flying, and they tested the system out. We just couldn’t come to agreement on a business model.”

“We’ve been the leader in free, fast Wi-Fi. We are confident there will be more than one LEO product in the world other than Starlink, and I’m confident Amazon has the capability to do a great job. Customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi. We’ve been out with a great product from Viasat, which we’ve got two new satellites in the sky. It’s not Starlink caliber but it’s pretty darn close.”

“This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”At the #F500Innovation Forum, @Delta CEO Ed Bastian told @ajs that the airline helped Elon Musk’s satellite Wi-Fi “get started in aviation,” but the two sides “just couldn’t come to… pic.twitter.com/xmSERJNjjH

Look, before I get too deep into this, let me make several points that I think no one reasonable will disagree with (which is not to say some commenters won’t disagree!):

When Bastian formally unveiled plans for free Wi-Fi at CES 2023 in Las Vegas, he said the following:

“At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different. Our vision has long been to deliver an experience at 30,000 feet that feels similar to what our customers have available on the ground.”

“We didn’t just want free Wi-Fi to offer base-level service – we wanted it to be transformative for the entire onboard experience. It is imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home, and we’ve put this system through meticulous tests to make that possible.”

Earlier this year, when announcing plans to partner with Amazon Leo for connectivity, Bastian said that “we need to stay the leader” in inflight connectivity. Obviously that won’t be the case for a long time.

As I see it, Delta’s problem here is pretty simple. Customers absolutely notice a difference between Viasat and Starlink. The issue isn’t that people will stop flying Delta altogether. The issue is that Delta has built its entire brand on being the industry leader, and on being on the forefront of technology.

There’s no denying that this sentiment among the public changes over time, because inflight Wi-Fi is easily one of the top amenities that passengers notice nowadays. Seriously, I can’t count the number of people I’ve heard from or just overheard talking about their first Starlink experience, and how blown away they were.

I guess to look at it from another angle, there’s no airline that loves talking about how premium it is more than Delta. What makes Delta premium? If we’re going to believe that Delta is premium, it’s not based on any one single thing, but rather, it’s based on the sum of the experience. And I think anyone who thinks a major Wi-Fi disadvantage lasting for years isn’t part of what contributes to consumer sentiment is lying to themselves.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is now downplaying the importance of inflight Wi-Fi. He’s arguing that “customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi,” which in isolation, is probably true. But he’s also arguing that Viasat is “pretty darn close” to Starlink, which is most definitely not true, as I see it.

I wouldn’t be so critical of these statements if it weren’t for Bastian spending years hyping up how it’s “imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home,” while also saying “we need to stay the leader.” And for that matter, Delta has of course also long hyped how premium it is — if that’s to be believed, it’s not about any one feature, but instead, it’s about the sum of the experience.

What do you make of Bastian’s inflight connectivity comments?

The  is getting a significant overhaul, pairing a higher annual fee with new Atmos Rewards earning rates and a collection of perks for businesses that regularly fly on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

Starting Nov. 18, new applicants can earn 10 points per dollar on qualifying flights booked through Atmos™ for Business, receive four Alaska Lounge passes annually and work toward flight discounts and bonus status points through spending.

The biggest winners may be companies with multiple employee cardholders that regularly book Alaska or Hawaiian flights. They'll pay a flat $195 annual fee regardless of how many employee cards they issue, while benefiting from new travel perks.

However, the refresh also eliminates some valuable benefits, including the annual $99 Companion Fare and the $100 discount on an Alaska Lounge+ membership. Existing cardholders won't automatically transition to the new version and can keep their current benefits.

New applicants can earn a limited-time offer of 90,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases within the first 90 days of account opening, worth about $1,440 based on TPG's November 2026 valuations. By point total, that's the largest offer in TPG's recorded history for the card, but it's not the richest because the new offer doesn't include Alaska's famous $99 Companion Fare.

Starting Nov. 18, the Atmos Rewards Business card will feature a new flat annual fee regardless of the number of cards, stronger rewards on flights booked through Atmos for Business and several new travel-day perks.

Annual fee: $195 for the company, with no additional fee for employee cards (was previously $70 + $25 per card, including for the primary cardholder)

The refresh also takes a few things away.

New cardholders will no longer earn 2 points per dollar spent on gas, electric vehicle charging, shipping and local transit/ride-hailing. New cardholders will also lose the ability to earn the annual Companion Fare through card spending and the $100 discount on an annual Alaska Lounge+ membership.

Overall, the theme is clear: The refreshed card concentrates its value around Alaska and Hawaiian travel, especially for companies willing to book through Atmos for Business and issue cards to multiple employees.

If you opened your before Nov. 18, 2026, you won't automatically receive the refreshed benefits or move to the new annual-fee structure.

Instead, Bank of America says existing cardholders will keep their current benefits, including the opportunity to earn the annual $99 Companion Fare under the previous card's terms.

If you're interested in switching to the refreshed card, you can call Bank of America at 1-800-892-3219 to explore your options.

Applications submitted before Nov. 18 will also remain under the previous card offering, even if they're still pending.

One of the biggest changes is the new annual-fee structure.

The previously charged $70 per company plus $25 per card, including the owner’s card. Now, it’s a flat $195 regardless of how many cards you have. A solo business owner will now pay more than double what they paid before, a company with five cards pays the same as before, and one with six or more pays less. This is arguably the most significant part of the refresh.

Each cardholder will continue to receive a free checked bag for themselves and up to six guests on the same reservation when the flight is paid for with the card. They also receive preferred boarding on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian flights.

That could make the card particularly appealing to small businesses with several West Coast or Hawaii-based road warriors. The more employees who consistently use the travel benefits, the easier it becomes to justify the companywide fee.

Solo owners who do not need employee cards may find one of the personal Atmos cards better suited to their needs.

In that case, you won't earn points from business spending, but you can enjoy similar perks with the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card for a lower annual fee or take advantage of more generous benefits (albeit with a higher fee) on the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card.

However, neither is a direct replacement for a business card, particularly for owners who want to separate business expenses or issue employee cards.

Related: Atmos Ascent vs. Atmos Summit: The Summit is better—but not for everyone

In addition to checked-bag and preferred-boarding perks, the refreshed card will include one Alaska Lounge pass per calendar quarter, for a total of four per account anniversary year. That cadence is best suited to a consultant or salesperson who flies throughout the year, rather than a company whose only major trip is an annual conference.

Meanwhile, the waived fee for same-day confirmed changes ($50 on most Alaska flights) could be particularly useful for employees whose meetings finish early, run late or move unexpectedly. That practical flexibility may save some employees frustration — and save the business itself money on fees.

The card also adds a $50 Instant Travel Delay Credit voucher, which can be used toward a meal or drink at the airport when an eligible flight is canceled or delayed by at least two hours on the day of travel.

Despite the new higher fee, even a solo business owner could potentially offset much of the $195 annual fee through these travel benefits. Someone who checks a bag on two round-trips would save $180; visit a lounge on each of those trips and you'll save another $130 compared to buying day passes.

Related: Alaska Airlines airport lounges: How to get access to this VIP space

Earning 10 points per dollar sounds exceptional, but it only applies to flights booked through the Atmos for Business website, the airlines’ self-managed booking platform. That means companies that don't qualify for Atmos for Business — it requires a minimum of $5,000 in annual travel spend — or businesses that book through a corporate travel agency or another platform won't earn this higher return.

Other eligible Alaska and Hawaiian purchases earn 3 points per dollar spent, dining earns 2 points per dollar spent and everything else earns 1 point per dollar. Companies with an eligible Bank of America business account also receive a 10% bonus on points earned from card purchases, effectively turning the 10-point rate into 11 points per dollar.

Lastly, travelers who select the Price Paid earning option and hold Atmos Platinum or Titanium status can earn 20 points or more per dollar on qualifying flights booked through Atmos for Business.

The card's weak general spending rate makes it better suited as a secondary card specifically for Alaska and Hawaiian spending than as a business’s only credit card.

The refreshed no longer includes its annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23), which cardholders prior to Nov. 18 earned after spending $6,000 during an account anniversary year.

That is a significant loss for owners who could redeem it for two travelers flying together. Four lounge passes and same-day change flexibility may be more useful for employees traveling alone, but they aren't an automatic replacement for a Companion Fare.

While the new discounts could be valuable for businesses with substantial spending, the $100,000 threshold is significantly higher than the previous $6,000 requirement for earning a Companion Fare.

The welcome offer drops the Companion Fare too, but it includes more points than past offers. Its 90,000 points are enough for three round-trip economy tickets between the West Coast and Hawaii on Alaska or Hawaiian, a one-way ticket on American Airlines in transatlantic business class or a round-trip premium economy ticket from Seattle to Tokyo on an Atmos partner airline.

The refreshed Atmos Rewards Business Card has a higher starting price, but it also has a clearer identity: It's built for companies with multiple cardholders and for recurring Alaska or Hawaiian travel.

Businesses that need employee cards, book substantial airfare through Atmos for Business and have employees who can use the lounge passes and same-day change waiver may come out well ahead.

However, the loss of the Companion Fare and several business spending bonus categories makes the card less appealing for some existing cardholders.

Sole proprietors or companies that don't book through Atmos for Business may still have a case for the card, but they'll need to run the numbers more carefully. And companies that rarely fly either airline or primarily need rewards on everyday operating expenses will likely find the card too specialized.

#6121. American Airlines’ Airbus A321neo Fleet Grows To 90, Expects 2 More & 1 A321XLR By Year’s End

American Airlines has expanded its Airbus A321neo fleet to 90 aircraft, with two more standard A321neos and one A321XLR expected before the end of 2026. The latest arrival continues the carrier's fleet modernization program, in which Airbus narrowbodies play an increasingly important role in its domestic and international networks.

The latest delivery follows an unusually busy period at the end of last month, when American received four A321-family aircraft in just seven days. Those deliveries included three standard A321neos and one A321XLR, registered N311NY. With no further Boeing deliveries expected this year, Airbus remains central to American's near-term fleet renewal strategy.

American's standard A321neo fleet has reached 90 aircraft, with two more expected before the end of the year. The airline is also anticipating one additional A321XLR, extending its investment in long-range, single-aisle aircraft. If all three outstanding deliveries arrive as planned, American will finish 2026 with 92 standard A321neos, alongside its growing fleet of 12 A321XLRs.

American's third-quarter financial disclosures showed that it had 165 Airbus A320-family aircraft on order as of September 30, with seven scheduled for delivery during the final quarter. The subsequent acceleration in October, when four A321-family aircraft arrived within a week, highlighted the program's pace. American also expects another 27 A321-family deliveries in 2027, although the precise split between the standard A321neo and A321XLR has not been disclosed.

The A321XLR is particularly important to American's international expansion, allowing it to serve longer routes with fewer passengers than a widebody aircraft would typically accommodate.

Brian Znotins, American's former Senior Vice President of Network Planning, highlighted the aircraft's importance when announcing the carrier's 2027 international expansion.

"The A321XLR is transforming our international network, expanding it to offer destinations to satisfy every travel palate. Combined with our investments enhancing our onboard product and in-flight experience, travelers have more reasons to choose American when they fly around the world."

American received its first A321XLR in October 2025, becoming the first US operator of the type. Its original 50-aircraft commitment was subsequently reduced to 40, including five delivered by the end of 2025. Each aircraft features 20 Flagship Suite business class seats, 12 premium economy seats, and 123 economy seats, emphasizing premium revenue over maximum capacity.

The XLR restores some of the long-range narrowbody capability American lost when it retired its 757s in 2020. Its economics make thinner transatlantic routes viable without deploying a much larger 787 Dreamliner. The aircraft initially entered service on premium transcontinental flights, before expanding into international markets as more aircraft became available.

American's 2027 schedule demonstrates its ambitions, with four additional European routes assigned to the XLR. Philadelphia-Vienna, measuring approximately 4,321 miles (6,955 km), is particularly notable as it will become the world's longest narrowbody flight. The route will operate daily from May 6 through January 2028, while New York gains new services to Amsterdam and Nice.

13 new routes were planned but now only seven are scheduled.

The standard A321neo remains central to American's high-capacity narrowbody strategy. With its fleet now at 90 aircraft, it still has firm orders for 126 more airframes as the airline continues investing in the type to support busy domestic routes and replace older aircraft.

Configured with 196 seats, including 20 First Class and 47 Main Cabin Extra seats, American's legacy A321neos accommodate 41 more passengers than the XLR. It is particularly valuable on busy domestic routes connecting American's major hubs and supports the gradual replacement of older narrowbodies. Its versatility extends internationally, with Philadelphia-Reykjavík scheduled to launch in May 2027.

American's Boeing 737 MAX 8s complement the A321neos, offering 172 seats on routes requiring less capacity. The airline also has substantial outstanding Boeing narrowbody orders, including the larger 737 MAX 10, although deliveries of that variant are not expected until 2029 or later. With an eventual planned fleet size of more than 250 A321-family aircraft, Airbus narrowbodies will continue to play a leading role in American's domestic modernization and expanding transatlantic network.

#6120. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially launched his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

#6119. An Airline You’ve Never Heard Of Will Fly From Seoul Incheon To Los Angeles

A very small international airline plans to add long haul, international flights to the United States as of next spring, and I feel pretty confident in saying that 99% of people have never heard of this airline (I had to look it up after seeing one of their planes at an airport several weeks back, and I know a thing or two about identifying airplanes). 😉

As reported by AeroRoutes, as of May 1, 2027, Parata Air will launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Los Angeles (LAX). The flight will operate with the following schedule:

WE301 Incheon to Los Angeles departing 12:00PM arriving 7:20AMWE302 Los Angeles to Incheon departing 9:50AM arriving 3:20PM (+1 days)

Parata Air will operate the route with an Airbus A330-200, featuring 260 seats, including 18 business class seats and 242 economy seats. The 5,944-mile flight is blocked at 11hr40min eastbound and 13hr30min westbound.

Tickets on the flight are now on sale, and I see fares starting at around $670 one-way in economy, and around $2,500 one-way in business class. Those aren’t exactly terribly attractive fares for a newcomer that appears to have a pretty lackluster onboard product.

For those not familiar with Parata Air, the airline launched operations back in 2019, but it has a fleet of just a handful of planes, including three Airbus A330s and two Airbus A320s. This will be the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. As I hinted at in the headline, I imagine this is a fully unknown player to most people, and I had never heard of the airline until a few weeks ago.

Random thought — can anyone think of a smaller international airline (in terms of fleet size) that added long haul flights to the United States? I know that’s very specific, but I can’t think of another one… it’s possible I’m missing something, though!

The airline acquired its three A330s secondhand from different sources, with the planes having flown for Garuda Indonesia, Hainan Airlines, and Thomas Cook (though that plane doesn’t have business class).

The Seoul Incheon to Los Angeles market is pretty well served in terms of capacity, but not so well served in terms of competition. That’s because no US carrier flies between Los Angeles and Seoul Incheon, and with Korean Air having acquired Asiana, there’s now only one South Korean flag carrier.

If you look at the market, you’ll see that Korean Air operates up to four daily flights, and Air Premia operates up to two daily flights. Now we’ll see a third airline from the country operating in the market, though with the lowest capacity, and arguably the worst product.

It’ll be interesting to see when we see some competition here on the US side. Delta might operate the route eventually, but that doesn’t actually increase competition, since the airline has a joint venture with Korean Air. American has (smartly, probably) given up on Los Angeles as a long haul hub. So that leaves United, and I could definitely see the airline eventually adding service in the market, as a competitive response against Delta and Korean Air, if nothing else.

As of May 2027, Parata Air will be launching a new nonstop route between Seoul Incheon and Los Angeles, representing the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. The airline will be operating daily in the market with Airbus A330s. With this, there will be three South Korean carriers flying this route, though no airlines from the United States.

What do you make of this new Parata Air service?
