#6118. Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex Review: Is The No Annual Fee Card Worth It?

American Express and Delta have had a close relationship for many years, and as part of that, they issue seven co-branded Delta Amex cards. This is my in-depth Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card review, as this is the entry-level personal Delta credit card with no annual fee (Rates & Fees), and probably the least talked about card in the lineup. It’s far from the most rewarding Delta credit card, but if you want to earn Delta miles and only fly the airline occasionally, it could be worth a look.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card

Before I get into the full Delta Blue Amex Card review, here’s an overview of the card’s main features, from its welcome bonus and earning rates, to other benefits:

Beyond that, here are my thoughts on the pros and cons of the Delta Blue Amex:

When applying for a credit card, the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and fees, are obviously major factors that people consider. With that in mind, let’s take a look at those details for the Delta Blue Amex Card. As you’d expect for this card, the lack of fees largely comes at expense of a smaller welcome offer.

The Blue Delta SkyMiles Amex has a welcome offer of 10,000 bonus SkyMiles after spending $1,000 within the first six months of your card membership. Based on my latest points & miles valuations, Delta SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each, making this bonus worth $110. We’ve seen this card’s bonus go a bit higher, but not by a huge amount.

The bonuses on all other Delta Amex cards are significantly higher, which isn’t a surprise, since cards with annual fees often have better bonuses than cards without annual fees. It’s hard to get excited about that offer, but I guess something is better than nothing?

The welcome offer on the Delta Blue Amex Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. The rules go beyond that, though.

You’re actually not eligible for the bonus on the card if you have or have had any of the more premium versions of the Delta Amex card portfolio, at least among the personal cards. This is true across the portfolio, and the idea is that you’re always eligible for the bonus on a more premium card, but not eligible for the bonus on a less premium card.

So if you do want to pick up multiple Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to first apply for the Delta Blue Amex, then the Delta Gold Amex, then the Delta Platinum Amex, and then the Delta Reserve Amex (or at least you’ll want to move in that general order).

Beyond that, Amex’s general card application restrictions apply, including that you can typically have at most five credit cards from Amex at a time (that doesn’t include hybrid cards).

Let me emphasize once again that the Blue Delta Amex has no annual fee. It’s great to see a trend whereby we’re seeing more airline credit cards with no annual fees, since it’s a nice option for someone who wants a co-branded credit card, but doesn’t want to pay an annual fee.

You can also add additional users to the card at no extra cost.

There’s no doubt that card issuers are moving toward offering more no annual fee cards with no foreign transaction fees, though it’s still not the standard. The Blue Delta Amex has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), which is awesome, since most Amex no annual fee cards do still have these fees.

When it comes to earning rewards, the Blue Delta SkyMiles Credit Card offers:

For a no annual fee product, it’s nice to see a card offering a bonus on dining. While some bonus categories are better than none, I don’t find the bonuses to be particularly compelling, as there are still better cards out there for airfare purchases and restaurant purchases.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or on Delta’s SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

The Delta Blue Amex is a decent no annual fee card in the sense that it offers 2x miles at restaurants and has no foreign transaction fees, but how are the perks on the card? Not surprisingly, this is an area where the card lags, and where the cards with annual fees offer significantly more value.

Nonetheless, there are some perks to the card that may prove valuable to the occasional Delta flyer.

If you have the Blue Delta Amex, then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food or alcoholic beverages, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

Having the Blue Delta Amex makes you eligible for the Delta Pay With Miles program. What is that? This allows those with co-branded Delta Amex cards to redeem miles for one cent each towards a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles towards flights, and then they still earn elite miles for taking those flights.

In other words, the 10,000 miles available as part of the welcome offer can be redeemed for a minimum of $100 worth of travel on Delta. This is obviously the lowest cost option for unlocking that benefit.

The Delta Blue Amex includes access to dedicated entrance lanes and fast lanes at stadiums and arenas that participate in the Amex Venue Collection program. As part of this benefit, you can also get 10% back on qualifying concessions purchases, up to $250 back per calendar year. (Enrollment required)

Amex Offers is a program that offers discounts for purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

The ideal situation is to have a no annual fee card (like this one), so you can get access to these offers without paying an annual fee to get access to this.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page.

The Delta Blue Amex comes with some basic travel and purchase protection benefits:

There are some coverage limits and exclusions to be aware of, so you’ll want to review the full details in the card’s benefits guide before assuming you’re insured.

Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

Many people who like Delta as a brand may be tempted to pick up the Delta Blue Amex — it allows you to earn miles with Delta, it has no annual fee, and it offers some perks that could add value (20% off inflight purchases, Amex Offers, access to Delta Pay With Miles, etc.).

However, in general, I wouldn’t recommend outright applying for this card:

Let me address both of those points below.

If you’re considering the Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex, let me make the case for applying for the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (learn more) instead, which currently has the limited-time offer:

You can always get the Gold Delta Amex, and then if you don’t find it to be worth the annual fee, you can downgrade it to the Blue Delta Amex after a year. That would allow you to maintain the card account, and you wouldn’t pay the annual fee when you downgrade (and you’d still get the elevated perks and bigger bonus for the first year).

At a minimum, it really is worth trying the Delta Gold Amex to see if you like it and to take advantage of the better bonus, and then you can downgrade at a later point if you find it’s not worthwhile.

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. That’s because these points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x), and 3x points on flights booked directly with airlines or at AmexTravel.com. That’s a much better return than you’ll get on this card, and it’s also quite easy to make the math on the card work.

If you’re absolutely committed to having a no annual fee card and want to maximize your return on spending, there are lots of excellent no annual fee cards to consider.

My favorite is the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card earns 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase (in the form of ThankYou points).

But it gets even better than that — rewards earned on this card can be converted into ThankYou points at a 1:1 ratio and can be moved to partner programs at the best possible ratio, assuming you have the card in conjunction with one earning premium ThankYou points, like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more).

That means the card earns two ThankYou points per dollar, and I value those points at 1.7 cents each, so that’s like a 3.4% return on everyday spending.

I appreciate that American Express and Delta offer a no annual fee option with the Delta Blue Amex. For someone absolutely committed to getting a Delta Amex Card and not paying an annual fee, this is the best/only option.

The card has no foreign transaction fees, offers 2x miles on dining, and gives you access to Pay With Miles and 20% discounts on inflight purchases.

However, for most people, I think it’s worth applying for the Delta Gold Amex. The card has a lot more perks and a much better bonus, and you can always downgrade the card to the Delta Blue Amex after at least a year.

If you want to learn more about the Blue Delta Amex Card, follow this link.

The following links will direct you to the rates and fees for mentioned American Express Cards. These include: Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card (Rates & Fees), and Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (Rates & Fees).

#6117. Surprise: Aer Lingus Unveils First-Ever Premium Economy, Coming To 10 A330s

Aer Lingus is getting on the premium economy hype. The Irish flag carrier has today announced it will introduce the cabin for the first time on 10 of its Airbus A330s, which will also feature new business and economy cabins (the product won’t be coming to the Airbus A321LR/XLR fleet).

This is quite a big change, and one that should give it a leg up in the highly competitive trans-Atlantic market.

The cabin will feature just four rows with 28 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. That’s about average when compared to other premium economy cabins. The narrow fuselage of the A330 means there’s only room for three seats in the middle section, rather than the four many other airlines offer.

As for the soft product, Aer Lingus promises three-course dining, drinks throughout the flight, a pillow and blanket, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing (not noise-canceling) headphones.

I actually really like the design and color scheme. It’s modern, looks elegant and premium, and most importantly of all for the airline of the Emerald Isle, the colors are quintessentially Irish.

Aer Lingus says premium economy fares will start from 700 Euros one-way, putting a return trip at around 1,400 Euros. That works out to around $1,534, and a few hundred dollars cheaper than United’s nonstop fares from Newark (EWR) to Dublin (DUB).

We’ll have to wait until October 1 next year to try Aer Lingus’ new premium economy out for ourselves. The airline hasn’t yet announced which routes will get the product first, but we should find out in the coming months.

The good news is, they’ll operate on many of the airline’s 18 nonstop routes from Dublin to the United States.

As a small, almost boutique-style airline with just 63 aircraft, Aer Lingus must remain competitive, especially in the saturated transatlantic market in which it predominantly operates. The addition of premium economy bridges the large gap between economy and business, and should open the airline up to a potential new customer base who’ve never flown it before.

I’ll be attending an event in Dublin tonight, so I should be back with more images and extra info soon!

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new premium economy?

#6116. Why Southwest Airlines Might Change Its Cabin Interior Again

Southwest Airlines completed the fleet-wide reconfiguration of its cabins to add extra legroom seating earlier this year. The 737 MAX 8s and 737-800s left the shop essentially the same as when they entered, but with the seat pitch adjusted to add the extra legroom section, while the 737-700s have lost one row to make room for the extra legroom seats.

The project was massive in scope, but the work itself was light and was even completed a week ahead of schedule. The reconfigurations represent the start of a new era at Southwest, in which the famous 'open seating' policy has been discontinued.

Today, there are now premium seating options, and passengers are paying to select specific seats online. The final Southwest flight with open seating, operating from Honolulu to LAX, departed on January 26, and when it arrived the following morning, Southwest was just like everyone else. However, could another interior modification be on the cards?

Southwest has recently changed the configurations of its entire 800+ Boeing 737 fleet. The primary change was to adjust the seat pitches of each aircraft to create a dedicated section of extra legroom seats. While the newest Boeing 737 MAX 8 deliveries feature Recaro R2 seats with special seat covers to denote that they offer added space, these seats will be largely indistinguishable on most aircraft.

This is because special seat covers have not been applied to the Collins Meridian or Innovator II seats found on older aircraft. The 737-800s and 737 MAX 8s are maintaining their maximum capacity of 175 seats, but 45 of these seats now feature 36 inches (91.44 cm) of legroom, per aeroLOPA.

The 737-700s, previously configured with 143 seats, will now feature 137 seats, as the thickness of the older Innovator II seats meant that a row had to be sacrificed to make room for the extra legroom seats. 40 of these are extra legroom seats, boasting an exceptional seat pitch of 38 inches (96.52 cm). Currently, only new 737 MAX 8s, along with some reconfigured 737-800s, feature the Recaro R2 seats.

The rest of the 737 MAX 8 fleet and most of the 737-800 fleet are equipped with the Collins Meridian. Meanwhile, some 737-800s, along with all 737-700s, are equipped with the B/E Aerospace (now part of Collins) Innovator II. Some 737-700s will be retrofitted with Collins Meridian seats, and all 737-800s with the Innovator II seats will receive the Recaro R2. All planes with the R2 feature in-seat power, and all aircraft with the Collins Meridian will be retrofitted with in-seat power.

Southwest's CEO Bob Jordan has confirmed that his company is seriously looking into adding a first class cabin onto its planes. No official announcement has been made since Jordan commented on this idea in January, and looking into a new cabin is hardly the same as a confirmation

However, in the current state of the US market, as well as Southwest's trajectory, Jordan's comments are essentially a confirmation that a first class cabin on Southwest is a matter of when, not if. Naturally, any details as to what this could look like are pure speculation. The company is partnering with Recaro for its newest economy seats, so the Recaro R4 or R5 would be the frontrunners.

Southwest is retrofitting its aircraft with in-seat power as well as Wi-Fi, so you can expect these amenities, but seatback entertainment is extremely unlikely. The carrier's pitch for extra legroom seats is among the best in the industry, so some inches would likely be taken out to make room for first class seats. Southwest Airlines traditionally positioned itself as a hybrid carrier, blurring the lines between a low-cost carrier and a legacy airline.

Now, however, budget airlines are increasingly moving upmarket as that's where the money is. Spirit long offered a stripped-down first class product called 'Big Front Seat' before its collapse, and Frontier is now also preparing to debut a new first class product. JetBlue, meanwhile, is working on a domestic first class product titled 'Mini Mint.'

Southwest Airlines once pulled off the impossible, using an ambitious strategy to save the company.

In any industry, premium products generally sell for high margins, but of course, face a smaller market than mainstream products. In the US airline industry, however, the market for premium seating has increased dramatically. As such, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and Alaska Airlines have been making all of the money.

Meanwhile, the rest (including American, which strategically moved downmarket before COVID) have been left behind. This is tied to the increasing importance of loyalty programs, which are the primary profit centers at Delta, United, and Alaska. Customers want to earn miles and use airline-sponsored credit cards so that they can then fly in Delta One, travel to Cape Town with United, or book an award ticket with an Alaska Atmos partner.

Earning Southwest Rapid Rewards points for redemptions in economy within the US simply doesn't have the same appeal, and so consumers are moving to the legacies. Adding a first class product increases the appeal of Southwest's Rapid Rewards program and gives potential loyalists more incentive to build status with the carrier.

First class seats are also higher-margin products than economy seats as a whole. Being cheap no longer sells, which is why the ultra-low-cost carriers are adding premium products, and Southwest's previous brand image of being a quirky airline with a uniform onboard product at largely affordable prices also doesn't cut it today.

There can be no denying that after Elliott Investment first boarded the airline in June 2024, it fundamentally changed Southwest's business model. Before Elliott, Southwest did not offer premium seating, it gave two checked bags for free, there were no airline partnerships, bookings could only be made on Southwest's website, there were no assigned seats, and no redeye flights.

Elliott aggressively argued that this needed to change. It is true that Southwest's finances greatly lagged behind industry leaders coming out of the COVID-19 pandemic, and the carrier had also been suffering from antiquated systems as well as outdated practices. Southwest's operational and sales changes, as such, have been a net positive.

However, many of the customer-facing changes have been controversial, to say the least. Southwest is now charging for previously complimentary services like checked bags, and it now assigns seats to passengers. Under Elliott, Southwest has been chasing ancillary revenue and attempting to move up-market with its premium seating options.

However, before the COVID-19 pandemic, Southwest had recorded nearly half a century of straight profits. This was possible because Southwest's unique attributes, such as open seating and two free checked bags, garnered it a cult following. This customer base kept Southwest in the green during previous downturns, but Southwest, under Elliott, has decided to shun its most loyal followers in favor of following industry trends.

Here's the latest in a long series of changes aimed at transforming Southwest into an entirely new, more profitable airline.

Southwest is now just like every other airline in the US, and the former loyalists now have no reason to stick with the carrier. Instead, the carrier is targeting a wider audience and offering an increasingly diverse selection of seating options to cater to a more premium clientele. It's competing mainly on price, schedule, and network.

While boosting ancillary revenue has increased the carrier's short-term financials, it's not sustainable to rely on this long-term. Without Southwest's former cult following, the carrier has to commit fully to its premium shift, even once Elliott Investment has left the company. First class is as popular with travelers as ever, and delaying Southwest's entry into this market space simply leaves money on the table.

Furthermore, the presence and availability of the product will make Rapid Rewards a more desirable loyalty program, a goal that Southwest has already been working towards with its foreign airline partnerships and changes to its credit cards. It's unclear when Southwest will commit to this move or how the product will look.

​​​​​​​However, the US airline industry is shifting towards one dominated by premium products and loyalty programs. Southwest, looking to emulate the profits made by the nation's most successful airlines, is adapting to emulate their business models. As such, first class could be the next logical step.

#6115. At the Races: Regional realignment

By Daniela Altimari, Mary Ellen McIntire and Niels Lesniewski

New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, New England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.)

One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged New England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a new congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a new congressional map.

California contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Guv update: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Senator Morrison?  Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have launched a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is New Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, new members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”

Ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The New York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

How Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

Was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”

Song of the cycle: The New York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The New York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

If those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

#6114. GOP chairman demands answers on Trump's costly VA technology overhaul amid US-wide outages

President Donald Trump shares his administration's efforts to support veterans on Veterans Day.

Shifting timelines and ballooning costs of the Trump administration's contracts to modernize the federal government, including programs affecting veterans, are raising alarm bells on Capitol Hill.

House Veterans Affairs Committee Chairman Mike Bost, R-Ill., wrote to the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) this month asking for more information on an Oracle software rollout for streamlining employee data and what, if any, safeguards are in place to stop potential data breaches from leaking Americans' sensitive personal information. It comes as the country has grappled with multiple outages hitting the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), big banks and Microsoft, among other entities.

"I write to you today to express concern about the pace of the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Federal Human Resources (HR) 2.0 implementation, uncertainty surrounding VA’s transition costs and readiness, and the risks posed by another major Oracle implementation affecting the Department," the letter said.

"The House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs supports efforts to modernize HR systems and improve how VA manages and supports its workforce. However, modernization must proceed with clear accountability, adequate resources, and safeguards against disruption."

‘BIG BALLS’ OF DOGE FAME GIVES EXCLUSIVE LOOK AT NEW TRUMP MISSION TO OVERHAUL GOVERNMENT

Illinois Republican Rep. Mike Bost speaks alongside Rep. Lisa McClain, a Republican from Michigan, and Rep. Steve Scalise, a Republican from Louisiana, during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 9, 2025. (Annabelle Gordon/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Technology firm Cerner won a $10 billion government contract in 2018 to modernize record-keeping at VA-run hospitals over 10 years. Cerner was acquired by multinational tech company Oracle four years later.

ORACLE HEALTH DATA BREACH EXPOSES NEARLY 20 MILLION PATIENTS

It was later paused for several years during the Biden administration in an effort to root out performance issues affecting veterans and healthcare providers at VA hospitals, the department said at the time.

Since then, the VA announced earlier this year it would extend that contract through 2031 — with a new total price tag of $27 billion.

OFFICE OF PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT UNCOVERS $500M IN FRAUD AND WASTE IN FEDERAL HEALTH BENEFITS PROGRAMS

It's raised concerns among lawmakers on Capitol Hill, including Bost, who referenced those issues in his questions on the VA's use of Oracle for modernizing its employee data via HR 2.0.

"More than four months after Oracle was selected to provide the governmentwide platform underpinning HR 2.0, the Committee seeks detailed evidence of implementation progress and readiness at VA. In addition, VA’s years-long experience with Oracle’s Electronic Health Record Modernization (EHRM) program reinforces the need for caution," Bost wrote.

A Department of Veterans Affairs sign is displayed outside the Washington VA Medical Center on July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

Bost also cited system performance issues and problems with user satisfaction with EHRM highlighted by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), but he said only four of GAO's 18 recommendations have been fully implemented as of this past August.

In June 2026, Oracle was awarded a $395.8 million contract to modernize the federal government's human resources systems.

DHS INVESTIGATES MASSIVE DATA BREACH EXPOSING 40,000 EMPLOYEES, INCLUDING ICE AND BORDER PATROL AGENTS

An independent government watchdog "identified inconsistent completion targets, concentrated security and authorization risk, vendor-dependent data migration, and persistent staffing gaps" with HR 2.0 software implementation in October, Bost noted.

"The report describes completion targets shifting from July 4, 2027, to as late as March 2028, while the Wave 2 timeline remains unset," he wrote.

He also raised concerns about the potential for a data breach after the FBI was targeted by hackers in September.

Though he noted existing reports about that hack do not link it to potential issues with Oracle's software at the VA, Bost suggested that staffing gaps and HR 2.0's "centralized authorization approach" could allow for vulnerabilities that need to be accounted for before the rollout is complete.

Fears of tech vulnerabilities are at an all-time high in the U.S. after multiple private and public entities experienced disruptions in service. Travelers were hit with chaos last week after an issue with air traffic control towers caused a nationwide ground stop of flights, while Amtrak's booking system also went offline for several hours.

Just on Monday, major banks like JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America experienced some service disruptions and transaction delays.

The incidents have not been connected so far.

In his letter, Bost also called on more transparency with HR 2.0's funding, warning it should not take away from resources aimed at Oracle's contract on veterans' healthcare systems.

"Identify VA’s projected costs, savings, funding sources, and funding gaps for fiscal years 2027 through 2029," Bost asked. "Explain how OPM and the VA will protect resources needed for EHRM and veterans’ services, avoid duplicative implementation spending, and ensure timely retirement of legacy systems."

When reached for comment, an OPM official told Fox News Digital the office "is working closely with agencies and stakeholders throughout implementation to drive adoption, manage change effectively, and continuously improve the platform over time. We take concerns over data security seriously and also want to highlight that HCM will be leveraging Oracle Fusion Cloud HCM, not PeopleSoft."

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

#6113. Aer Lingus Retrofitting A330s With New Business, Premium Economy, Economy Cabins

It’s not just Aer Lingus’ premium economy stealing the headlines in Ireland today. Expected to fly passengers for the first time on October 1, 2027, the new cabins are part of a comprehensive Airbus A330 tip-to-tail retrofit that will include new business and economy cabins. We covered the premium economy cabin in a separate article story.

The same 10 Airbus A330s that will get the airline’s new premium economy will also get a swanky new business class. The airline’s Airbus A321XLRs aren’t included in this cabin update.

Aer Lingus opted for its take on the ever-popular Collins Elevation suite. There’ll be 28 seats in a 1-2-1 configuration that stretch out to 78 inches long when in lie-flat mode.

The color palette of Irish greens, whites, and light wood gives the seat an elegant yet distinctly non-corporate feel. It’s a thumbs-up from me.

In terms of updated tech, each seat has 4K HD screens (in all cabins) as well as wireless and USB-C charging. While nothing revolutionary, these touches will significantly modernize Aer Lingus A330 cabins.

Aer Lingus is also introducing a self-service bar stocked with snacks and drinks. I wonder if this will include Champagne…

The airline will also serve up a whole new in-flight dining experience featuring dishes inspired by both Irish ingredients and its transatlantic destinations.

It wouldn’t be a full retrofit without sprucing up economy.

Per the renderings, Aer Lingus has done a great job again with the cabin’s look and feel. The emerald green Shamrocks are a lovely touch.

Seats are configured in the A330’s classic 2-4-2 configuration — a favorite for those traveling in pairs.

While the recline looks a bit modest here, the seat’s thickness looks like it’ll provide more support than some of those ultra-thin, rigid seats airlines are sneaking in these days.

The six-way adjustable headrests should also mean less head-wobbling when catching some shut-eye.

The curved design of the seat backs should hopefully mean noticeably more knee space.

Aer Lingus is also upping its food and beverage ante for economy passengers. In addition to a snack bar, a new mid-flight snack will be offered.

A retrofit program like this was essential for Aer Lingus to remain competitive in the transatlantic market. The introduction of premium economy was a great move, especially since the cabin is known to be highly profitable.

Aer Lingus has also done a great job of matching the Irish color scheme and sleek design across all cabins, which is more than can be said for some airlines these days. 😉

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new A330 cabins?

#6111. Chase Ink Business Preferred Card Bonus: 100K Points Welcome Offer

The Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card has a phenomenal sign-up bonus of 100,000 points after spending $8,000 within three first three months, and there’s lots of value to this card in the long term, especially thanks to its reasonable $95 annual fee — read my Ink Preferred review here. If you’re eligible for the card, there’s no reason not to apply.

This is part of the Chase Ink Business card portfolio, and it’s arguably Chase’s most rewarding and best value business credit card. In this post I’d like to go over the Ink Business Preferred bonus details, including eligibility requirements.

Link: Learn more about the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card with 100K bonus points

The Chase Ink Preferred Card currently has a welcome offer of 100,000 Ultimate Rewards points after spending $8,000 within the first three months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each, meaning the 100,000 points are worth $1,700 to me, which is among the best bonuses out there. There are lots of great uses of Chase points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners.

Chase Ultimate Rewards partners with programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club, United MileagePlus, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, World of Hyatt, and more. If you want to cash out Chase points (which I wouldn’t recommend), you can get one cent of value per point, meaning the 100,000 points would be worth $1,000.

Just to give some examples of possible uses of the points, you could transfer 34,000 points to Iberia Club for a one-way Iberia business class ticket from Boston to Madrid, or 60,000 points to Flying Blue for a one-way Air France or KLM business class ticket from Miami to Paris. You can stretch your points even further by taking advantage of transfer bonuses.

Let me emphasize that the Chase Ink Preferred 100K bonus is the best publicly available sign-up bonus that’s currently available on the card, and it has been the standard offer since November 2025. How do the previous Chase Ink Preferred offers compare, though?

As you can see, the Ink Business Preferred sign-up bonus on the card has varied from 80,000 points to 120,000 points, and the current bonus of 100,000 points is 10,000 points better than the previous offer, which was for up to 90,000 points.

Everyone has to decide for themselves if it’s worth waiting for the possibility of another welcome bonus of over 100,000 points. Personally I probably wouldn’t wait, since we have no reason to believe such an offer is returning soon. Furthermore, with the card’s useful points categories for spending, there’s potentially quite an opportunity cost to waiting. But still, if you’re in no rush, it could be worth waiting.

When it comes to getting approved for the Chase Ink Preferred Card and earning the welcome bonus, what rules should you be aware of? Well, there are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Chase policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:

The new cardmember bonus may not be available to you if you have ever had this card. We may also consider factors pertinent to your business in determining your bonus eligibility.

As you can see, officially the welcome bonus may not be available to you if you currently have this card, or if you’ve had it in the past. However, eligibility for the card (including the bonus) is unrelated to whether you have any other Chase business card.

In other words, you’re eligible for this card, including the bonus, if you have other cards from Chase, including cards in the business lineup. Speaking of which, those cards have some amazing bonuses as well, which are worth considering:

Beyond that, there are some general Chase rules to be aware of:

While Chase business cards can be tough to get approved for, they offer such fantastic bonuses and perks, so it’s worth the effort, in my opinion. Furthermore, it’s nice how the eligibility requirements aren’t too strict in terms of qualifying for the bonus.

The Chase Ink Preferred Card has a $95 annual fee (with no cost for additional employee cards), and offers all kinds of amazing perks that make it worth holding onto. Among other things, here’s what makes the card so valuable:

Let me acknowledge that the Ink Preferred isn’t right for everyone. As I see it, the Ink Preferred is all about the rewards structure and the strong purchase and travel protection, while also having a reasonable cost. If you’re looking for airport lounge access or a card with all kinds of premium perks and credits, then consider the Sapphire Reserve Business, which many people will find to be worthwhile for the Chase Sapphire Lounge access, Priority Pass membership, travel credits, and more.

The Chase Ink Preferred Card is one of the best business cards out there, and if you’re eligible for the card, there’s lots of merit to applying.

Not only does the card have a big bonus, but it’s worth holding onto for the great rewards structure, excellent protection benefits, and the ability to maximize other cards in the Chase ecosystem. With the changes we’ve seen to other Chase cards in recent times, this card is arguably even more compelling than in the past.

Do you have the Chase Ink Preferred Card, and if so, what has your experience been?

#6110. Democrats mulling Iran war funding cutoff strategy

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

“I know it’s going to be my main push,” he said. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”

Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”

“When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators said. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., said earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”

While ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the new Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how quickly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, said that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”

Democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

"I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries said.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro said earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

The administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks said. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#6109. Why Boeing Added New Engines To 1 Of Its 2 Longest-Running Aircraft In Production

Wikimedia Commons, Andreas Zeitler | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Inside Boeing's gigantic Washington plants, two of the longest-running jets in commercial aviation history are headed toward very different destinations. Workers in Renton installed huge 69-inch CFM LEAP-1B turbofans on the 737 MAX to bring the 1960s airframe up to 21st-century standards. However, thirty miles north in Everett, Boeing is winding down production of its twin-aisle 767 in 2027, despite being decades newer with its 1980s-era engineering.

Still, the doors have not shuttered yet, and thanks to a lifeline from Congress, the classic widebody is continuing to roll off the line with the same engines. Inside those historic walls, Boeing’s engineers constantly push the cutting edge of aerospace technology. Yet they applied that innovation unevenly between their two oldest active product lines, pouring $3 billion into modernizing the 737 while letting the veteran 767 face its looming sunset.

Boeing's decision to abandon the 767 results from both significant changes in the global cargo industry and commercial realities. The 737 MAX's extensive wing and engine redesigns were justified by thousands of airline orders, but the 767's niche cargo demand could never justify a similar overhaul, particularly since shippers are shifting their focus to the upcoming 777-8F freighter and the 777-200F passenger-to-freighter conversions are being slowed down by a severe shortage of used donor airframes.

Boeing scrapped plans for a brand-new single-aisle aircraft after Airbus received over 1,000 bookings for its A320neo and former exclusive customer American Airlines threatened to defect, as Leeham News wrote. Rather, the 737 airframe, whose fundamental cabin cross-section dates back to the 1954 Dash 80 prototype, was modified with CFM LEAP-1B turbofans at a cost of almost $3 billion. In order to preserve single-aisle market dominance, the 737 MAX upgrade served as a crucial stopgap. It quickly compensated for itself with hundreds of airline orders and allowed Boeing to develop a future clean-sheet replacement.

While building the next-generation 777-8F and awaiting the availability of used passenger 777 donor airframes for P2F conversions, Boeing continued to operate the twin-aisle 767-300F as a temporary freight bridge. Freighter sales were restricted to a few dozen aircraft a year since commercial airlines switched from ordering passenger 767s to the lightweight, composite 787 Dreamliner in 2014.

As global e-commerce and pandemic-era cargo demand increased, the 767-300F, powered by its reliable but thirsty 1980s-era General Electric CF6-80C2 or Pratt & Whitney PW4062 engines, performed adequately as a temporary stopgap. However, the International Civil Aviation Organization's carbon emission regulations, which go into effect on January 1, 2028, cannot be met by those older engines. After that cutoff, a temporary cargo stopgap would become a permanent commercial closure because the 767 could not lawfully comply with international routes without contemporary engines.

With the 737 MAX, massive narrowbody order volume turned an aging fuselage into a multi-decade cash engine that absorbed billions in engineering upgrades. With the 767-300F, low production rates meant Boeing treated the jet purely as a low-cost bridge to hold cargo customers until the 777-8F arrived and P2F conversion lines ramped up, willingly letting regulatory deadlines retire the commercial airframe rather than sinking new capital into a sunsetting program.

By enacting a rule that exempted freight jets weighing between 396,832 and 529,109 pounds from new carbon restrictions until 2033, Congress attempted to give Boeing a crutch. This effectively shielded the 412,000-pound 767-300F. However, Stephanie Pope and Kelly Ortberg, Boeing executives, declined to rely on a complete legislative rescue. Foreign authorities in Europe and Asia could prohibit the aircraft from landing because a US exemption has no power outside the US, keeping brand-new freighters behind American borders and damaging their resale value for international carriers like FedEx and UPS.

Instead of leaning on political life support, Boeing chose to shut down commercial 767 production in 2027 and absorb a $400 million charge. Unlike the 737 MAX, where massive passenger volume easily funded complex structural and engine upgrades, the low-volume 767 could never justify a multi-billion-dollar overhaul. Boeing recognized that stretching an outdated freighter through domestic loopholes made far less sense than focusing its engineering muscle on programs with real global demand.

Everett's widebody engineers are advancing the next-generation 777X family toward final FAA certification in early 2027, opening the door for the new 777-8F freighter, while the 737 MAX line continues to produce the high-volume revenue flow required to finance ongoing enhancements. Instead of producing geographically limited 767s, Boeing allowed the commercial line to shut down on time, keeping Everett's equipment focused on military KC-46 tankers while its new widebodies get ready to take over international cargo routes.

The demise of the sawtooth jet engines in the era of next-gen turbofans.

Putting new engines on the 737 was no simple bolt-on modification despite the appearance to a casual observer. The modern LEAP-1B engine featured a huge 69-inch fan, forcing engineers to stretch the 737’s nose landing gear by eight inches and mount the engines further forward and higher on its low-slung 1960s wing. Applying the same MAX upgrade formula to the 767 seemed promising on paper because both aircraft have similar profiles and basic construction, though the 767 has a larger fuselage.

Boeing’s engineering resources and factory tooling were already locked onto far bigger, future-ready platforms than the 767. Instead of pouring capital into a temporary bridge, Boeing preserved its engineering capacity for the next-generation 777-8F and more popular 777-200F, letting the 767 finish its final bridge run before handing its crucial air freight mission over to its successors.

The engineering compromises that brought a 1960s jet into the 21st Century.

Bolting a modern engine onto the 767 would require gutting the airplane’s internal structures and essentially changing every aspect. Its legacy aluminum wings were engineered to carry older engines weighing roughly 9,800 pounds each. Swapping in an advanced turbofan like the GEnx-1B would add over 3,700 pounds of extra dead weight per side. Supporting that heavy overhang would force Boeing to rebuild the wing’s internal ribs, spars, and titanium mounts, triggering a multi-billion-dollar safety certification that niche cargo sales could never pay back.

The technology gap inside the engines was just as wide. 21st-century jets squeeze every drop of energy from fuel by running at extreme pressures and blistering heat, using space-age ceramic parts and single-crystal metal blades that survive temperatures above 3,000 degrees. That intense efficiency lets new engines burn far less fuel and easily pass tough global pollution rules.

By contrast, the 767’s 1980s-era engines run at much lower pressures with traditional metal blades that cannot handle extreme heat. Those older thermal limits mean higher fuel burn and heavier exhaust that fail modern clean-air standards. Faced with rebuilding the entire wing just to carry heavier, hotter engines, Boeing accepted that upgrading the 767 was an engineering dead end.

Analyzing why Atlas Air broke its all Boeing streak for the first time.

Before the 2028 carbon cutoff, the commercial 767's demise was cemented by a market squeeze. After FedEx Express took delivery of its 152nd and final new 767-300F in May 2026, only 15 civilian orders remained on Boeing’s books, including seven for UPS and eight for an undisclosed buyer. Once those final commercial jets leave Everett before the 2027 deadline, the civil 767 will vanish permanently from Boeing’s lineup.

By carrying 116,000 pounds of cargo across 3,255 nautical miles without burning as much fuel as larger widebodies, the 767-300F maintained a profitable middle ground for decades. That mid-size niche is mostly gone now. While extra-large twinjets like the Airbus A350F, Boeing 777F, and forthcoming 777-8F exceed the 767 in every parameter on long-haul international routes, upgraded single-aisle freighters increasingly dominate short domestic e-commerce flights.

However, a military lifeline has ensured that the Everett assembly line itself continues to operate well into the 2030s. To fulfill significant orders for the KC-46A Pegasus aerial refueling tanker for the US Air Force and allies like Japan and Israel, Boeing will keep its 767 tooling operational because defense aircraft are exempt from commercial pollution regulations. This will close a legendary commercial chapter while solidifying its future as a military powerhouse.

That military transformation sets the stage for the next chapter of this 1980s airframe’s remarkable survival. Outfitted with fly-by-wire refueling booms, defensive armor, and advanced cockpit displays borrowed from the 787 Dreamliner, the KC-46A Pegasus is quietly evolving far beyond its commercial roots. While the civilian 767 fades into history, its combat-ready twin is taking on high-stakes global refueling missions that will keep Everett’s assembly line vital for decades to come.

#6108. World Of Hyatt 2027 Updates: Milestone Rewards From 10 Nights, New Rewards, And More

World of Hyatt members can expect more flexibility and choice from January 1, 2027. Highlights of the update include earning Milestone Rewards sooner, a bunch of new Milestone Rewards, and more flexibility when redeeming rewards and paying for stays. There’s actually no huge catch, and the changes I learned about last night on an intimate call with the Hyatt team are genuinely member-focused.

The update follows the new Hyatt-Delta relationship, which also launched this week.

Starting January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will start enjoying Milestone Rewards after 10 nights stayed or 20,000 base points. That’s great news for relatively infrequent Hyatt guests (like myself), who will no longer have to stay 20 nights or earn 35,000 base points to earn their first Milestone Reward.

At 10 nights or 20,000 base points, members will be able to choose from:

Milestone Rewards will be unlocked at every ten nights, up to 150 nights.

Not only is it about to become quicker to earn Milestone Rewards, but there’ll also be new awards to choose from each level. Here are a few examples of the 20+ new rewards:

The downside of free parking becoming a Milestone Reward means that World of Hyatt members who earn Globalist from 2027 onwards will no longer enjoy it as a permanent status perk on award stays. This will be a notable downgrade to Globalists who value their parking perk.

Hyatt has published a handy new infographic with all the details.

There are also two more important Milestone Reward changes to note, both of which aren’t such positive news:

For the first time, World of Hyatt members will be able to stack multiple awards on a single stay. For example, you can use a Suite Upgrade Voucher, a Guest of Honor Award, and claim free parking, all on the same stay.

All awards will also expire after 365 of being issued. That’s great for awards that used to only last 180 days.

I think this could be my favorite update. Hyatt is enhancing its Pay My Way option to allow guests to choose how to pay for each night of a stay. As someone who struggles to rack up Hyatt points (Hyatt isn’t a transfer partner of any cards in the U.K.), this should certainly streamline booking stays for me.

The booking page will display each award applied to each individual night and provide guests with a drop-down menu to select how they’d like to pay for each night.

At a time when we’re plagued with loyalty program devaluations, these changes coming to World of Hyatt appear to be a genuinely positive slew of updates. Even when you consider some of the less favorable updates, like Globalists losing free parking and some award expiration dates being limited to 365 days, the changes will be positive overall for the vast majority of World of Hyatt members.

What do you make of these World of Hyatt changes?

#6107. Lufthansa’s A380 Business Class Seat Retrofit Nearly Done, But It Isn’t Allegris

In January 2026, Lufthansa formally announced plans to retrofit its Airbus A380s with new business class seats. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026, and Lufthansa had committed to retrofitting all the planes by the middle of 2027.

There’s now a positive update, as it looks like Lufthansa is running way ahead on that schedule, and all A380s should be retrofitted within the coming weeks…

Lufthansa is introducing a new business class product on its entire fleet of eight Airbus A380s. Rather interestingly, it’s only business class that’s getting new seats, while first class, premium economy, and economy, remain the same, aside from some minor upgrades (like improved inflight entertainment).

The first A380 with new interiors entered service in April 2026, and AeroRoutes flags how as of December 18, 2026, Lufthansa is exclusively showing the new business class configuration on all routes. So starting in the coming weeks, you can expect the entire A380 network to feature the new cabins.

Lufthansa A380s are based in Munich (MUC), and currently fly to Bangkok (BKK), Delhi (DEL), Los Angeles (LAX), Mumbai (BOM), San Francisco (SFO), and Washington (IAD). As you’d expect, there’s seasonal variation in the routes, though.

What’s interesting is that Lufthansa isn’t introducing its new Allegris business class on these planes, but instead, is introducing another “off the shelf” product. Specifically, the airline has opted for the Thompson Aero Vantage XL product, which is in a staggered configuration.

Each seat has direct aisle access, seat width of 58cm, and a bed length of at least two meters. Seats feature bluetooth connectivity and flexible partitions. Lufthansa is calling this “Premium XXL,” which… I’m not sure if that’s supposed to describe the seat, or if Lufthansa is taking some liberties on a new Grindr profile, somehow turning Vantage XL into Premium XXL.

As A380s are reconfigured, the business class cabin is shrinking in size by 10 seats, going from 78 seats to 68 seats. First class continues to have eight seats, premium economy continues to have 52 seats, and economy continues to have 371 seats.

It’s pretty cool to note how Lufthansa has reversed course on the A380. At the beginning of the pandemic, Lufthansa grounded its fleet of Airbus A380s, and the intent was that these planes would be retired, and would only reenter service “in the event of an unexpectedly rapid market recovery.”

With the strong recovery we’ve seen in transatlantic leisure demand, the airline made the decision to start bringing back Airbus A380s as of the summer of 2023, and eight of the initial 14 are now back in service (six of them were sold). At first, the return of the A380s was mostly described as a temporary measure, in light of delayed Boeing 777-9 deliveries. The airline didn’t commit to keeping these planes around in the long run, though that changed over time.

In recent years it has become clear that the A380 will have a long term place in Lufthansa’s fleet. Clearly this investment in the business class product reflects that.

Lufthansa of course has its new Allegris cabins, including the new Allegris business class and new Allegris first class. These cabins debuted on newly delivered Airbus A350-900s, and we’re also seeing them on newly delivered Boeing 787-9s (though without first class).

So why is Lufthansa not installing its new Allegris seats on the A380s? Well, I’d assume it comes down to a couple of factors. The biggest reason is quite straightforward — Lufthansa has had a really tough time getting its new Allegris seats certified, and these seats need to be certified on each individual aircraft. The idea is that by picking an “off the shelf” product, these seats are already certified, and therefore the airline could actually rely on getting them into service immediately.

Second of all, I imagine that given the narrower fuselage of the A380 upper deck, it might’ve required even more complicated customization to fit the new Allegris seats up there.

For once, I’d say Lufthansa made a wise decision by just picking a generic product for its A380s. I think the big mystery is why Lufthansa just didn’t do this for its other planes, to avoid this entire mess. Separately, Lufthansa is reconfiguring its Boeing 747-8s, in a complicated two-part process. Initially, we’ll see the new Allegris business class seats on the lower deck, while the same business class seats will remain on the upper deck.

Lufthansa is wrapping up the process of introducing a new business class product on its Airbus A380s. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026. While the initial plan was for all planes to be reconfigured as of the middle of 2027, it looks like that project will instead wrap up by December 2026, which is amazing.

Rather than installing the new Allegris business class seats, the airline is instead installing a more generic product, the Thompson Aero Vantage XL seat, which is a significant improvement over the product you’ll otherwise find on these jets. As planes are reconfigured, business class capacity is being reduced by 10 seats, from 78 to 68.

Lufthansa sure is all over the place when it comes to modernizing its cabins. Either way, this change is good to see.

What do you make of Lufthansa’s new A380 business class?

#6106. Trump set for economic showdown with Xi as unfulfilled promises leave billions hanging in balance

Ryan M. Yonk, a scholar at the American Institute for Economic Research, breaks down what the U.S. needs to do if it wants concrete results on trade with China.

President Donald Trump later today will meet with President Xi Jinping in China, where the pair are expected to discuss trade between the two nations after what one expert describes as years of broad promises but few executed deals.

Tariffs, agricultural purchases and rare earth minerals are all potential topics of conversation, and are in many ways intertwined, according to Ryan Yonk, an economic scholar and research fellow at the American Institute for Economic Research who specializes in relations between the United States and China.

At a summit in Beijing in May, China agreed to purchase 25 million metric tons of American soybeans, one of its U.S. largest imports, annually. China also agreed to purchase $17 billion worth of other agricultural products this year, in 2027 and in 2028.

President Donald Trump walks on a red carpet after greeting Chinese President Xi Jinping during an arrival ceremony at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland., on Sept. 23, 2026. Trump is hosting Xi for a three-day state visit to Washington, D.C., where the leaders are expected to discuss trade practices, artificial intelligence and furthering "strategic stability" between their countries. (Getty Images)

TRUMP HEADS TO BEIJING FOR HIGH-STAKES XI TALKS AS TAIWAN TENSIONS, TRADE DISPUTES TEST US STRENGTH

"There has been a very sort of large-scale discussion, particularly about soy purchases from U.S. producers that got derailed as the tariff debate and argument increased across time," Yonk said.

Those purchases, Yonk said, were widely believed to be one area where China would make the first move in purchasing U.S. products given the current tariff arrangement, in large part because China simply lacks the domestic capability to produce soy at the quantity it needs.

When Xi visited the U.S. in September, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the two countries had agreed to extend a tariff truce and reduce restrictions on trade for certain products until January.

They left the door open to hammer out a more permanent deal during Trump's visit to China Wednesday.

A combine harvester during a soybean harvest at a farm in Harvard, Illinois, Oct. 17, 2025. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

Yonk thinks that without a "fundamental rebalancing of the trade agreements on both sides," China will not act first in making large scale purchases from the United States.

WHAT XI WANTS FROM TRUMP AS BEIJING SEEKS LEVERAGE IN HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT

"I think [it] is unrealistic, because an expectation that China will act first with very little reciprocal action on the U.S. side isn't traditionally how China has acted," he said.

That calculation is not just economic, but political, Yonk explained. Neither Trump nor Xi wants to act first for fear of the appearance that one is giving in to the other.

He is not confident that high-level talks between the two world leaders will lead to concrete change in trade policy.

"And so, if we're going to get real progress, it's going to likely have to be not simply between the two leaders meeting and agreeing, but actual trade negotiations that involve sub-cabinets, officials actually going through and identifying what specific restrictions can be lowered," he said, adding that those tactics have not yet been employed in a meaningful way between the two nations.

DOUG BURGUM SAYS TRUMP ENTERS CHINA SUMMIT IN 'STRONGEST POSITION' OF ANY US LEADER EVER

Trump already vowed on Tuesday to break China's grip on rare earth minerals, which are used to build everything from fighter jets to cell phones.

"We're doing very well," Trump said. "We're making rare earth at a level that we've never made before. We're going to catch [China] within 10 months, they say. We'll catch them. Everything we need, we'll have in 10 months."

President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping attend a bilateral meeting at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. President Trump is meeting with President Xi Jinping in Beijing to address the Iran conflict, trade imbalances and the Taiwan situation while establishing new bilateral boards for economic and AI oversight. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

AMERICA DEPENDS TOO MUCH ON CHINA FOR ESSENTIAL MINERALS. WE NEED TO DIG OUR FUTURE

Yonk said the U.S. does have a large supply of rare earth minerals available within its borders. But it is more cautious of the environmental concerns that come along with mining and refining them than China. Thus, China has been a major source of America's rare earth minerals.

China is experiencing economic pain that keeps it coming back to the negotiating table, Yonk said, noting that the U.S. has its own share of pain with high levels of inflation. But ultimately, he surmised, China is worse off than the United States, using the analogy that if the United States catches a cold, China will catch a "fairly severe flu."

"And so the stakes are very high for China getting the trade arrangements right. It pushes us back into, if we're going make real progress, it's going be often item by item," he said. "It's going to be trade line by trade line and understanding what those bilateral trade agreements can really look like."

"It always sounds good to say we're going to solve it all at once, but most of the trade agreements we've had with China that have succeeded have been line by line, product area by product area, and it requires a holistic look at the relationship rather than mere platitudes."
