Squeezing the most value out of every dollar on a cruise is a top goal for most travelers. It doesn't matter if you're on a quick escape cruise from a local port or an exotic luxury cruise halfway around the globe, you never want to end it feeling like you should have gotten more for your money.

Cruises are the ultimate all-inclusive vacation, with meals, transportation and entertainment included, and there is even more value-adds on board that you may have never thought to look for. The trick is to hone in on built-in value early, in the cruise shopping and purchasing stage, and then pay attention to every detail that might enhance your experience along the way. Here are 14 tricks to get the most possible value from any cruise you take.

It can feel like you’re bombarded with emails after you book a cruise, but some of them contain hidden treasure.

Royal Caribbean, Celebrity, Princess, MSC and Virgin Voyages are among the cruise lines that use a bidding process to manage unsold cabins as the sailing date gets closer. Carnival Cruise Line offers upgrades without bidding. Pay attention to your email, and you might nab a nicer cabin for less than you’d pay by booking it outright.

Emails also alert you to discounted packages or bundles for Wi-Fi, shore excursions, specialty dining, drinks and even spa treatments. Much of the same information can be found on the cruise planner on the cruise line's website, but unless you log in often, watch those emails for value-oriented offers.

While it's tempting to always look at the newest (and often the biggest) ships, you may find that switching to an older or smaller ship, which may be just slightly less in demand, often helps squeeze more from your cruise budget without limiting your vacation fun.

You can also save hundreds of dollars by opting for inside staterooms, rooms with partially blocked views or those with less-than-perfect locations on the ship. This even works within suite zones or exclusive ship-within-a-ship areas. My dermatologist recently confided that he always chooses an inside suite within the Yacht Club when he cruises with MSC; he gets all the VIP perks, including exclusive dining and entertainment venues, for thousands less than the suites with balconies.

And don't rule out the cruise cabin guarantee option. Regardless of the cabin type, allowing the cruise line to select your stateroom is almost always the better value option than picking a specific room.

While most lines sign you up for loyalty programs automatically after your first sailing, you might need to opt in. Some lines allow you to sign up even before your first cruise, giving you advance offers to entice you to go ahead and book that first cruise.

Status matches between cruise lines are a huge bonus. MSC offers a status match with other cruise lines, hotel brands and tour operators. You can do this before your first booking and get Voyagers Club benefits on your first cruise with the line. These could be as simple as a welcome beverage or as elaborate as a complimentary tasting menu dinner. Ultra-luxury sister brand, Explora Journeys, offers a one-time status match with MSC and comparable luxury lines.

Royal Caribbean, Celebrity and Silversea have an ongoing status match across the three sister brands. That means you can reap rewards on a luxury line by earning status on a mainstream brand.

Similarly, Viking’s loyalty program spans its river, ocean and expedition arms. Once you’ve cruised with the line, you’ll get benefits fleetwide, even if you try out a different kind of ship.

Some lines offer casino status matches with land- and sea-based casinos that might even earn you a free cruise. These often come with exceptions; your casino status on Carnival won't get you a free cruise on sister line Princess, but casino status on Celebrity might. And don't be afraid of free cruise certificates handed out by reputable casinos on land where you have status. They’re the real deal, often based on long-standing partnerships between the casino and cruise lines. The reverse is also true. I’ve never been to WinStar Casino in Oklahoma, but they send me offers of free hotel nights using postcards featuring the Carnival logo, with which I have casino status.

While not every loyalty perk holds a huge value for you, little freebies definitely add up on vacation. For example, Carnival gives you a free 1.5-liter bottle of water on your second cruise. That's one less bottle you might have to buy.

As you move up the loyalty ladder, cruise by cruise, the perks improve. For example, you may be eligible for free laundry, drinks and specialty dining the higher up you go. I once met a couple who were on a five-night Royal Caribbean cruise for the sole purpose of moving up to the top loyalty tier before going on a much longer cruise. The higher tier would give them free Wi-Fi and a handful of other valuable perks for the duration of their longer cruise.

Often the onboard perks are loaded on your cabin keycard, but you might have to ask how to use them. For example, if you are entitled to a free bag of laundry at your loyalty level, nobody will hand you a bag and say, "Fill it up; it's free." It's up to you to know the perks you are entitled to and follow through on getting them.

Amid the barrage of marketing messages for beverage packages of all sorts, it's easy to forget that certain beverages are included in your cruise fare.

Every cruise ship offers standard drip coffee, water, iced tea, hot cocoa, punch or lemonade and a variety of tea bags free of charge. Milk and juice are available at breakfast. Look for self-serve stations at the buffet, or ask your server.

Sodas are included on premium lines like Windstar, Oceania and Viking, as well as on luxury lines like Seabourn, Silversea and Regent Seven Seas Cruises. Disney Cruise Line also offers free soft drinks but only from the beverage dispensers by the pool.

It's surprising how many free (or included) alcoholic drinks you can procure once on board a ship. I've been offered sparkling wine at art auctions, galley tours and captain's events.

Royal Caribbean and Celebrity both have free drinks for the top three tiers of loyalty status.

Celebrity Cruises offers free drinks for anyone gambling in the casino. Carnival and Virgin Voyages are among the lines offering free drinks to select gamblers based on their prior gambling history. You might be eligible for those, even if you only gamble on land.

The cabin you book might come with valuable perks, so know what they are so you don’t miss out.

For example, Celebrity’s AquaClass cabins come with not only thermal suite access and exclusive dining in the line’s health-forward restaurant called Blu, but also a choice of exercise equipment. Yoga mats are supposed to be in the closet when you board, but you'll have to ask for any of the other items listed on the menu provided.

Suites on most lines come with extra perks like included drink packages and specialty dining. On certain ships, even some smaller suite categories come with exclusive dining rooms only for the occupants of those categories. The food in these exclusive eateries is often a step above the main dining room and not to be missed if you are staying in the entitled category.

The same goes for suite lounge access. You generally find snack and beverage stations stocked with specialty treats you won’t find elsewhere on board, making it worthwhile to at least sneak a peek at the lounge offerings if you paid for a category that comes with access.

The cost of going out to the movies these days makes a cruise movie night a big value. Now that most of us watch movies by streaming them at home, actually going to the movies is a treat in and of itself.

Movie nights on a ship are a step above your local movie theater. You might enjoy films on a giant poolside screen while you float in the pool or relax on a lounge chair with bar servers bringing the drinks to you. Disney Cruise Line screens first-run films for free, with costumed characters in attendance. Many lines serve free popcorn wherever movies are being shown.

If staying in for a movie night in your jammies sounds good, take advantage of free or pay-per-view movies on your cabin’s TV. Disney is among the cruise lines with popcorn on the room service menu. On a Silversea cruise, I once told our butler we were staying in for an evening movie. His immediate reply was, "Shall I pop some corn for you?" The answer, of course, was, "Yes, please."

Live music, comedy acts, magic shows and musical theater are luxuries you can pay dearly for on land — but all of those are available on cruise lines at no charge. The larger the ship, the more entertainment options you will have.

Free live music is found daily in lounges, pool areas, atriums and on stage in the main auditorium. Audience participation game shows, sometimes raucous in nature, usually take over lounge space a few nights of the cruise.

The main stage will have a show nightly, either song-and-dance revues featuring an onboard cast or guest magicians, musicians and comedians, some with TV credits to their name. Larger ships might have separate comedy club venues to keep the laughs flowing every night of the cruise, with both family-friendly and adults-only shows. Clubs on dry land where these same performers appear often charge a $30-40 cover. On a recent Carnival cruise, I estimate my visits to the comedy club alone would have cost me several hundred dollars.

Some lines lean heavily into specialty performances. Look for ice skating, aquatic high-diving and dance shows on select Royal Caribbean ships and acrobatic performances on Virgin Voyages and MSC Cruises. Royal Caribbean and Norwegian Cruise Line both offer Broadway musicals, while Disney produces live musical performances based on its popular animated movies.

With so much free entertainment that would certainly cost a family hundreds in ticket prices on land, you’ll get a ton of value from your cruise if you attend the shows that most appeal to you.

When the night's entertainment winds down, it's time to dance the night away and go clubbing — and cruise ship clubs don’t have a cover. Big ships crank up the party vibe after the last show in the main theater, so you can make the most of every second you’re awake. Hop from dance parties on the pool deck to karaoke in smaller bar venues and even silent discos in the atrium to keep the fun going into the wee hours.

Eating out and trying local restaurants are hallmarks of vacation, but you can blow your budget doing that on land. You can spend a lot on specialty restaurants on board, too, but pay attention to timing to get the most value out of the free dining on board. If you know you would enjoy steak and lobster, do a little research to figure out which night they will be served in the main dining room. You don’t want to find out too late that you booked a specialty restaurant on the same night you could have been eating surf and turf at no additional cost. Themed brunches and afternoon tea are also main dining room events you don’t want to miss.

Looking beyond the buffet and main dining room might turn up surprising food choices you didn't even know were included in your cruise fare. Pool grills serving juicy hamburgers, specialty coffee shops with snacks and even sandwiches and healthy choice salads near the solarium are all yummy examples of freebies tucked away in spots you might not think to look.

As for the specialty restaurants, those are generally still a bargain compared to a similar meal at a land-based restaurant. Carnival's Steakhouse is a good example. The cost is $52 per person. That sounds steep, but if you've priced a filet mignon in a nice restaurant lately, you'll know that $52 barely covers the steak. At Fahrenheit 555, you'll be treated to appetizers, sides and desserts, making the cover charge a vacation value. Book your Steakhouse dinner for the first night of a sailing, and Carnival will usually throw in a complimentary bottle of house wine.

For lounging in your cabin, free or low-cost room service boosts your cruise value. My personal favorite (especially on sea days) is enjoying a "first breakfast" of coffee and croissants from room service before heading out for a more substantial second breakfast.

Private island experiences provide an inexpensive break from paying for excursions in other ports. First things first, the beach is free. Use of the lounge chairs is free (not always the case at some vacation destinations). Swimming in the ocean and in some pools is free.

Depending on the island, you might find hammocks, hiking trails, game and sports areas and interesting snorkeling spots. Rental equipment for snorkeling and other water activities is usually reasonably priced, but you can bring your own gear.

The major private islands all have complimentary barbecue buffets and occasionally other food trucks or fast-casual offerings. As with specialty dining on the ship, even the up-charged food won’t cost as much as at a theme park or on the beach at a vacation destination.

Relying on shore excursions offered by the cruise line is the easy way to plan your days in port. It also keeps you safe from becoming one of those pier-running late-comers at departure time. Those tours are not always the best value, however. Lower-priced reputable port tours may take a bit more research on your part, but can save hundreds of dollars.

I recently enjoyed a 4-hour kayak tour in Ketchikan with pickup near the pier and guaranteed on-time return that I booked directly on the Ketchikan Kayak Company's website, which saved me roughly $60 per person compared to the similar tour offered by the ship.

And don’t forget that skipping organized tours altogether can also net you an amazing day in port. If tours aren't your jam, or you just don’t want the scheduling hassle in every port, consider simply venturing out on your own in search of fun. If the town is walkable, start with that. Or consider renting a car or simply hiring a taxi driver. I've visited Cozumel dozens of times on cruise ships, but had never seen the far side of the island. Last fall, a group of friends and family rented two Jeeps online from a rental agency located walking distance from the pier. We had a marvelous time stopping wherever we wanted, including for an impromptu tequila tasting (for the non-drivers, of course).

Whether you're talking about something as simple as miniature golf, basketball, pickleball or table tennis, or as elaborate as surf simulators and multideck dry slides, cruise lines often load their ships’ upper decks with free fun. As with all things on a cruise, certain activities come with a cost, but you’ll find plenty of fun that does not add to your cruise bill.

On land, you typically need to pay to access waterslides, splash parks, rock climbing walls and adventure and zip lines, but on many cruises, these active onboard attractions come free. Certain activities might require reservations or specific attire (like closed-toe shoes), so check out the details in advance.

Did you know that some cruise lines let you buy VIP packages pre-cruise for a bundle of preferential treatment similar to suite category perks? The real value of these programs lies in not paying for an expensive suite while enjoying extra perks as if you did.

Royal Caribbean's The Key includes early boarding times, a welcome lunch, fast lane access to select onboard activities, premium theater seating, departure day perks and free internet access for each guest who purchases the package.

Celebrity's Premium Access is a similar bundle. The combination of complimentary room service and Premium Wi-Fi for two devices makes this package a cruise value.

Holland America's Club Orange includes a complimentary cabin upgrade when available, priority check-in, priority lines at Guest Services and Shore Excursion desks, bathrobes, an expanded room service menu, a complimentary glass of sparkling wine, exclusive events like behind-the-scenes tours and coffee chats with performers and even separate dining rooms on some ships. With a bit of strategy, the cabin upgrade alone can justify the cost of the Club Orange add-on. This works best in Oceanview and Verandah categories where you can choose an obstructed view cabin at a low cost, banking on the Club Orange upgrade to a full-view room.

Carnival’s Faster to the Fun offers early cabin access, express luggage delivery and priority check-in and embarkation, shuttle boarding, dining reservations, Guest Services line and debarkation. Note that Carnival blocks access to FTTF for some loyalty guests, including some casino loyalty members, to avoid stacking of perks.

Norwegian Cruise Line’s Priority Access includes priority security, check-in and boarding processes on embarkation day, plus skip-the-line tendering and debarkation, complimentary standard room service and a $50 spa discount on port days.

Cruises come with so much value bundled into the cost of the fare that it can be easy to overlook all the goodies that aren't costing you anything extra. Adding value to your cruise vacation can be as simple as reading the daily planner or taking a walk around the ship to discover all the included attractions. Whether it’s free entertainment in your favorite lounge, a dance lesson or no-cost prime rib in the main dining room, all those onboard freebies and low-cost add-ons make it possible to get outsize value from your cruise vacation.

#6081. Democrats Have the Electoral College in Their Sights

Will the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact soon cross the 270-vote threshold?

Delegates point to an electoral map at the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia, Pa., in 2016.

The blue wave washed over a slew of state legislative chambers and six new governorships. Next year, a majority of Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governing trifecta. One of the biggest dangers of Democrats’ new political clout is that they will now push to override the Electoral College and effectively force the country into a nationwide presidential popular voting system as early as 2028.

Their vehicle is called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote, no matter which candidate carries each state. The compact was born after former President George W. Bush’s narrow Electoral College victory in 2000, and it was turbocharged following Donald Trump’s 2016 win despite his losing the popular vote. The District of Columbia and 18 states have joined, accounting for 222 electoral votes.

John Fund is National Review’s national-affairs reporter.

#6080. American Airlines Plans To Nearly Triple Its Phoenix A Gates Lounge Space—And Add 150% More Seats

American Airlines Phoenix lounges are one of the biggest holes in the airline’s effort to offer a better product. They’re been too small, crowded dated, and barely worth visiting even when you have access. Already American expects 18 million lounge visits in 2026 up 80% from 10 million in 2016 while passenger traffic is up just 12.1%. What may have worked in the past no longer does. And American is finally announcing substantial investment in all three Admirals Clubs, adding enough room that getting away from a crowded gate might actually mean getting away from a crowd. Here’s what’s changing: Location   Planned Changes A19–A21   Near term: new food service area, infrastructure for expanded food and drink offerings, and facility updates. B5–B7   New self-service food and beverage area, 20% more seats, refreshed interiors and improved support space. Both A clubs, including A7–A9   Longer term: nearly triple their combined footprint, approximately 150% more seats, and refreshed furnishings and finishes. A club seating would become about 2.5 times current level. American isn’t sharing expected completion dates, actual seat counts or square footage. And there’s no Phoenix Flagship Lounge announcement. What’s perhaps most interesting to me is they’re spending on Terminal 4 even as they committed to invest as the anchor airline for Phoenix’s planned $4.5 billion West Terminal. The airport expects a late 2033 opening (so sometime after that, natch). That’s seven years away. American can’t sell a premium experience today on the promise that its lounges will become better in the mid-2030s. But the American I’ve come to known wouldn’t invest today when they’ll also be investing later. Phoenix unveiled its preferred West Terminal concept at Tuesday’s Industry Day, which American CEO Robert Isom attended. So the timing of this announcement wasn’t a coincidence. American, though, is investing in its lounges in a real turnaround. I suggested last year that I’d believe their commitment to becoming a more premium carrier and focusing on revenue growth rather than just cost control when the capital investments started – clubs and new planes. We’re still waitin on the expected aircraft order, but American is planning to deliver a new, renovated or expanded lounge nearly every month on average over two to three years. Phoenix had been a real omission from the announced pipeline. After years of club closures and renovations I described as “modern hospital,” American developed a much warmer design. Washington National’s E concourse club, followed by Denver, Newark and Philadelphia, showed what they could do with better lighting, wood, and places that are actually comfortable to sit and work. The food has been improving as well. I covered the additional hot dishes and better charcuterie in Admirals Clubs. And Flagship lounge food is getting better. Flagship Dining now offers sit down meals and good wine for long haul business class passengers. The current lounge pipeline includes: Airport   Project Charlotte   More than 40,000 square feet above the atrium, plus a separately announced Flagship Lounge. Dallas–Fort Worth   A 37,000 square foot Terminal C club and Terminal F Provisions. Miami   A new Flagship Lounge and expanded D30 Admirals Club, nearly doubling total lounge space. Chicago O’Hare   A replacement Concourse L club exceeding 10,000 square feet. Washington National   Rebuilding the D club with 50% more seats. Austin   More than 12,000 square feet with an outdoor terrace. Permits are in hand, and I expect a 2027 opening. Nashville   About 17,400 square feet with outdoor terraces. Construction is targeted for 2027. New York JFK   A 3,700 square foot Provisions location with a dedicated barista bar. San Antonio’s new terminal plans also include its first Admirals Club. And Los Angeles Flagship Dining reopened November 5. American announced Citi branding at Admirals Club entrances. It’s part of their new card agreement that is more of a joint venture than supplier relationship. Citi gets an airport lounge presence through American’s network. The Executive card includes membership, while Globe and Strata Elite each provide four passes a year. The clubs help sell three different credit cards. Lounge pricing pushes frequent flyers toward Citi. The Executive card’s annual fee is $695 for new applicants. A full standalone Admirals Club membership is $1,200–$1,400, while even the restricted $750 Single membership costs more than the card and leaves out guests and partner lounges. American is making the card the obvious way to buy access. Better clubs help get customers to apply and give them a reason to renew. Once they’re carrying the card, American and Citi have more opportunities to get their spending. And with Globe and Strata Elite distributing passes alongside Executive memberships, American needs more seats./ Topics on this pageAdmirals ClubAirport loungeAmerican AirlinesCitibankPhoenix Sky Harbor International AirportAustinChicagoDenverMiamiNashvilleNew YorkO'HarePhiladelphiaPhoenixRobert IsomSan AntonioTerminal 4+12 more More From View from the Wing

#6079. Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

#6078. Trump-Xi showdown revives 25-year-old Clinton China 'mistake' as Senate vet demands reversal

President Donald Trump warned Iran on Monday that it would face unprecedented retaliation if it were to carry out an attack on Washington, D.C.

Former Trump Ambassador Sam Brownback is urging Washington to reverse a decades-old trade decision and strip China of its permanent normal trade relations status, arguing the United States must rethink its economic relationship with Beijing as President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

"I think it's time we back up and correct the mistake we made 25 years ago in granting normal trade relations with China, a country that seeks our demise and doesn't grant human rights, and remove that," Brownback told Fox News Digital in an interview.

Trump is traveling to China this week for his third meeting of the year with Xi, with the two leaders scheduled to hold talks Thursday in Shenzhen before joining Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral meeting, amid ongoing trade tensions and concerns over American dependence on Chinese supplies.

TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS

"I think, tactically, President Trump is playing through this right," Brownback said. "But we're in a tough spot right now."

Brownback, who served as ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom during Trump's first administration, pointed to Washington's decision more than two decades ago to establish permanent normal trade relations with China.

President Bill Clinton signed legislation authorizing permanent normal trade relations with China in 2000, and President George W. Bush formally granted the trade status in December 2001, following China's accession to the World Trade Organization.

Revoking China's permanent normal trade relations status would generally subject Chinese imports to higher tariffs, rather than automatically ending trade between the two countries.

Brownback said that reducing those dependencies and restructuring trade relations would require years rather than an immediate break with Beijing.

TRUMP SHOULD PRESS XI ON CHINA’S PERSECUTION OF BELIEVERS AT HOME AND ABROAD

Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump visit the Temple of Heaven on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Brendan Smialowski - Pool/Getty Images)

Brownback argued that the United States should now consider reversing that decision through an orderly process that would pressure Beijing to respect human rights and religious freedom.

He suggested reaching a "Helsinki Accords 2.0" deal, modeled on a landmark 1975 Cold War agreement that incorporated human rights into broader discussions between the United States, its European allies and the Soviet Union.

The agreement, Brownback said, would allow Washington to negotiate with Beijing over trade and religious freedom while warning that continued abuses could jeopardize normal trade relations.

"Either you grant human rights and religious freedom to your own people, or we're pulling back normal trade relations," Brownback said.

China's first lady Peng Liyuan, China's President Xi Jinping, President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump pose on the North Portico steps of the White House ahead of a state dinner in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 24, 2026. President Xi is on a state visit to the United States from Sept. 23 to 25. (SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images)

Brownback also urged Trump to raise religious persecution directly with Xi, arguing that Beijing's treatment of Christians and other religious groups should become a central part of future negotiations.

THE CCP’S NEW ‘UNITY’ LAW TURNS CHINA’S REPRESSION INTO A GLOBAL THREAT

The U.S. Department of Labor estimated in 2022 that 100,000 Uyghurs and other ethnic minority former detainees in China may have been working under forced-labor conditions following detention in re-education camps.

"We can't trade with you if you're going to continue to operate the way you are, particularly towards people of faith, towards Christians," Brownback said.

Brownback said stabilizing the relationship would itself represent a meaningful achievement while the United States works to reduce its dependence on Chinese supplies.

"I think a successful trip is a continuation of the current situation right now, just stabilizing the relationship, not having it deteriorate further until we get in a better position on dealing with things like rare earth minerals and pharmaceutical supplies," Brownback said.

AMERICA DEPENDS TOO MUCH ON CHINA FOR ESSENTIAL MINERALS. WE NEED TO DIG OUR FUTURE

Sam Brownback urges reversing normal trade relations with China, citing human rights abuses and a long-term threat, as President Trump meets Xi Jinping. (Sarah Silbiger/Getty Images)

He also argued that religious freedom represents a strategic vulnerability for China's communist leadership, which he said views independent religious institutions as a threat to its authority.

"They now have a bigger navy than we do, but they fear religious freedom more than they do our aircraft carriers or our missiles," Brownback said.

#6075. Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

#6074. A Trump–Xi–Putin Summit Could Remake the World Order

Can a triangle of the U.S., China, and Russia create a sustainable equilibrium of power, rules, and values?

From left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping

NR illustration; Alexander Kazakov, Kevin Lamarque, Tingshu Wang/Reuters

The proposed Trump–Xi–Putin meeting in Shenzhen this month could become one of the most consequential diplomatic encounters since the Cold War. Whatever the three leaders might negotiate concerning Ukraine, Taiwan, trade, nuclear weapons, or artificial intelligence, its larger significance would be unmistakable: The three powers most capable of shaping the international order would be gathering not primarily to defend it but to renegotiate their positions within, or against, it.

The irony is extraordinary. Russia seeks to overturn an order from which it believes itself excluded. China seeks to reshape an order from which it has benefited enormously. The United States, which created and sustained that order, increasingly regards its maintenance as an excessive burden. The revolutionary, the reformer, and the reluctant guardian have become, in different ways, revisionists.

From left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping

NR illustration; Alexander Kazakov, Kevin Lamarque, Tingshu Wang/Reuters

#6067. James Talarico’s ‘Incarnational Politics’

The new senator from Texas has bad ideas about Christianity and democracy, but the press seems okay with that.

The day after the Democrats trounced the Republicans in the midterm elections, Ezra Klein of the New York Times tweeted, “One of the more exciting parts of this election — among many — is the return of a religious left.” Accompanying the enthusiastic remark was a clip from his interview earlier this year with James Talarico, the Democrat who won the Texas senatorial race. In the clip, Talarico — a Presbyterian seminarian — advocates a political attitude in which Americans recognize each other as being made in God’s image and treat each other accordingly. He calls this “an incarnational politics.”

Incarnational politics — hoo boy. The term, a nearly paradoxical union of the sacred and the profane, sounds just enough like intersectional politics to catch the attention of progressives. It also sounds like an edgy indie band that never quite made it. (“I saw Incarnational Politics open for Bad Religion in ’91.”)

#6066. China's Xi surprises Trump at tarmac, reciprocating gesture shown months ago

President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen, China, for the APEC summit, where Chinese President Xi Jinping greets him on the tarmac with an elaborate welcome ceremony. Bill Melugin reports on the high-stakes arrival and national security analyst Dr. Rebecca Grant analyzes the diplomatic significance of the meeting.

President Donald Trump said he expected a special reception from China's Xi Jinping, and Wednesday morning's reception did not disappoint.

After Trump's in-person welcome of Xi at Joint Base Andrews in September, Xi personally greeted Trump at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport, a rare airport welcome ahead of a three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Putin, who has met with Xi dozens of times and arrived at the same Shenzhen airport earlier Wednesday, did not receive a personal greeting from the Chinese leader. Instead, senior Chinese Communist Party advisor Cai Qi welcomed Putin upon arrival.

'RED CARPET FOR A DESPOT': TRUMP'S LAVISH XI WELCOME COLLIDES WITH GOP ANTI-COMMUNISM MESSAGE

Some Democratic and Republican lawmakers had criticized Trump over that September airport greeting, but it has brought Xi to reciprocate.

The Trump greeting marked a sharp contrast with Trump's previous visit to China in May, when Chinese Vice President Han Zheng met him at the airport in Beijing. Xi, who has led China for more than a decade, has rarely — if ever — appeared at an airport to welcome a visiting foreign leader, according to reports.

XI PRAISES US STATE VISIT 'PERFECTION' AS TRUMP CALLS MEETINGS 'VERY PRODUCTIVE'

President Donald Trump speaks with China's President Xi Jinping as he arrives at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Mark Schiefelbein - Pool/Getty Images)

As Trump stepped off Air Force One, a handshake between the two leaders turned into a brief hug while military regiments and performers dressed in pink and turquoise stood at attention. A military band played the U.S. and Chinese national anthems as dancers waved flowers, pompoms and American and Chinese flags.

U.S. President Donald Trump is greeted by China's President Xi Jinping at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on Nov. 18, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"China is a nation that values courtesy and has a tradition of returning goodwill with goodwill," a report in China's Xinhua read.

REAL WINNER OF XI SUMMIT REVEALED AS TRUMP LOOKS TO USHER IN NEW ERA WITH CHINA

The leaders' exchange represents a new U.S.-China relationship of "respect, fairness, and reciprocity," Dean Wu Xinbo of Fudan University in Shanghai told The New York Times.

It showed China will "still treat him seriously and would like to continue to work with him," he added.

TRUMP SET FOR ECONOMIC SHOWDOWN WITH XI AS UNFULFILLED PROMISES LEAVE BILLIONS HANGING IN BALANCE

International Crisis Group senior analyst William Yang noted the gesture before potentially turbulent talks to come.

"It’s important to highlight the reciprocity that Xi gave to Trump by receiving him on the tarmac," Yang wrote Wednesday morning on X. "This gesture likely reflects Xi and Beijing’s desire to show respect to Trump, which they know the US President enjoys, and it is likely also an attempt to uphold the positive rapport between Xi and Trump ahead of a potentially turbulent period in U.S.-China relations in the coming months."

TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES

Trump, Xi and Putin are in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The three leaders are scheduled to meet together Thursday on the sidelines of the economic gathering — an unprecedented three-way session.

Ahead of a one-on-one meeting with Xi on Wednesday, Putin said he expected "great potential benefits" from Thursday's three-way discussion. The session has drawn concern from officials in Ukraine, Iran and Taiwan, who worry the leaders of the world's three most powerful nations could make decisions affecting their futures without their participation.

During a briefing last week, a senior U.S. official said the three-way meeting is unlikely to produce any formal denuclearization agreement, calling it an "entry point" and "the first conversation."

Trump will meet Putin one-on-one tomorrow on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, a U.S. official confirmed to Fox News.

Earlier Wednesday morning, Trump recapped his trip to the Philippines.

"I am now heading to China, from the Philippines, where we had a wonderful meeting on Trade, National Security, and other subjects," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "I am pleased to announce that we made a new and completely different Trade Deal with the Philippines, one that will be a true landmark and, in particular, a Deal that will be great for our Farmers and those in the business of 'Energy.'

"President Marcos is a powerful leader, and a man of high integrity and substance. It was an Honor to be with him, and his beautiful wife and son. See you in China!"

Fox News' Lucas Tomlinson contributed to this report.

When you're traveling for work, a canceled flight is more than a hassle. It can mean missing an important meeting or paying up for a last-minute fare.

Through the end of January 2027, Capital One is giving select business cardholders a new way to manage flight disruptions. Eligible flights booked through Capital One Business Travel will automatically include free rebooking on another airline after a qualifying cancellation or delay, with Capital One covering the new ticket up to $5,000 per traveler.

When travelers book flights through Capital One Business Travel, Capital One will monitor eligible itineraries beginning 24 hours before departure. If the flight is canceled or delayed by at least three hours, the traveler will receive a notification and gain access to a self-service rebooking tool.

The benefit covers several types of disruptions, including:

Last week's ground stop, which backed flights up for days, is a good example of when this benefit could be a huge help.

And unlike traditional airline rebooking, which may be limited to flights operated by the original carrier or its partners, Capital One's tool allows eligible travelers to select a replacement flight on another airline, with the new ticket covered up to $5,000 per traveler.

The flexibility to jump to a competing airline is the standout feature. When one carrier is sold out, another airline may still have space. Re-routing through a different connecting airport can also be strategic to avoid weather issues altogether.

Replacement flights must depart on the same or following day, serve the original destination or a nearby airport and be booked in the same (or lower) fare class. Despite these terms, this will still give travelers far more flexibility than handling things independently.

Travelers can also contact a live agent for 24/7 support.

Capital One Business Travel is available to cardholders with several Capital One business cards, including the following:

Holding one of these cards does not guarantee the free add-on. To check, log in to Capital One Business Travel. If the complimentary rebooking feature is available to you, it will be automatically added to your eligible flight at checkout.

The Venture X Business is particularly relevant for frequent flyers because it earns 5 miles per dollar spent on flights booked through Capital One Business Travel. Plus, it comes with a $300 annual credit for bookings made through Capital One Business Travel.

New applicants can potentially get even more value from Capital One Business Travel through the card's current welcome offer, which includes up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 travel credit after meeting two spending thresholds:

The information for the Capital One Spark Classic for Business, Capital One Spark Miles for Business, Capital One Spark Miles Select for Business, Capital One Spark Pro and Capital One Spark Classic Miles for Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: Capital One Venture X Business review: High earning rates and premium perks for businesses

This is useful protection, but it comes with restrictions. The original ticket must be booked through Capital One Business Travel, and the disruption must meet the three-hour threshold within 24 hours of departure.

It's also temporary. The complimentary is available for eligible bookings made through the end of January 2027, while supplies last. Capital One hasn't published a final eligible departure date.

Still, this could be valuable for business travelers with time-sensitive trips. It can also eliminate business travel bottlenecks, such as waiting for a manager to approve a costly replacement ticket.

Related: Getting a refund for a canceled or delayed flight

Capital One's new feature will help you with rebooking options, but it won't cover the other costs of getting stranded.

For example, if you're rebooked on a flight the following day, you may need to pay for a hotel, meals or transportation. That's where eligible credit card trip delay coverage could help.

Trip delay insurance covers unexpected costs related to qualifying delays, such as accommodations, meals or transportation while waiting out your delay.

That gap can be especially important during weather or air traffic control disruptions, when airlines generally do not pay for stranded travelers' hotels or meals.

Not every eligible card includes trip delay coverage, though. The Venture X Business covers up to $500 per ticket for meals and lodging when a trip is delayed six hours or more or requires an overnight stay.* Cash-back cards like the Spark Cash don't include it. Check your card's benefits guide before you travel.

Related: Flight delayed? 4 things to do to get trip delay reimbursement from your credit card

#6063. Former Washington Rep. Jim McDermott dies at 89

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call)

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

“Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”

When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”

Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a new life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

“I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”

As he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

“Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”

#6060. We Need a Better GOP

President Donald Trump attends the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, September 9, 2026.

The old Republican establishment could be out of touch, unimaginative, and too comfortable with revolving-door practices that enriched former officeholders and staffers, among other failings.

Beginning in 2016, Donald Trump burned this establishment to the ground and created a new one that has its own myriad deficiencies, some of which echo the failings of yore; the extremely online elements of today’s establishment, for instance, have found a whole new way to be out of touch.

We say this not to pine for yesterday’s establishment — parties never go back, only forward — but to make the point that every party elite reaches its point of exhaustion, and that’s where the Trump establishment is now.

There is a robust intramural argument on the right over how to interpret the historic loss in the midterms. We have our own views, but the most elemental need is a better GOP — one that is not beholden to the will of one man, doesn’t tolerate corruption, insists on strict adherence to the rule of law, encourages Congress to take up its allotted role in our constitutional system, rewards policy entrepreneurship on the part of officeholders, and focuses on results rather than performative provocations.

It’s possible to imagine any number of people leading such a national party, and it could have different ideological colorations depending on that leader and underlying circumstances. All that is TBD and should be a matter of fierce debate and competition. But unless the party moves beyond today’s establishment and renews itself, it risks subsequent devastating votes of no confidence from the American public.

Consider the issue of corruption, which was one of the biggest concerns of voters in the midterms. It is one thing for a party to suffer politically in the course of making progress on an important priority — say, stepped-up immigration enforcement. It is another to suffer from the perception — and, sadly, the reality — that politically connected people are engaged in untoward schemes for their own enrichment. The former is an inevitable political trade-off; the latter is a party’s elite feasting on its power and connections with no heed to the consequences for the larger cause.

President Trump, who has an overawing dominance over the party, is the source of many of the GOP’s current discontents. His influence is not going to drastically diminish anytime soon, and we know that many good Republicans have considered him better than the alternative, or have thrilled to his no-holds-barred assaults on the left. However one evaluates the Trump phenomenon, though, attempts to rely on the tropes that fueled his rise beginning in 2016, or ape his political style, will almost certainly fail — for the simple reasons that times change and Trump’s persona is not replicable.

The GOP could do much worse than look to the states, where Republican governors and legislators have cut taxes, restrained spending, pared back regulations, protected unborn children, and pursued reforms of schooling and housing. One reason that Florida constituted high ground beyond the reach of the blue wave is that it has been so well governed for so long, and it has had a series of reformist Republican governors focused on results.

At the national level, the GOP obviously needs a cost-of-living agenda that addresses high costs in health care, medicine, and education, and there’s much work that’s been done on these issues at the state level and among conservative policy thinkers. But arriving at a coherent agenda will require a seriousness of purpose and substantive focus that have been lacking for years now. That doesn’t mean the party should be dull and conventional — much can be learned from Trump’s zest for combat and vivid political branding — but it needs to recover a sense of institutional self-respect.

The new establishment, via President Trump, has worked its way back around to what were widely considered weaknesses of the old one. Republicans were once determined to make another push for amnesty after every election loss, and now, the president has floated that idea in response to the Democratic midterm victory; Republicans were once too soft on China, and Trump has been notably conciliatory in his second term; the GOP once talked a good game on deficit spending but didn’t do nearly enough to curtail it, while we are now adding to the debt hand over fist during a time of economic expansion and relative peace; the Tom DeLay–led Republican House was much too cozy with lobbyists, but prior GOP ethical lapses have been eclipsed over the past two years.

The old establishment had reached its expiration date and, regardless, isn’t coming back, while the current establishment is harmful to the party’s image and interests and an obstacle to change.

As Lincoln said, it is a time to think anew and act anew. The GOP desperately needs something fresh and different, with ideas and policies designed to meet the challenges of the day.

The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

#6059. Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from new software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin said “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work."

Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications."

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment."

Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a new one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and said their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

At issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

It's here! Frontier Airlines is now offering its GoWild All You Can Fly Pass for 2027, letting travelers take to the skies at a deep discount for an entire year (and potentially longer).

For a limited time, flyers can purchase a GoWild Pass good through 2027 for just $399. Members of the airline's Discount Den can score the pass for $349.

While that's not quite as good as some offers we've seen in past years (but better than some in other years), it can add up to significant savings if you fly the airline a lot. You must be a Frontier Miles member to purchase one.

Keep in mind that passholders pay $0.01 in airfare plus applicable taxes, fees and charges at the time of booking, so the pass gets you out of the regular airfare, but you're still on the hook for taxes and fees as well as other charges for things like optional seat selection and bags. While taxes on domestic legs are low, international ones can incur $60-$110 each way, depending on the destination.

Sneak peek: Frontier's new first-class seats are finally on sale, set for March debut

Multiple passholders can book travel at the same time, but you can't mix and match passholders with non-passholders on the same reservation.

Likewise, different types of fares can be combined each way on itineraries as long as all passengers hold a valid GoWild Pass at the time of booking and the primary passenger holds a Discount Den membership if Discount Den fares are selected.

One other big caveat: GoWild passes autorenew, so if you want to cancel when your current pass expires, you'll need to contact the airline to do so. Your renewal date will be stated in your confirmation email when purchasing the pass.

The GoWild Pass is valid for flights to over 100 destinations across Frontier's route network, including both domestic gateways and international cities in Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America. The airline's route network changes frequently, though, so stay on top of it to make sure your route will be in service when it's time to book.

Travel begins after purchase (meaning as soon as today) and is available through Dec. 31, 2027, meaning potentially over a full year of flying.

There are no blackout dates, like we've seen in some past instances, but on peak dates, you can expect to pay $59-$199 extra per segment.

Here's the kicker: Standard bookings for eligible GoWild fares begin a day before departure for domestic flights and 10 days before departure for international flights. If your return flight is outside that window, then you'll have to try to make an additional booking when the window opens for that flight.

If you do want to book more in advance than that, however, you can pay an additional charge to do so, though this can vary based on the date and the route.

Also keep in mind that just because a seat is open on the flight you want does not mean it's eligible for a GoWild booking.

You can earn Frontier Miles on the purchase of the pass as well as any extras, like seat assignments, bag fees or priority boarding that you purchase.

If you hold elite status with Frontier, you are still eligible for your benefits, including free seats and bags, so that can be a great way to save on optional fees that non-elites have to pay.

All-you-can-fly airline passes are a rarity these days and come with lots of limitations. Frontier Airlines' GoWild All You Can Fly Pass is no exception.

Still, if you fly the airline a lot, have flexibility (and a bit of spontaneity) in your plans and don't need a ton of extra amenities like preferred seats or checked bags, these fares can be a good way to save a bit on flights you'd be taking anyway ... or perhaps some fun last-minute fares you wouldn't be able to take advantage of otherwise.

From left: Sr. Christine Cosgrove, O.P., the author, Sr. Martha Kunesh, O.P., and speaker Kristen Hanson, an advocate against assisted suicide, at a National Review Institute/Sheen Center event on the virtue of hope.

Could anything sound more exotic today? This opening line comes from a 16th-century prayer by the Carmelite reformer St. Teresa of Avila. She carried it in the breviary she used for daily prayer. (the initials stand for “Order of Preachers”), who entered a Dominican convent just before the opening of the Second Vatican Council. #6051. This week: Permitting bill hits Senate floor amid aviation funding fight

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new issue is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel."

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is currently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

#6049. Standing Athwart Pumpkin Tyranny

Through October and November, this mediocre flavor and scent are in everything everywhere all the time.

A display of Trader Joe’s pumpkin and fall-themed products at a grocery store in Lafayette, Calif., September 25, 2026.

A pumpkin spice latte is on the menu at every coffee shop. Sometimes, the drink is served in a pumpkin-shaped mug. To lure in customers for brunch, quaint cafes serving pumpkin pancakes put a chalkboard sign on the sidewalk saying, “COME IN FOR GOURD VIBRATIONS!” Each bakery has pumpkin scones, pumpkin pie, pumpkin banana bread, and pumpkin coffee cake. An attempt to order an old fashioned will be met with an invitation from the demoralized bartender, “Do you want to try our pumpkin spice old fashioned?” The pen at the bank is topped with a rubber pumpkin; this way, customers know that all the money is kept safe. Little plastic pumpkins are in the windows displays at clothing shops, or beside the cashiers (who work in front of pumpkin-flavored nicotine patches). Squashes are piled high in cardboard bins by the entrance of every grocery store. I reach for what I think is my favorite chai tea blend on the shelves — but alas! It is now pumpkin chai with an orange label.

Through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time. Anything edible is infused, swirled, drizzled, and dusted with pumpkin. You cannot escape the flavor: pumpkin cereal, pumpkin protein powder, pumpkin bagels with pumpkin cream cheese. The Asian aisle has frozen Kung Pao-mpkin Dumplings. Dog treats are flavored like a pumpkin spice latte because everyone must participate, no exceptions. Longstanding favorites are replaced, so French fries are now pumpkin fries. That peculiar squash always sneaks its way into a dish, and so the stuffed raviolis have a little bit of pumpkin. Despite its omnipresence, the pumpkin surprises you: The waiter arrives at the table with a salad that is topped — just for this week — with toasted pumpkin seeds. (Of course, the utensils are wrapped in a flimsy brown napkin dotted with little orange pumpkins.) Even things we thought were reliably mint, like gum and the dentist’s fluoride, are pumpkin spice.

Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

It is now pumpkin chai with an orange label.

Through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time. Anything edible is infused, swirled, drizzled, and dusted with pumpkin. You cannot escape the flavor: pumpkin cereal, pumpkin protein powder, pumpkin bagels with pumpkin cream cheese. The Asian aisle has frozen Kung Pao-mpkin Dumplings. Dog treats are flavored like a pumpkin spice latte because everyone must participate, no exceptions. Longstanding favorites are replaced, so French fries are now pumpkin fries. That peculiar squash always sneaks its way into a dish, and so the stuffed raviolis have a little bit of pumpkin. Despite its omnipresence, the pumpkin surprises you: The waiter arrives at the table with a salad that is topped — just for this week — with toasted pumpkin seeds. (Of course, the utensils are wrapped in a flimsy brown napkin dotted with little orange pumpkins.) Even things we thought were reliably mint, like gum and the dentist’s fluoride, are pumpkin spice.

Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.
